q028.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse. The warehouse uses row- level security (RLS).

You create a Direct Lake semantic model that uses the Delta tables and RLS of the warehouse.

When users interact with a report built from the model, which mode will be used by the DAX queries?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Import

Why it is correct: The expected answer for this question is Import. When the warehouse enforces row-level security, the Direct Lake model does not serve those queries straight from the Delta/Parquet files, and this question treats the resulting mode as Import.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the Microsoft documentation states that when a Direct Lake semantic model reads from a warehouse (or SQL analytics endpoint) that enforces row-level security, queries that reference tables with RLS fall back to DirectQuery mode so that the security defined in the SQL engine is honored (and fail if DirectQuery fallback is disabled). Import is a storage mode, not a mode that Direct Lake falls back to, so option A (DirectQuery) could also be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security in Fabric data warehousing and Direct Lake security integration
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. DirectQuery

Why it is incorrect: This is not the expected answer for this question, although it is what the documentation describes: with RLS in the warehouse, the Direct Lake semantic model falls back to DirectQuery for the DAX queries that touch the secured tables.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake security integration

B. Dual

Why it is incorrect: Dual is a storage mode for individual tables in composite models (a table can be served from cache or through DirectQuery depending on the query). It is not a query mode that Direct Lake switches to when RLS is present.

  • Official documentation: Manage storage mode in Power BI Desktop

C. Direct Lake

Why it is incorrect: Direct Lake loads Parquet/Delta column data directly from OneLake, which would bypass the RLS rules defined in the warehouse's SQL engine. For that reason, queries involving tables with SQL-engine RLS cannot be served in Direct Lake mode and fall back instead.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview

q029.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a complex semantic model. The model is based on a star schema and contains many tables, including a fact table named Sales.

You need to create a diagram of the model. The diagram must contain only the Sales table and related tables.

What should you use from Microsoft Power BI Desktop?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Model view

Why it is correct: In Power BI Desktop, Model view (modeling view) shows the tables and relationships of the semantic model as a diagram. In it you can create additional layouts (diagram tabs) and drag in just the tables you need; with the Add related tables option on a table (for example Sales), Desktop adds the fact table and every table directly related to it to that layout. This gives a focused star-schema diagram of Sales and its dimensions, without the other tables of a complex model.

  • Official documentation: Work with Modeling view in Power BI Desktop
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. data categories

Why it is incorrect: Data categories are column properties (for example City, Country or Web URL) that tell Power BI how to treat the data in visuals. They do not produce a diagram of tables.

  • Official documentation: Work with Modeling view in Power BI Desktop

B. Data view

Why it is incorrect: Data view shows the rows and columns of a single table as a grid for inspection. It does not display relationships or let you build a diagram of related tables.

  • Official documentation: Work with Modeling view in Power BI Desktop

D. DAX query view

Why it is incorrect: DAX query view is an editor for writing and running DAX queries (and DAX scripts) against the model. It returns result tables, not a visual diagram of tables and relationships.

  • Official documentation: Work with Modeling view in Power BI Desktop

q030.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model uses Direct Lake mode.

You suspect that some DAX queries load unnecessary columns into memory.

You need to identify the frequently used columns that are loaded into memory.

What are two ways to achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: Use the Analyze in Excel feature.
Query the DISCOVER_MEMORYGRANT dynamic management view (DMV).

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Use the Analyze in Excel feature.
  • Option C: Query the $System.DISCOVER_STORAGE_TABLE_COLUMN_SEGMENTS dynamic management view (DMV).

Why it is correct: In Direct Lake mode, columns are loaded into memory on demand (transcoding) when a DAX query first needs them, and are later evicted. To see which columns are resident, you need to inspect the model's storage metadata.

  1. Option C: the $SYSTEM.DISCOVER_STORAGE_TABLE_COLUMN_SEGMENTS DMV, queried through the XMLA endpoint (for example from DAX Studio, SSMS or a notebook), returns per-column segment information, including which column segments are loaded in memory, their size and how recently they were used. That is exactly the data needed to find frequently used columns that have been loaded.

  2. Option A: Analyze in Excel is the other accepted solution: you can connect a PivotTable to the model and run queries that cause columns to load.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but Analyze in Excel only consumes data and does not report which columns are in memory, while the Vertipaq Analyzer tool (option B), built on the same storage DMVs, is the documented way to analyze column memory usage, including Direct Lake columns. B and C could therefore also be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Analyze query processing for Direct Lake semantic models and Understand Direct Lake storage
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Use the Vertipaq Analyzer tool.

Why it is incorrect: This is not the expected answer for this question, but Vertipaq Analyzer reads the model's storage DMVs/DMV-equivalent information (such as the column segment DMV used in option C) and presents table and column sizes and residency, so it is a valid way to inspect which Direct Lake columns are in memory. That is why B and C can also be argued.

  • Official documentation: Understand Direct Lake storage

D. Query the DISCOVER_MEMORYGRANT dynamic management view (DMV).

Why it is incorrect: DISCOVER_MEMORYGRANT reports memory grants of the engine (how much memory the running operations were allocated). It says nothing about which columns of a model are loaded in memory or how frequently they are used.

  • Official documentation: Analyze query processing for Direct Lake semantic models

q031.stem:
You have the source data model shown in the following exhibit.

The primary keys of the tables are indicated by a key symbol beside the columns involved in each key.

You need to create a dimensional data model that will enable the analysis of order items by date, product, and customer.

What should you include in the solution? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • The relationship between OrderItem and Product must be based on: Both the CompanyID and the ProductID columns
  • The Company entity must be: Denormalized into the Customer and Product entities

Analysis of "The relationship between OrderItem and Product must be based on": In the source model the primary key of Product is the composite key (CompanyID, ProductID), so ProductID alone is not unique: two companies can use the same ProductID for different products. OrderItem carries both CompanyID and ProductID, and a relationship (a foreign key) must reference the complete primary key of the target, not part of it.

  • Both the CompanyID and the ProductID columns (correct): This is the only join that identifies exactly one product row for every order item, so it keeps the grain of the fact table intact and avoids wrong or duplicated matches.

  • The ProductID column (incorrect): It references only part of a composite key. ProductID values repeat across companies, so each order item could match several products and the relationship would be many-to-many, producing wrong totals.

  • A new key that combines CompanyID and ProductID (incorrect as the stated answer): A surrogate or concatenated key is a legitimate dimensional-modeling technique, but the question asks what the relationship must be based on in the model shown. The existing keys already uniquely identify the product, so the direct two-column relationship is the answer the exam expects without inventing extra columns.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

Analysis of "The Company entity must be": The goal is a dimensional (star) model that analyzes order items by date, product and customer. Company is not one of the requested analysis dimensions, and it only exists in the source as a normalized, snowflaked parent of Product and Customer (both carry CompanyID as part of their keys).

  • Denormalized into the Customer and Product entities (correct): In a star schema, dimension tables are denormalized so that the attributes of related entities live in the dimension itself. Company attributes are therefore copied into both Product and Customer, which removes the extra Company table and the snowflake hops, and the model stays a simple star with OrderItem as the fact table and Date, Product and Customer as dimensions.

  • Omitted (incorrect): Dropping Company would lose its attributes, and the CompanyID column would still be needed to identify products and customers, since it is part of their keys. Information that belongs to the business would disappear from the analysis.

  • Denormalized into the Product entity only (incorrect): Customer also depends on Company (CompanyID is part of its primary key). Flattening Company into only one of the two dimensions would leave Customer snowflaked to Company, so the model would not be a true star schema, and a CompanyID cannot simply be pushed into Product alone.

  • Official documentation: Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse

Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse

q032.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1. Model1 uses Import mode. Model1 contains a table named Orders. Orders has 100 million rows and the following fields.

You need to reduce the memory used by Model1 and the time it takes to refresh the model.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: Split OrderDateTime into separate date and time columns.
Replace TotalQuantity with a calculated column.
Convert Quantity into the Text data type.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Replace TotalQuantity with a calculated column.
  • Option D: Replace TotalSalesAmount with a measure.

Why it is correct: Model1 uses Import mode, so every column is stored in memory (compressed by the VertiPaq engine) and is read from the source during each refresh. The goal is to reduce memory use and refresh time for a table with 100 million rows.

  • Option D is the clear win. TotalSalesAmount is currently a calculated column (Quantity multiplied by Price). A calculated column is computed at refresh time and materialized for all 100 million rows, which consumes memory and lengthens the refresh. Replacing it with a measure such as SUMX(Orders, Orders[Quantity] * Orders[Price]) stores nothing; the value is calculated at query time only for the filtered rows.
  • Option B is the second accepted action for this question: the TotalQuantity field is replaced by a calculated column, as the question's expected selection.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but in the exhibit TotalQuantity already appears to be a measure, and turning a measure into a calculated column would add stored data rather than reduce it. Splitting OrderDateTime into separate date and time columns (option A) is a documented data-reduction technique that lowers cardinality and could be argued as the second action instead. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Power BI
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Split OrderDateTime into separate date and time columns.

Why it is not the expected answer: It is not the selection expected for this question. In practice, though, it is a recognized optimization: a Date/Time column with seconds has very high cardinality, which compresses poorly. Splitting it into a Date column (at most a few thousand distinct values) and a Time column (at most 86,400 values, or fewer if rounded) lowers cardinality and the dictionary size and so reduces memory, so it is a valid technique in its own right.

  • Official documentation: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Power BI

C. Convert Quantity into the Text data type.

Why it is incorrect: Text columns compress worse than integers and Quantity is numeric, so it should stay an Integer. Converting it to Text would increase memory consumption, and it would break numeric aggregation such as summing Quantity. Choosing the most compact data type is part of the recommended data reduction techniques.

  • Official documentation: Optimization guide for Power BI

Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Power BI

q033.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model.

You need to prevent report creators from populating visuals by using implicit measures.

What are two tools that you can use to achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Microsoft Power BI Desktop
  • Option C: Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)

Why it is correct: Implicit measures are created when a report creator drags a numeric column straight into a visual and Power BI aggregates it automatically (Sum, Average, and so on). To prevent this, the semantic model property Discourage implicit measures (DiscourageImplicitMeasures) is turned on. When it is enabled, the summation symbol disappears from the columns in the Data pane and columns cannot be added to visuals as aggregated values, so report creators must use explicit DAX measures.

  • Power BI Desktop (A): In Model view, Model explorer, you select the semantic model and set the Discourage implicit measures property in the Properties pane.
  • SSMS (C): SSMS can connect to a semantic model through the XMLA endpoint and can script and alter model objects (TMSL/XMLA), which allows the property to be changed that way.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but SSMS has no dedicated UI for the Discourage implicit measures property (it only works through XMLA/TMSL scripting), whereas Tabular Editor (option B) exposes it directly as the DiscourageImplicitMeasures property and could also be argued as a valid tool. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Model explorer in Power BI Desktop
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Tabular Editor

Why it is not the expected answer: It is not the selection expected for this question, although in practice Tabular Editor is an external tool that edits the model metadata directly, including the DiscourageImplicitMeasures property of the semantic model, and is widely considered a valid tool for this requirement.

  • Official documentation: Model explorer in Power BI Desktop

D. DAX Studio

Why it is incorrect: DAX Studio is a tool for writing, running and profiling DAX queries and for analyzing model performance. It connects to the model for querying, and it is not used to change model properties such as discouraging implicit measures, so it cannot enforce the requirement.

  • Official documentation: Guidance for Power BI

Model explorer in Power BI Desktop
Guidance for Power BI

q034.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains two lakehouses.

You are building a dataflow that will combine data from the lakehouses. The applied steps from one of the queries in the dataflow is shown in the following exhibit.

Use the drop-down menus to select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented in the graphic.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • [Answer choice] of the transformation steps in the query will fold: Some
  • The Added custom step will be performed in: the Microsoft Power Query engine

Analysis of the first statement: The Applied steps pane shows query folding indicators next to each step. The first steps (Source, Navigation) show the indicator that means the step folds, that is, it is translated into a query evaluated by the data source. The "Capitalized each word" step shows an indicator that is different (orange/red), which signals that folding stops there: that step and the ones after it are not pushed to the source. Because some steps fold and others do not, the answer is Some.

  • All (incorrect): The indicators clearly distinguish steps that do not fold, and the context menu options "View data source query" and "View query plan" are greyed out for the selected step, so not every step folds.

  • None (incorrect): The initial steps (Source and Navigation) do fold, so it is not the case that nothing folds.

  • Official documentation: Query folding indicators

Analysis of the second statement: Once a step breaks query folding, every following step (Appended query, Changed column type, Added custom, Filtered rows) is evaluated locally. The "Added custom" step comes after the step that breaks folding, so it is executed in the Microsoft Power Query engine (the mashup engine, which in Dataflow Gen2 runs in the dataflow's compute).

  • Each lakehouse's query engine (incorrect): The lakehouses can only run the steps that were folded into the query sent to them; a custom step after the folding break is not sent. Also, the query combines data from two lakehouses, so the combination happens in Power Query.

  • The source lakehouse query engine (incorrect): Same reason: the source only evaluates the part that folded, not the steps after the break.

  • Official documentation: Overview of query evaluation and query folding in Power Query

links.t: Query folding indicators
Overview of query evaluation and query folding in Power Query

q035.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse’.

Lakehouse1 contains a table named Tablet.

You are creating a new data pipeline.

You plan to copy external data to Table’. The schema of the external data changes regularly.

You need the copy operation to meet the following requirements:

Replace Table1 with the schema of the external data.

Replace all the data in Table1 with the rows in the external data.

You add a Copy data activity to the pipeline.

What should you do for the Copy data activity?
options: From the Source tab, add additional columns.
From the Destination tab, set Table action to Overwrite.
From the Settings tab, select Enable staging.
From the Source tab, select Enable partition discovery.
From the Source tab, select Recursively.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: From the Destination tab, set Table action to Overwrite.

Why it is correct: The two requirements are to replace the schema of Table1 with the schema of the external data and to replace all the rows. For a Lakehouse table destination, the Copy data activity offers the Table action setting. Overwrite "overwrites the existing data and schema in the table using the new values", which meets both requirements, even when the source schema changes regularly. With Append the old rows would be kept and the existing schema would not be replaced.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. From the Source tab, add additional columns.

Why it is incorrect: Additional columns add extra fields (such as a file path or a static value) to the data copied from the source. This does not control whether the destination table is replaced or appended to.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity

C. From the Settings tab, select Enable staging.

Why it is incorrect: Staging uses an intermediate storage location to improve performance for some copy scenarios. It does not define how the destination table is written, so it does not replace the schema or the data.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity

D. From the Source tab, select Enable partition discovery.

Why it is incorrect: Partition discovery makes the source read partition information from the folder structure of file-based sources (for example year=2024/month=01) and expose it as columns. It is a read-side feature and has no effect on replacing the destination table.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity

E. From the Source tab, select Recursively.

Why it is incorrect: Recursively only controls whether the copy reads files from subfolders of the source folder. It does not change how the destination is written.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity

q036.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse.

You plan to query sales data files by using the SQL endpoint. The files will be in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) storage bucket.

You need to recommend which file format to use and where to create a shortcut.

Which two actions should you include in the recommendation? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: Create a shortcut in the Files section.
Create a shortcut in the Tables section.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Use the CSV format.
  • Option D: Create a shortcut in the Tables section.

Why it is correct: To query data with the SQL analytics endpoint of a lakehouse, the data has to be exposed as a table, and tables come from the Tables section. Shortcuts created in the Tables section make external data (here, the Amazon S3 bucket) available for SQL queries, whereas the Files section holds unmanaged data that is not registered as tables. That is why D is correct.

  • Option C is the expected selection for the format: the files in the shortcut are CSV.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint only exposes Delta tables, and a Tables-section shortcut is recognized as a table only when the target holds Delta data, so CSV could not be queried that way. The alternative of a Tables shortcut plus the Delta format (options D and E) could therefore be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse shortcuts and What is a lakehouse in Microsoft Fabric?
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Create a shortcut in the Files section.

Why it is incorrect: A shortcut in the Files section can point to any folder in any format, but the data is not automatically registered as a table, so the SQL analytics endpoint does not see it. Spark can read it, but the requirement is to query with the SQL endpoint.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse shortcuts

B. Use the Parquet format

Why it is incorrect: Parquet is not Delta. The SQL analytics endpoint only exposes Delta tables, so unmanaged Parquet files in a shortcut are not queryable as tables.

  • Official documentation: What is a lakehouse in Microsoft Fabric?

E. Use the delta format.

Why it is not the expected answer: It is not the selection expected for this question. Technically, though, Delta is the format that the SQL analytics endpoint requires for tables.

  • Official documentation: What is a lakehouse in Microsoft Fabric?

q037.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains a subfolder named Subfolder1 that contains CSV files.

You need to convert the CSV files into the delta format that has V-Order optimization enabled.

What should you do from Lakehouse explorer?
options: Use the Load to Tables feature.
Create a new shortcut in the Files section.
Create a new shortcut in the Tables section.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Use the Load to Tables feature.

Why it is correct: In Lakehouse explorer, you can right-click a folder or file in the Files section and choose Load to Tables. The feature converts CSV (or Parquet) files into a Delta table, and tables loaded this way are always in the Delta Lake format with V-Order optimization enabled. It therefore meets both requirements (conversion to Delta and V-Order) in a single action, without writing code.

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Create a new shortcut in the Files section.

Why it is incorrect: A shortcut only creates a pointer to existing data. It does not convert anything: the CSV files stay CSV.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse shortcuts

C. Create a new shortcut in the Tables section.

Why it is incorrect: A Tables-section shortcut also only references existing data, and it is recognized as a table only if the target is already in Delta format. It does not convert CSV into Delta and does not apply V-Order.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse shortcuts

D. Use the Optimize feature.

Why it is incorrect: Table maintenance (Optimize) compacts small files and can apply V-Order, but only on tables that already are Delta. It cannot turn a folder of CSV files into a Delta table.

q038.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains an unpartitioned table named Table1.

You plan to copy data to Table1 and partition the table based on a date column in the source data.

You create a Copy activity to copy the data to Table1.

You need to specify the partition column in the Destination settings of the Copy activity.

What should you do first?
options: From the Destination tab, set Mode to Append.
From the Destination tab, select the partition column.
From the Source tab, select Enable partition discovery.
From the Destination tabs, set Mode to Overwrite.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: From the Destination tabs, set Mode to Overwrite.

Why it is correct: Partitioning is configured in the Advanced options of the Lakehouse table destination of the Copy activity (Enable Partition, then Partition column name). Since Table1 already exists and is unpartitioned, the partition layout can only be applied by rewriting the table, and that is what Overwrite does (it replaces the data and the schema). The first thing to do is therefore to set the table action to Overwrite; once that is set, you can enable partitioning and select the date column in the destination columns. When you append to an existing table, the partition columns are derived from the existing table, so an unpartitioned table cannot be partitioned with Append.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity and Load data to Lakehouse using partition in a data pipeline
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. From the Destination tab, set Mode to Append.

Why it is incorrect: With Append on an existing table, the partition columns are taken from the existing table, which is unpartitioned, so you cannot introduce a new partitioning scheme this way. The existing data would also remain unpartitioned.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity

B. From the Destination tab, select the partition column.

Why it is incorrect: This is the step you want to reach, but not the first one: the partition options depend on the table action, and for an existing unpartitioned table you must first choose Overwrite. The question asks what to do first.

  • Official documentation: Load data to Lakehouse using partition in a data pipeline

C. From the Source tab, select Enable partition discovery.

Why it is incorrect: Partition discovery is a source-side setting that reads partition folders of file-based sources as columns. It does not define how the destination table is partitioned.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity

q039.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains a fact table named FactSales that has one billion rows.

You run the following T-SQL statement.

CREATE TABLE test.FactSales AS CLONE OF Dbo.FactSales;

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • A replica of dbo.Sales is created in the test schema by copying the metadata only: Yes
  • Additional schema changes to dbo.FactSales will also apply to test.FactSales (first occurrence): No
  • Additional schema changes to dbo.FactSales will also apply to test.FactSales (second occurrence): No

Analysis of statement 1 (Yes): CREATE TABLE test.FactSales AS CLONE OF dbo.FactSales creates a zero-copy clone in Fabric Warehouse. Only the metadata of the source table is copied, and the clone points to the same underlying Parquet files in OneLake, so a table of one billion rows is cloned almost instantly with no data duplication. (The statement names dbo.Sales instead of dbo.FactSales, which is a typo in the question; the intended meaning is that the replica is created in the test schema by copying metadata only, so the answer is Yes.)

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric

Analysis of statements 2 and 3 (No, No): Both statements are identical. A clone is an independent table: after it is created, changes made to the source (including schema changes, data changes and later schema evolution) are not propagated to the clone, and changes to the clone are not reflected in the source. The two tables only share the original data files until either one is modified, at which point the modified table writes its own new files.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric

q040.stem:
You have source data in a folder on a local computer.

You need to create a solution that will use Fabric to populate a data store. The solution must meet the following requirements:

Support the use of dataflows to load and append data to the data store.

Ensure that Delta tables are V-Order optimized and compacted automatically.

Which type of data store should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: a lakehouse

Why it is correct: The requirements are to use dataflows to load and append data, and to have Delta tables that are V-Order optimized and compacted automatically. A lakehouse stores its tables in Delta format, is a supported destination for Dataflow Gen2 (with Append or Replace as the update method), and the Spark engine writes Delta tables with V-Order and the lakehouse supports automatic table maintenance such as compaction. A dataflow can also read files from a local folder, so the source data can be uploaded and loaded.

  • Official documentation: Dataflow Gen2 data destinations and managed settings and Delta Lake table optimization and V-Order
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. an Azure SQL database

Why it is incorrect: An Azure SQL database is not a Fabric item that stores Delta tables, so the Delta V-Order and automatic compaction requirements do not apply to it. It stores data in its own relational format.

  • Official documentation: Dataflow Gen2 data destinations and managed settings

C. a warehouse

Why it is incorrect: A warehouse also stores its data as Delta in OneLake and applies V-Order, but the requirement describes Delta tables that you manage and that are compacted automatically in the lakehouse scenario with dataflows loading and appending data. The comparison the exam intends is that lakehouse is the store that fits dataflows plus Delta table optimization, while a warehouse is a T-SQL-centric engine.

  • Official documentation: Understand V-Order for Microsoft Fabric Warehouse

D. a KQL database

Why it is incorrect: A KQL database (in an eventhouse) is designed for real-time and time-series data queried with KQL, and its storage is not managed as V-Order Delta tables for dataflow-based loading in this scenario.

  • Official documentation: Dataflow Gen2 data destinations and managed settings

q041.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse.

You are using a Fabric notebook to save a large DataFrame by using the following code. df.write.partitionBy(“year”, “month”,

“day”).mode(“overwrite”).parquet(“Files/SalesOrder”)

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Statement 1 - The results will form a hierarchy of folders for each partition key: Yes
  • Statement 2 - The resulting file partitions can be read in parallel across multiple nodes: Yes
  • Statement 3 - The resulting file partitions will use file compression: No

Statement 1 (Yes). partitionBy("year", "month", "day") makes Spark write the data in a Hive-style directory layout, one nested level per partition column and in the order given: Files/SalesOrder/year=2024/month=5/day=17/part-....parquet. The result is therefore a hierarchy of folders (year, then month, then day). The alternative "No" is wrong because partitioning is precisely what creates that folder tree; without partitionBy all part files would sit directly under Files/SalesOrder. Note also that the target is the Files section of the lakehouse, so the output is plain Parquet files (unmanaged), not a Delta table.

  • Official documentation: partitionBy (DataFrameWriter) and Load data into your lakehouse with a notebook - Microsoft Fabric

Statement 2 (Yes). The write produces many independent Parquet part files spread across the partition folders. Spark distributes the read of those files as tasks across the executors (nodes) of the Spark pool, and a later query that filters on year, month or day can also skip entire folders (partition pruning). Parquet is a splittable, columnar format, so parallel reads across nodes are the normal behavior. "No" would only be true for a single non-splittable file read by one task, which is not this case.

  • Official documentation: Read and write Parquet files

Statement 3 (No). The statement says that the file partitions "will use file compression" as a consequence of this code. The code does not configure any compression option, so nothing in this write explicitly enables it. The point of the item is that compression is a property of the file format/codec setting, not something that partitionBy or mode("overwrite") provides.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but Spark's default Parquet codec (snappy) does compress the pages inside each file, so "Yes" could also be argued for this statement. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Read and write Parquet files

q042.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a data flow named Dataflow1 contains a query that returns the data shown in the following exhibit.

You need to transform the data columns into attribute-value pairs, where columns become rows.

You select the VendorID column.

Which transformation should you select from the context menu of the VendorID column?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Unpivot other columns

Why it is correct: The exhibit shows a wide table: one VendorID column followed by one column per date (2015-01-01, 2015-01-02, ...). To turn the date columns into rows you need attribute-value pairs, where the attribute column holds the former column names (the dates) and the value column holds the numbers. Because you selected only VendorID (the column that must stay as an identifier), the right command is Unpivot other columns: it keeps the selected column(s) as they are and unpivots every other column, including date columns that might be added later (it generates Table.UnpivotOtherColumns). The result has the columns VendorID, Attribute, Value.

  • Official documentation: Unpivot columns - Power Query and Table.UnpivotOtherColumns - PowerQuery M
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Group by

Why it is incorrect: Group by aggregates rows (sum, count, etc.) by one or more key columns. It reduces the number of rows and does not convert column headers into rows.

  • Official documentation: Unpivot columns - Power Query

B. Unpivot columns

Why it is incorrect: "Unpivot columns" unpivots only the columns that are selected. Since the selected column is VendorID, it would unpivot that single column and leave all the date columns as columns, which is the opposite of what is needed. You would have to select all the date columns instead, and the step would not pick up new date columns automatically.

  • Official documentation: Unpivot columns - Power Query

D. Split column

Why it is incorrect: Split column divides the contents of a column into several columns (by delimiter, number of characters, etc.). It does not rotate columns into rows.

  • Official documentation: Unpivot columns - Power Query

E. Remove other columns

Why it is incorrect: It deletes every column except the selected one, so you would keep only VendorID and lose all the data. It is a projection, not a reshape.

  • Official documentation: Unpivot columns - Power Query

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a data pipeline.

You need to ensure that the pipeline runs every four hours on Mondays and Fridays.

To what should you set Repeat for the schedule?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Hourly

Why it is correct: The Hourly repeat option lets you run the pipeline every N hours (1 to 72), so "every four hours" is a native setting of this option.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the scenario also requires running only on Mondays and Fridays, and in the Fabric scheduler selecting specific weekdays is available only with the Weekly repeat option (where you pick the days and add run times such as 00:00, 04:00, 08:00, 12:00, 16:00 and 20:00). The Hourly option exposes only an interval, so by itself it would run every day, which makes C (Weekly) arguable. Check it against the linked documentation.

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Daily

Why it is incorrect: Daily schedules run every day (with up to a few run times) and have no weekday selection, so they cannot be restricted to Monday and Friday.

  • Official documentation: Job Scheduler in Microsoft Fabric

B. By the minute

Why it is incorrect: Minute-based schedules repeat every 1 to 720 minutes. Four hours is 240 minutes, so the interval would fit, but the option has no weekday filter and would run all seven days.

  • Official documentation: Job Scheduler in Microsoft Fabric

C. Weekly

Why it is incorrect: It is not the expected answer for this question, although Weekly is the only option that lets you choose Monday and Friday and add several times of day (every four hours), which is why it could be argued in practice.

q044.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.

Several times a day, the performance of all warehouse queries degrades. You suspect that Fabric is throttling the compute used by the warehouse.

What should you use to identify whether throttling is occurring?
options: the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app

Why it is correct: Warehouse queries consume capacity units (CU) from the Fabric capacity. When usage exceeds the purchased capacity, Fabric first smooths the load and then applies throttling (delays or rejections) to interactive operations, which shows up as periodic slowdowns of every query. The tool built to see this is the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app: its Compute page and the throttling/overage views show CU utilization over time, background and interactive smoothing, and when the capacity entered throttling states. Matching the times of the slowdowns with those charts confirms or rules out throttling for the warehouse.

  • Official documentation: Understand capacity throttling and smoothing, Capacity Metrics app compute page and Monitoring scenarios in the Capacity Metrics app
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. the Capacity settings

Why it is incorrect: The capacity settings in the admin portal let you configure a capacity (size, notifications, workload settings, delegation). They are not a monitoring tool and do not show historical utilization or throttling events.

  • Official documentation: Understand capacity throttling and smoothing

B. the Monitoring hub

Why it is incorrect: The Monitoring hub lists the activities and their status (running, failed, duration) for Fabric items, such as pipeline runs and refreshes. It does not report capacity-level CU consumption or throttling state.

  • Official documentation: Monitoring scenarios in the Capacity Metrics app

C. dynamic management views (DMVs)

Why it is incorrect: DMVs show live connections, sessions and requests inside the warehouse (for example, which query is running or blocked), not whether the capacity is throttling. A query being slow because of throttling would look just like any other slow query in a DMV.

  • Official documentation: Monitor connections, sessions, and requests using DMVs

q045.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that uses the default Spark starter pool and runtime version 1.2.

You plan to read a CSV file named Sales_raw.csv in a lakehouse, select columns, and save the data as a Delta table to the managed area of the lakehouse.

Sales_raw.csv contains 12 columns.

You have the following code.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Statement 1 - The Spark engine will read only the SalesOrderNumber, OrderDate, CustomerName and UnitPrice columns from Sales_raw.csv: Yes
  • Statement 2 - Removing the partition will reduce the execution time of the query: No
  • Statement 3 - Adding inferSchema='true' to the options will increase the execution time of the query: Yes

Statement 1 (Yes). Spark evaluates lazily: the select(...) that follows load(...) is folded by the Catalyst optimizer into the file scan, so only the four columns needed (plus OrderDate, which feeds Year) are materialized from the 12-column CSV. This column pruning applies to the CSV data source too. The objection that a CSV text file must be read entirely is true at the I/O level, because each line must be scanned, but the engine parses and keeps only the required columns.

  • Official documentation: Load data into your lakehouse with a notebook - Microsoft Fabric

Statement 2 (No). The partition (partitionBy('Year')) only affects the write phase: it creates one folder per year in the managed sales Delta table. With a low-cardinality column such as year it adds negligible overhead, and the cost of the job is dominated by reading and parsing the CSV, which does not change when you remove it. Removing it therefore does not meaningfully reduce execution time (and it would hurt later queries that filter by year).

  • Official documentation: Delta Lake table optimization and V-Order and Tune file size

Statement 3 (Yes). With inferSchema set to true, Spark has to make an additional pass over the CSV file to sample the values and infer the type of every column before the real read. That extra scan increases the execution time compared with using the default (all columns as strings) or an explicit schema, which is the recommended approach for large files.

  • Official documentation: Load data into your lakehouse with a notebook - Microsoft Fabric

q046.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.

A user discovers that a report that usually takes two minutes to render has been running for 45 minutes and has still not rendered.

You need to identify what is preventing the report query from completing.

Which dynamic management view (DMV) should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: sys.dm_exec_requests

Why it is correct: The report query has been running for 45 minutes and you need to know what is holding it back. sys.dm_exec_requests returns one row per request that is currently executing in the warehouse, including its status, start_time, total_elapsed_time, and the wait information (wait_type, wait_time, blocking_session_id), so you can see whether the request is suspended, waiting or blocked. In Fabric Data Warehouse the documented DMVs are sys.dm_exec_connections, sys.dm_exec_sessions and sys.dm_exec_requests; you join them (by session_id) to get the login and the SQL text of the running statement.

  • Official documentation: Monitor connections, sessions, and requests using DMVs - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. sys.dm_exec_sessions

Why it is incorrect: It describes authenticated sessions (login, host, program, status, last request time), but not the execution state of the query or what it is waiting on. It helps to identify who is connected, not what blocks the request.

  • Official documentation: Monitor connections, sessions, and requests using DMVs - Microsoft Fabric

C. sys.dm_exec_connections

Why it is incorrect: It shows connection-level information (client address, protocol, encryption, bytes read and written). It has no per-query status or wait data, so it cannot tell you why a statement is not finishing. It is the least useful of the three for this purpose.

  • Official documentation: sys.dm_exec_connections (Transact-SQL)

D. sys.dm_pdw_exec_requests

Why it is incorrect: This is a view of Azure Synapse dedicated SQL pool (Parallel Data Warehouse architecture). Fabric Data Warehouse does not use the dm_pdw_* views; it exposes the standard sys.dm_exec_* DMVs described in the Fabric documentation.

  • Official documentation: Monitor connections, sessions, and requests using DMVs - Microsoft Fabric

q047.stem:
You are creating a data flow in Fabric to ingest data from an Azure SQL database by using a T-SQL statement.

You need to ensure that any foldable Power Query transformation steps are processed by the Microsoft SQL Server engine.

How should you complete the code? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (object before the dot): Value
  • Second box (function after the dot): NativeQuery
  • Third box (record field set to true): EnableFolding

The completed code is Query = Value.NativeQuery(Database, "SELECT * FROM customer WHERE country IN ('USA', 'UK')", null, [EnableFolding = true]).

Value.NativeQuery. The function that sends a native statement (here T-SQL) to the data source is Value.NativeQuery, and it belongs to the Value library, so the pair is Value + NativeQuery. Alternatives: Table would require a Table.* function (there is no Table.NativeQuery), and Record likewise has no such function. Without it you could not run the T-SQL statement against the Azure SQL database.

  • Official documentation: Native query folding in Power Query

EnableFolding = true. By default Power Query does not fold any later steps after a native query, so every subsequent transformation (filters, column selection, group by) is evaluated in the mashup engine after downloading the result. Passing the options record [EnableFolding = true] as the fourth argument of Value.NativeQuery tells Power Query that the foldable steps that follow can be translated and pushed down to the SQL Server engine, which is exactly the requirement. StopFolding is the opposite behavior, and Optimize is not an option of this function; NativeQuery was already used in the function name, and Record/Table are data types, not field names for the options record.

  • Official documentation: Native query folding in Power Query

q048.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Readings from 100 IoT devices are appended to a Delta table in Lakehouse1.

Each set of readings is approximately 25 KB. Approximately 10 GB of data is received daily.

All the table and SparkSession settings are set to the default.

You discover that queries are slow to execute. In addition, the lakehouse storage contains data and log files that are no longer used.

You need to remove the files that are no longer used and combine small files into larger files with a target size of 1 GB per file.

What should you do? To answer, drag the appropriate actions to the correct requirements. Each action may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Remove the files: Run the VACUUM command on a schedule.
  • Combine the files: Run the OPTIMIZE command on a schedule.

Remove the files (VACUUM). After updates, deletes, overwrites and OPTIMIZE, Delta Lake keeps the previous data files and log entries so that time travel works. They are no longer referenced by the current table version but still occupy storage. VACUUM deletes the data files that are unreferenced and older than the retention threshold (7 days by default). Because the problem states that the storage holds unused data and log files, the action that removes them is VACUUM, and it has to be run (for example from a scheduled notebook or the lakehouse maintenance feature) because it is not automatic. Setting parallelDelete only changes how fast a VACUUM deletes files; it does not remove anything by itself.

  • Official documentation: Delta table maintenance in Microsoft Fabric

Combine the files (OPTIMIZE). 100 devices append around 25 KB readings continuously (about 10 GB per day), which produces a huge number of tiny Parquet files and slows queries. OPTIMIZE bin-packs small files into larger ones, and you can target about 1 GB per file (OPTIMIZE ... with the max file size setting or spark.databricks.delta.optimize.maxFileSize), so running it on a schedule is the requirement for compacting existing files. The other candidates do not meet the stated need: the optimizeWrite and autoCompact table or SparkSession settings improve files written from now on (they are preventive and, with default settings, are not enabled for append patterns of this kind), and they do not combine the small files already in the table nor remove obsolete ones, and they are not tied to a 1 GB target.

q049.stem:
You need to create a data loading pattern for a Type 1 slowly changing dimension (SCD).

Which two actions should you include in the process? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: Update rows when the non-key attributes have changed.
Insert new rows when the natural key exists in the dimension table, and the non-key attribute values have changed.
Update the effective end date of rows when the non-key attribute values have changed.
Insert new records when the natural key is a new value in the table.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Update rows when the non-key attributes have changed.
  • Option C: Update the effective end date of rows when the non-key attribute values have changed.

Why it is correct: Option A is the defining behavior of a Type 1 SCD: when a natural key already exists and an attribute changed, the existing row is overwritten, so no history is kept. Option C is the second action accepted for this question: the load also maintains the effective end date of rows whose non-key attribute values changed.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but updating an effective end date is part of a Type 2 pattern (the old row is closed and a new current row is inserted), while Type 1 keeps no history. A Type 1 load is usually described as updating changed rows (A) and inserting rows whose natural key is new (D), so A and D could also be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 1 and Modeling dimension tables in Warehouse
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Insert new rows when the natural key exists in the dimension table, and the non-key attribute values have changed.

Why it is incorrect: Inserting a new version of a row for an existing key preserves history, which is the Type 2 pattern. Type 1 overwrites in place.

  • Official documentation: Load tables in a dimensional model

D. Insert new records when the natural key is a new value in the table.

Why it is incorrect: It is not the expected answer for this question, although inserting rows for natural keys that do not yet exist is a standard part of every SCD load, including Type 1 (an upsert/MERGE: update matched, insert not matched).

  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 1

q051.stem:
You are analyzing customer purchases in a Fabric notebook by using PySpark.

You have the following DataFrames:

transactions: Contains five columns named transaction_id, customer_id, product_id, amount, and date and has 10 million rows, with each row

representing a transaction. customers: Contains customer details in 1,000 rows and three columns named customer_id, name, and country.

You need to join the DataFrames on the customer_id column. The solution must minimize data shuffling.

You write the following code.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

results =

Which code should you run to populate the results DataFrame?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: transactions.join(F.broadcast(customers), transactions.customer_id == customers.customer_id)

Why it is correct: The transactions DataFrame is large (10 million rows) while customers is tiny (1,000 rows). With a regular join Spark would normally pick a sort-merge join, which shuffles both sides across the cluster so that rows with the same customer_id end up on the same executor. By wrapping the small DataFrame in F.broadcast(), you tell Spark to use a broadcast hash join: the 1,000 customer rows are copied once to every executor and each executor joins them against its local partitions of transactions. The large table is never repartitioned, so the shuffle of the 10 million rows is avoided, which is exactly the requirement of the scenario ("minimize data shuffling").

  • Official documentation: Join hints (BROADCAST) in Spark SQL and Data processing optimization for Apache Spark
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. transactions.join(customers, transactions.customer_id == customers.customer_id).distinct()

Why it is incorrect: This does not influence the join strategy at all, and .distinct() adds an extra wide transformation (another shuffle to deduplicate the whole result). It therefore increases shuffling instead of minimizing it, and it may even remove legitimate duplicate rows.

  • Official documentation: Data processing optimization for Apache Spark

C. transactions.join(customers, transactions.customer_id == customers.customer_id)

Why it is incorrect: It is a valid inner join, but without a hint Spark relies on its automatic choice. Although Spark can auto-broadcast small tables under a size threshold, that depends on statistics and configuration and is not guaranteed; the explicit broadcast() is the way to guarantee that the small side is broadcast and the large side is not shuffled. This option does not explicitly minimize the shuffle, so it is not the best answer.

  • Official documentation: Join hints in Spark SQL

D. transactions.crossJoin(customers).where(transactions.customer_id == customers.customer_id)

Why it is incorrect: A cross join first builds the Cartesian product (10 million x 1,000 = 10 billion rows) and only then filters it. This is extremely expensive in data movement and compute, is the opposite of an optimization and is a classic anti-pattern when an equi-join is what you need.

  • Official documentation: Data processing optimization for Apache Spark

From Power BI Desktop, you open Performance analyzer as shown in the following exhibit.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • The query for the table visual is executed by using: Direct Query

Analysis of "The Direct Lake fallback behavior is set to":

The Performance analyzer output shows two Card visuals. The first one has only DAX query, Visual display and Other (no Direct query entry), so it was answered by Direct Lake. The second one has a Direct query entry of 8,660 ms, which means that this query could not be answered by Direct Lake and Power BI fell back to DirectQuery against the SQL analytics endpoint. Because the same model used Direct Lake for one visual and DirectQuery for another, fallback is enabled and Automatic is the setting that allows both behaviors.

  • DirectLakeOnly is incorrect: it disables fallback, so a query that cannot use Direct Lake would fail with an error instead of running through DirectQuery. A Direct query entry could never appear.

  • DirectQueryOnly is incorrect: all queries would always use DirectQuery and no visual would be served by Direct Lake, but the first card shows no Direct query activity.

Analysis of "The query for the table visual is executed by using":

The visual that shows the Direct query duration (the last one in the capture) is the one executed through Direct Query: the "Direct query" line is the time spent by the DirectQuery connection to the source SQL endpoint, and it accounts for most of the 9,055 ms DAX query. Note that the Direct query line is only displayed when fallback happens.

  • Direct Lake is incorrect: Direct Lake queries load column data from OneLake into the VertiPaq engine and do not show a Direct query entry in Performance analyzer, as the first card shows.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains a table named Nyctaxi_raw. Nyctaxi_row contains the following table:

You create a Fabric notebook and attach it to Lakehouse1.

You need to use PySpark code to transform the data. The solution must meet the following requirements:

Add a column named pickupDate that will contain only the date portion of pickupDateTime.

Filter the DataFrame to include only rows where fareAmount is a positive number that is less than 100.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Box 1 (the method on df): df.withColumnsRenamed
  • Box 2 (the conversion): .cast('date')
  • Box 3 (the row filter): .filter("fareAmount > 0 AND farAmount < 100")

Analysis of Box 1:

The call has the shape <method>("pickupDate", df['pickupDateTime']), that is, a new column name plus a Column expression. The accepted choice for this box is df.withColumnsRenamed, which is the option that produces the pickupDate column from the converted pickupDateTime value in this exercise. The other options do not fit: df.columns is just a list of column names and cannot be called with a name and a Column, and df.select would need a list of columns and would drop all the others.

  • Official documentation: Transform data using notebooks in Microsoft Fabric

Analysis of Box 2:

pickupDateTime is a Timestamp. To keep only the date portion you cast it to the date type: .cast('date') truncates the time portion and returns a DateType column. .alias('date') would only change the name of the expression to "date", it does not change the data type. .cast('pickupDate') is not a valid data type name, and .getField('date') extracts a field from a struct, which a timestamp is not.

  • Official documentation: Transform data using notebooks in Microsoft Fabric

Analysis of Box 3:

The requirement is a positive fareAmount below 100, that is fareAmount > 0 AND fareAmount < 100. Passing a SQL expression string to .filter() is valid PySpark (the exhibit contains a typo, "farAmount", that is ignored for the selection). .filter(col("fareAmount").contains("1..100")) does a string-contains test and is not a numeric range. .when(...) is a conditional expression used inside withColumn/select, not a DataFrame row filter. .where(df.fareAmount.isin([1,100])) keeps only rows where the fare is exactly 1 or 100, not a range.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but in PySpark withColumnsRenamed (and withColumnRenamed) only rename existing columns (the former takes a dict of old name to new name), whereas the shape <method>("pickupDate", df['pickupDateTime']) matches df.withColumn, which is the method that adds a new column as the requirement states. Check it against the linked documentation.

Which two actions should you recommend performing from the Fabric Admin portal? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

answer.correct:

  • Option B: Enable the Users can try Microsoft Fabric paid features option for specific security groups.
  • Option E: Enable the Users can create Fabric items option for specific security groups.

Why it is correct: The Litware case states that Fabric features will be enabled in the existing tenant, that only the analytics team (and the Fabric administrators) may see the PoC items, that the remaining users get access to Fabric features only after the PoC, that the PoC runs on a Fabric trial capacity, and that the principle of least privilege must be followed.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Authentication method: Single sign-on (SSO) authentication
  • Mode: Direct Lake

Analysis of each selection:

Mode: Direct Lake. The customer satisfaction report must (1) show data as soon as it is updated in the data store, (2) minimize query execution time, and (3) use the data store (a Fabric lakehouse or warehouse in the AnalyticsPOC workspace) as the sole source. Direct Lake loads Delta/Parquet column data straight from OneLake into the VertiPaq engine on demand, so there is no scheduled copy to wait for (the model is refreshed by a lightweight framing operation) and queries run at in-memory speed. Import mode would be fast but only shows new data after a refresh, which violates "as soon as the data is updated". DirectQuery shows fresh data but sends every visual query to the source, so it is slower and does not minimize execution time.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - Microsoft Fabric

Authentication method: Single sign-on (SSO). The report must also respect any table-level security defined in the source data store. With SSO (the default for Direct Lake), the effective permissions of the interactive user decide what that user can read, so security defined in the warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint (including object-level and row-level security) is evaluated per user. With a service principal (fixed identity), every report consumer would use the permissions of that single identity, so the source-level security would be bypassed and every viewer would see what the identity sees. Basic authentication is not a supported way to connect a Direct Lake model to OneLake and would not flow user identity either.

What are two ways to achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

Populate the date dimension table by using a Copy activity in a pipeline.
Populate the date dimension view by using T-SQL.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option C: Populate the date dimension view by using T-SQL.
  • Option D: Populate the date dimension table by using a Stored procedure activity in a pipeline.

Why they are correct: The technical requirements say the dimensional model must contain a date dimension, that there is no existing data source for it, that the fiscal year equals the calendar year, and that it must always contain dates from 2010 through the end of the current year. Because there is nothing to extract, the dates must be generated by code that runs inside the data store, which the case defines as a warehouse/lakehouse queried with T-SQL.

  • C: A view defined with T-SQL can generate the full date series (for example with a numbers/series expression or a CTE) and derive year, quarter, month and so on. Because the upper bound is computed from the current date (for example the end of the current year), the view always covers 2010 through the end of the current year with no maintenance. It is also a valid object for the dimensional model, which may contain tables or views.
  • D: A Stored procedure activity in the pipeline that already orchestrates the daily load can run a T-SQL stored procedure that generates the dates and inserts the missing ones into the date dimension table. Running it on each load keeps the table extended through the end of the current year.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but option A is also technically valid: a Dataflow Gen2 can generate the date series with Power Query (M) and write it to a table, so A and D could also be argued as a pair. The expected answer here favors generating the dates with T-SQL inside the data store. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Stored procedure activity - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Populate the date dimension table by using a dataflow.

Why it is incorrect: A Dataflow Gen2 can technically generate a list of dates with Power Query (M) and write it to a destination table, so this approach can work in practice, but it is not the expected answer for this question. The dimensional model is built with T-SQL logic in the data store, and a dataflow would add another authoring tool and refresh for something that a few lines of T-SQL do directly.

You need to ensure the data loading activities in the AnalyticsPOC workspace are executed in the appropriate sequence. The solution must meet the technical requirements.

Create and schedule a Spark notebook.
Create and schedule a Spark job definition.
Create a pipeline that has dependencies between activities and schedule the pipeline.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Create a pipeline that has dependencies between activities and schedule the pipeline.

Why it is correct: The technical requirements say the raw and cleansed data must be updated completely before the dimensional model is populated, and the analytics engineers load the AnalyticsPOC store daily using a mix of tools (low-code ingestion, dataflows, notebooks and T-SQL). A Fabric data pipeline is the orchestration item: you chain activities (Copy, Dataflow, Notebook, Stored procedure, and so on) with dependency conditions such as On success, so an activity starts only when the previous one has finished successfully, and you attach a schedule to run the whole chain daily. That guarantees the required order with minimal effort.

A. Create a dataflow that has multiple steps and schedule the dataflow.

A dataflow cannot sequence notebooks, stored procedures or other items, and the case lets engineers pick any transformation tool.

B. Create and schedule a Spark notebook.

Why it is incorrect: A scheduled notebook only runs its own code. It is not designed to coordinate the other load items (dataflows, copy jobs, T-SQL procedures) and would require custom orchestration code. A pipeline Notebook activity is the right way to include notebooks in a sequence.

You are implementing a medallion architecture in a single Fabric workspace.

You have a lakehouse that contains the Bronze and Silver layers and a warehouse that contains the Gold layer.

You create the items required to populate the layers as shown in the following table.

You need to ensure that the layers are populated daily in sequential order such that Silver is populated only after Bronze is complete, and Gold is populated only after Silver is complete. The solution must minimize development effort and complexity.

  • Orchestration pipeline: A schedule
  • Bronze layer: A pipeline Copy activity
  • Silver layer: A pipeline Dataflow activity
  • Gold layer: A pipeline Stored procedure activity

Analysis of each selection:

Orchestration pipeline: A schedule. The layers must be populated daily and in order. The single orchestration pipeline that chains the three stages is started by a schedule (a daily trigger on the pipeline), and its activity dependencies (On success) enforce Bronze, then Silver, then Gold. A Copy activity, Dataflow activity, Stored procedure activity or Spark job definition cannot trigger the run on a recurring basis, and an Invoke pipeline activity is something that sits inside a pipeline, not what starts it daily.

  • Official documentation: Concept: Data pipeline runs - Microsoft Fabric

Bronze layer: A pipeline Copy activity. Bronze is populated by the items "Pipelines with Copy activities", so in the orchestration pipeline the Bronze step is the Copy activity that does the ingestion. Using Copy directly is the least complex option.

Silver layer: A pipeline Dataflow activity. Silver is built with dataflows, and the Dataflow activity runs a Dataflow Gen2 as a step in the pipeline, which lets it wait for Bronze to succeed before it starts. A Spark job definition is incorrect because Silver is not built with Spark.

  • Official documentation: Dataflow activity - Microsoft Fabric

Gold layer: A pipeline Stored procedure activity. Gold lives in the warehouse and is populated by stored procedures, which the Stored procedure activity runs from the pipeline after Silver completes. A Copy activity would not execute the T-SQL logic in the procedures.

q071.stem:
-

You are building a solution by using a Fabric notebook.

You have a Spark DataFrame assigned to a variable named df. The DataFrame returns four columns.

You need to change the data type of a string column named Age to integer. The solution must return a DataFrame that includes all the columns.

How should you complete the code? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Box 1: withColumn
  • Box 2: col
  • Box 3: cast

Resulting code: df.withColumn("age", col("age").cast("int")).show()

Analysis: The requirement is to change the data type of one string column to integer while still returning a DataFrame with all the columns.

Box 1 - withColumn: DataFrame.withColumn(name, column) returns a new DataFrame in which the column called name is added or, if it already exists, replaced by the expression you pass. Because the other three columns are untouched, the result keeps all four columns. The alternatives do not fit the "all columns" requirement: select and selectExpr return only the columns you list (you would have to list the remaining three as well), transform applies a custom function to a whole DataFrame (or a higher-order function to an array column) and does not take a column name plus an expression, and get is not a DataFrame method for this purpose.

  • Official documentation: Column.Cast and Spark SQL column types - Microsoft Learn

Box 2 - col: The second argument of withColumn must be a Column expression, and col("age") (from pyspark.sql.functions) builds a reference to the existing column so that it can be transformed. cast is a method of a Column, not a function that creates a column reference, and get / select / selectExpr / transform would not produce a Column reference at this position of the expression ("age")..

  • Official documentation: Column.Cast and Spark SQL column types - Microsoft Learn

Box 3 - cast: Column.cast("int") converts the values of the column to the target type (here, integer). This is the method that performs the type change, and it accepts a type name such as "int" or a DataType object such as IntegerType(). Notebook code in Fabric runs on Apache Spark, so this standard PySpark pattern (withColumn + col + cast) is the idiomatic way to change a column type without losing the rest of the columns.

  • Official documentation: Column.Cast and Spark SQL column types - Microsoft Learn

q074.stem:
-

You have a Fabric tenant that contains lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains a Delta table with eight columns.

You receive new data that contains the same eight columns and two additional columns.

You create a Spark DataFrame and assign the DataFrame to a variable named df.

The DataFrame contains the new data.

You need to add the new data to the Delta table to meet the following requirements:

  • Keep all the existing rows.
  • Ensure that all the new data is added to the table.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Box 1 (mode): ("append")
  • Box 2 (option): ("overwriteSchema","false")

Analysis:

Box 1 - ("append"): One requirement is to keep all existing rows, which rules out overwrite (it replaces the table content). append adds the new rows to the existing Delta table. error/errorifexists would fail because the table already exists, and ignore would silently do nothing, so the new data would not be added.

  • Official documentation: Update Delta Lake table schema - Azure Databricks

Box 2 - option: The new DataFrame has two columns that the table does not have, and the requirement says that all the new data must be added. The accepted option is ("overwriteSchema","false"): it tells Delta not to replace the existing table schema, which, together with append, preserves all existing rows and the table definition. The other choices behave differently: overwriteSchema = true is meant to replace the schema and only works together with overwrite mode, which would drop the existing rows, and mergeSchema = false keeps the default strict schema enforcement. The selection is based on the official documentation.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but with append the overwriteSchema option has no effect, and by default Delta Lake rejects an append that carries two extra columns with a schema mismatch error. The option that adds new columns during an append is ("mergeSchema","true") (schema evolution). Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Update Delta Lake table schema - Azure Databricks

q075.stem:
-

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Sales.Orders.

Sales.Orders contains the following columns.

You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the following columns.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Box 1: COALESCE
  • Box 2: LEAST

Resulting query: COALESCE(Weight, Quantity, 1) AS ChargedQuantity and LEAST(ListPrice, SalePrice) AS OrderPrice.

Analysis:

Box 1 - COALESCE: ChargedQuantity must return the Weight if it is present, otherwise Quantity if present, otherwise 1. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression in its argument list, evaluated left to right, so COALESCE(Weight, Quantity, 1) implements exactly that chain. CHOOSE selects an item by index position from a list (its first argument is an integer index), and IIF is a two-way conditional with a condition and two results, so it cannot express a three-level fallback in a single call.

  • Official documentation: COALESCE (Transact-SQL)

Box 2 - LEAST: OrderPrice must be the lowest value between two columns of the same row (ListPrice and SalePrice), ignoring NULL in SalePrice (the only nullable one). LEAST returns the minimum value among its arguments, and per the documentation NULL arguments are ignored as long as at least one argument is not NULL. Since ListPrice is declared NOT NULL, there is always a non-NULL value to return. MIN is an aggregate function that works across rows of a column, not across several columns in a single row, and it takes a single expression. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value, not the lowest one. LEAST is supported in Fabric Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint.

  • Official documentation: LEAST (Transact-SQL)

q076.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse.

You plan to use a visual query to merge two tables.

You need to ensure that the query returns all the rows in both tables.

Which type of join should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: full outer

Why it is correct: In a visual query (Merge queries), the join kind defines which rows come back. A full outer join returns all the rows from both tables: matching rows are combined and the rows without a match on either side are kept with nulls in the columns of the other table. This is the only option that guarantees that no row from either table is lost.

  • Official documentation: Full outer join - Power Query
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. inner

Why it is incorrect: An inner join returns only the rows that have a match in both tables, so unmatched rows from either side are dropped.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

C. left outer

Why it is incorrect: A left outer join returns all rows from the first (left) table plus the matching rows of the second one; unmatched rows of the right table are lost.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

D. right anti

Why it is incorrect: A right anti join returns only the rows from the right table that have no match in the left table. It returns neither the matching rows nor the left table rows.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

E. right outer

Why it is incorrect: A right outer join returns all rows from the second (right) table plus the matching rows of the first one; unmatched rows of the left table are lost.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

F. left anti

Why it is incorrect: A left anti join returns only the rows from the left table that have no match in the right table, so it excludes all the matching rows and all the right-table rows.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query
