q077.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains a Delta table that has one million Parquet files.

You need to remove files that were NOT referenced by the table during the past 30 days. The solution must ensure that the transaction log remains consistent, and the ACID properties of the table are maintained.

What should you do?
options: From OneLake file explorer, delete the files.
Run the OPTIMIZE command and specify the Z-order parameter.
Run the OPTIMIZE command and specify the V-order parameter.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Run the VACUUM command.

Why it is correct: Delta tables keep old Parquet files that are no longer referenced by the current table version (for example after updates, deletes or OPTIMIZE) so that time travel and concurrent readers keep working. VACUUM removes the files that are no longer referenced by the Delta transaction log and are older than the retention threshold. Because it goes through the Delta engine, the transaction log stays consistent and ACID guarantees are maintained. The requirement of "not referenced during the past 30 days" maps to a retention interval of 30 days (720 hours); the Fabric default retention threshold is 7 days, so you would specify the retention explicitly (and in the lakehouse UI you can run the table maintenance with VACUUM and a custom retention).

  • Official documentation: Delta Lake table optimization and V-Order - Lakehouse table maintenance - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. From OneLake file explorer, delete the files.

Why it is incorrect: Deleting Parquet files by hand bypasses the Delta transaction log, which still references them. This can corrupt the table (queries fail with missing files) and breaks consistency and ACID guarantees. Furthermore, doing it for one million files by hand is impractical and you cannot reliably know which ones are unreferenced.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse table maintenance - Microsoft Fabric

B. Run the OPTIMIZE command and specify the Z-order parameter.

Why it is incorrect: OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into fewer larger ones (and Z-order co-locates related data to improve data skipping). It does not delete the old files; they remain on storage as unreferenced files until VACUUM is run. It can even create more unreferenced files.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse table maintenance - Microsoft Fabric

C. Run the OPTIMIZE command and specify the V-order parameter.

Why it is incorrect: V-Order is a write-time optimization of the Parquet layout that improves read performance. Combined with OPTIMIZE it rewrites files, but it does not remove the unreferenced ones, so it does not meet the requirement.

You are implementing two dimension tables named Customers and Products in a Fabric warehouse.

You need to use slowly changing dimension (SCD) to manage the versioning of data. The solution must meet the requirements shown in the following table.

Which type of SCD should you use for each table? To answer, drag the appropriate SCD types to the correct tables. Each SCD type may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Customers: Type 2
  • Products: Type 1

Analysis: The requirements table says that for Customers a change must create a new version of the row, and for Products the change must overwrite the existing value in the latest row.

Customers - Type 2: A Type 2 slowly changing dimension keeps history by inserting a new row (a new version, typically with surrogate key, validity dates and/or a current flag) each time a tracked attribute changes, while the previous row is marked as no longer current. That is precisely "create a new version of the row". Type 0 would ignore changes, Type 1 would overwrite them losing history, and Type 3 stores only the previous value in an extra column rather than a new row.

  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric

Products - Type 1: A Type 1 SCD simply overwrites the attribute value in the existing row, so no history is kept and only the latest value exists. That matches "overwrite the existing value in the latest row". Type 2 would add rows, Type 3 would add a previous-value column, and Type 0 never changes the values.

  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 1 - Microsoft Fabric and Dimensional modeling: dimension tables - Microsoft Fabric

Slowly changing dimension type 1 - Microsoft Fabric

q079.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 and an Azure SQL database.

You plan to create a dataflow that will read data from the database, and then transform the data by performing an inner join.

You need to ignore spaces in the values when performing the inner join. The solution must minimize development effort.

What should you do?
options: Append the queries by using fuzzy matching.
Merge the queries by using fuzzy matching.
Append the queries by using a lookup table.
Merge the queries by using a lookup table.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Merge the queries by using fuzzy matching.

Why it is correct: In a dataflow (Power Query), an inner join between two queries is done with Merge queries (join kind = Inner). To make values match even when they differ in spaces, you enable Use fuzzy matching to perform the merge in the merge dialog. Fuzzy matching has options such as ignoring case and ignoring spaces (and similarity threshold), so no additional transformation steps to clean the data are needed, which minimizes development effort.

  • Official documentation: Fuzzy merge - Power Query
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Append the queries by using fuzzy matching.

Why it is incorrect: Append stacks the rows of one query on top of another (like UNION); it does not perform a join, and there is no fuzzy matching in append.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

C. Append the queries by using a lookup table.

Why it is incorrect: Append does not perform an inner join, so it cannot satisfy the requirement, and a lookup table adds extra work.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

D. Merge the queries by using a lookup table.

Why it is incorrect: Merge is the right operation, but a lookup table (a mapping of values with and without spaces) would have to be built and maintained manually. That is far more development effort than ticking the fuzzy matching option and its ignore-spaces setting.

  • Official documentation: Fuzzy merge - Power Query

q080.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains two schemas name schema1 and schema2 and a table named schema1.city.

You need to make a copy of schema1.city in schema2. The solution must minimize the copying of data.

Which T-SQL statement should you run?
options: INSERT INTO schema2.city SELECT * FROM schema1.city;
CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS CLONE OF schema1.city;
CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS SELECT * FROM schema1.city;

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS CLONE OF schema1.city;

Why it is correct: In a Fabric warehouse, CREATE TABLE ... AS CLONE OF creates a zero-copy clone: only the metadata is copied and the clone points to the same underlying Parquet data files in OneLake, so the operation is almost instantaneous and does not duplicate data (storage is only consumed later when the clone or the source change). A clone can be created in a different schema of the same warehouse, which is what is requested.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. INSERT INTO schema2.city SELECT * FROM schema1.city;

Why it is incorrect: It requires the destination table to already exist and physically copies every row, so data is duplicated.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric

B. SELECT * INTO schema2.city FROM schema1.city;

Why it is incorrect: It creates the table but also physically copies all the data, writing new files.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric

D. CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS SELECT * FROM schema1.city;

Why it is incorrect: CTAS reads the source and writes a full new copy of the data, so it does not minimize the copying of data (it works, but the requirement is to minimize data copy).

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric

q081.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You need to prevent new tables added to Lakehouse1 from being added

automatically to the default semantic model of the lakehouse.

What should you configure?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: the SQL analytics endpoint settings

Why it is correct: Every lakehouse has a SQL analytics endpoint, and the default semantic model of the lakehouse is managed from that endpoint. Its settings contain the Default Power BI semantic model option (called "Sync the default Power BI semantic model"). While it is on, new tables created in the lakehouse are added automatically to the default semantic model. Turning it off stops the automatic sync, so new tables in Lakehouse1 are no longer added and you decide which objects to include manually. The setting is opened from the SQL analytics endpoint item (or the warehouse item in the case of a warehouse), which is exactly what the question asks for.

  • Official documentation: Default Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Fabric - Add or remove objects and Semantic models in Fabric Data Warehouse
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. the semantic model settings

Why it is incorrect: The settings of the semantic model cover things like refresh, credentials, endorsement or permissions. The behavior that automatically adds new lakehouse tables to the default model is not controlled there; it is a property of the SQL analytics endpoint that generates and syncs the model.

  • Official documentation: Default Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Fabric

C. the workspace settings

Why it is incorrect: Workspace settings manage general aspects of the workspace (license mode, Spark settings, OneLake options, and so on). They do not include a switch to stop new lakehouse tables being synced to the default semantic model of one specific lakehouse.

  • Official documentation: Semantic models in Fabric Data Warehouse

D. the Lakehouse1 settings

Why it is incorrect: The lakehouse item settings (name, description, sensitivity and so on) do not expose the sync option. That option sits one level lower, in the settings of the lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint, which is a separate item.

  • Official documentation: Default Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Fabric

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1 and a warehouse named Warehouse1.

You need to create a new table in Warehouse1 named POSCustomers by

querying the customer table in Lakehouse1.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First drop-down (statement): CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers AS SELECT
  • Second drop-down (FROM clause): FROM lakehouse1.dbo.customer

First selection: CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT (CTAS). The goal is to create a new table in Warehouse1 and populate it with the result of a query over data that lives in Lakehouse1. CTAS does both in one statement: it creates the table and loads it with the rows returned by the SELECT (here SELECT DISTINCT customerid, customer, postalcode, category). A plain CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers would only define a table and would not accept a SELECT after it. CREATE TABLE ... AS CLONE OF is wrong because a clone is a zero-copy, metadata-based copy of an existing table in the same warehouse. It cannot take a column list or a DISTINCT query, and table clones across different warehouses/items in a workspace are not supported, so it cannot copy a lakehouse table into a warehouse.

  • Official documentation: Ingest data into your Warehouse using Transact-SQL and Clone table in Microsoft Fabric - Limitations

Second selection: FROM lakehouse1.dbo.customer. Lakehouse1 and Warehouse1 are in the same workspace, so the warehouse can query the lakehouse through a cross-database query using three-part naming (<item>.<schema>.<table>). FROM dbo.Customer would look for a table in the current database (Warehouse1), where the table does not exist. FROM dbo.POSCustomers would reference the table that is being created, which makes no sense as the source. Only the three-part name lakehouse1.dbo.customer points to the table in the lakehouse (through its SQL analytics endpoint).

  • Official documentation: Query the SQL analytics endpoint or Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric (cross-database queries) and Tutorial: Create cross-warehouse queries with the SQL query editor

q083.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You are creating an Azure Data Factory pipeline.

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Lookup

Why it is correct: The Lookup activity can retrieve data from a source, and it can also execute a stored procedure and return the result set. Its output (a single row or an array of rows) is exposed through the activity output, so downstream activities can reference it with expressions such as @activity('Lookup1').output.firstRow.ActiveCustomers. Here the stored procedure returns two values (the number of active customers and the average sales), and they must be consumed by later activities, which is the typical use of Lookup.

  • Official documentation: Use the Lookup activity to look up data from a data source - Microsoft Fabric and Lookup activity in Azure Data Factory
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Switch

Why it is incorrect: Switch is a control-flow activity that evaluates an expression and runs one of several branches of activities. It does not call stored procedures and does not return data.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

B. Copy data

Why it is incorrect: Copy data moves data from a source to a destination. It can use a stored procedure as a source, but its purpose is to write the rows to a sink; its output only contains run metadata (rows read, rows written, duration), not the returned values for use by downstream activities.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

C. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: Append variable only adds a value to an existing array variable. It cannot execute a stored procedure in a warehouse.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

q084.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains two workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2. Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Workspace2 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse2. Lakehouse1 contains a table named dbo.Sales. Lakehouse2 contains a table named dbo.Customers.

You need to ensure that you can write queries that reference both dbo.Sales and dbo.Customers in the same SQL query without making additional copies of the tables.

What should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: a view

Why it is correct: The requirement is to write one SQL query that references dbo.Sales (Lakehouse1, Workspace1) and dbo.Customers (Lakehouse2, Workspace2) without copying the data. A view is a virtual object that stores only a query definition, not data, so it satisfies "no additional copies": a view that joins the two tables exposes them as a single queryable object. Keep in mind that a SQL analytics endpoint only sees items from its own workspace, so in practice the table of the other workspace must first be made reachable (for example with a OneLake shortcut), and the view is then built on top of it.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but a SQL analytics endpoint cannot see tables in another workspace directly. The usual approach is a OneLake shortcut that exposes the other workspace's table without copying data, so "a shortcut" (option A) could also be argued, since it is the only option that puts both tables in the same query scope. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Query the SQL analytics endpoint or Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric and OneLake shortcuts
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. a shortcut

Why it is not the expected answer: A shortcut is a very good way to avoid copies, because it makes data from another lakehouse (even in another workspace) appear in your lakehouse as a reference. However, a shortcut by itself only exposes the table; the expected answer is the object that lets you write the query combining both tables. In practice a shortcut is often the piece that makes the second table reachable, so it is arguably right, but it is not the expected answer for this question.

  • Official documentation: Create a same-tenant OneLake shortcut

B. a dataflow

Why it is incorrect: A dataflow (Dataflow Gen2) is an ETL tool that ingests and transforms data, and typically writes the results to a destination, which creates a copy of the data. That contradicts the requirement.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts (reference data without copying it)

D. a managed table

Why it is incorrect: A managed table stores its own Delta data in the lakehouse. Creating one from the other table would physically duplicate the data, which is exactly what the question forbids.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts

q085.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.

You are designing a star schema model that will contain a customer dimension.

The customer dimension table will be a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD).

You need to recommend which columns to add to the table. The columns must NOT already exist in the source.

Which three types of columns should you recommend? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: an effective end date and time
an effective start date and time

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: an effective end date and time
  • Option D: a surrogate key
  • Option E: an effective start date and time

Why it is correct: A Type 2 slowly changing dimension keeps history by inserting a new row each time a tracked attribute changes, instead of overwriting the old one. That requires columns that the source system does not have:

  • Surrogate key: because the same business entity (customer) now appears in several rows (one per version), the natural key is no longer unique. A warehouse-generated surrogate key uniquely identifies each version and is the key that fact tables reference.

  • Effective start date and time and effective end date and time: they define the period during which each version of the row was valid, so you can find the current version (for example, end date is null or in the far future) and join facts to the version that was valid at the time of the transaction.

  • Official documentation: Dimension tables in dimensional modeling - Microsoft Fabric and Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. a foreign key

Why it is incorrect: In a star schema, foreign keys live in the fact table and point to the dimensions. A dimension table does not need a foreign key to implement SCD Type 2.

  • Official documentation: Dimension tables in dimensional modeling - Microsoft Fabric

B. a natural key

Why it is incorrect: The natural (business) key is the identifier that already comes from the source system, for example the customer number. The question asks for columns that do NOT already exist in the source, so the natural key is not something you add; you keep it and use it to detect changes.

  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric

Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric

q086.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You plan to create a data pipeline named Pipeline1. Pipeline1 will include two activities that will execute in sequence.

You need to ensure that a failure of the first activity will NOT block the second activity.

Which conditional path should you configure between the first activity and the second activity?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Upon Completion

Why it is correct: In a Fabric data pipeline, the connection between two activities has a conditional path: Upon success, Upon fail, Upon completion and Upon skip. The Upon completion path runs the next activity once the previous one has finished, regardless of whether it succeeded or failed. This is exactly what is needed so that a failure of the first activity does not block the second.

  • Official documentation: Pipeline canvas experience - Microsoft Fabric and Errors and conditional execution - Azure Data Factory
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Upon Failure

Why it is incorrect: Upon failure runs the second activity only if the first fails. If the first activity succeeds, the second would not run, so it does block the second activity in the success case.

  • Official documentation: Errors and conditional execution - Azure Data Factory

C. Upon Skip

Why it is incorrect: Upon skip runs the second activity only when the first activity was skipped (because one of its own dependencies was not met). It does not cover the normal success or failure outcomes of the first activity.

  • Official documentation: Errors and conditional execution - Azure Data Factory

D. Upon Skip

Why it is incorrect: This option repeats option C (Upon Skip), and it does not meet the requirement. For comparison, Upon success would run only if the first activity succeeded, so a failure would block the second activity.

  • Official documentation: Pipeline canvas experience - Microsoft Fabric

q087.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model.

You need to identify any surrogate key columns in the model that have the Summarize By property set to a value other than to None. The solution must minimize effort.

What should you use?
options: Model explorer in Microsoft Power BI Desktop
Model view in Microsoft Power BI Desktop
Best Practice Analyzer in Tabular Editor

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Best Practice Analyzer in Tabular Editor

Why it is correct: Best Practice Analyzer (BPA) in Tabular Editor scans the whole semantic model against a set of rules and lists every object that breaks a rule. One of the commonly used rules is precisely that key columns (for example, columns ending in "Key" or "ID") should have Summarize By set to None. Running BPA therefore finds all the surrogate key columns with a different Summarize By value in one pass, with almost no manual effort, and the rule can even offer a fix.

  • Official documentation: Optimize a data model by using Best Practice Analyzer - Microsoft Learn and External tools in Power BI Desktop
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. DAX Formatter in DAX Studio

Why it is incorrect: DAX Formatter only reformats the text of DAX expressions to make them readable. It knows nothing about column properties such as Summarize By.

  • Official documentation: Troubleshoot DAX performance by using DAX Studio

B. Model explorer in Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Model explorer lets you browse the tables and columns and edit their properties, but you would have to inspect the columns one by one (or select several manually). It cannot automatically identify the columns that break a rule, so it does not minimize effort.

  • Official documentation: Model explorer - Power BI

C. Model view in Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Model view shows tables and relationships and gives access to the Properties pane, but it has the same limitation as Model explorer: no automated rule-based search for columns with a given property value.

  • Official documentation: Work with Modeling view in Power BI Desktop

q088.stem:
-

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a Microsoft Power BI report named Report1.

Report1 is slow to render. You suspect that an inefficient DAX query is being executed.

You need to identify the slowest DAX query, and then review how long the query spends in the formula engine as compared to the storage engine.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers (in order):

  1. From Performance analyzer, capture a recording.
  2. Sort the Duration (ms) column in descending order.
  3. Copy the first query to DAX Studio.
  4. Enable Query Timings and Server Timings. Run the query.
  5. View the Server Timings tab.

Analysis of the sequence:

  1. Capture a recording in Performance analyzer. Performance analyzer in Power BI Desktop records, for each visual, how long it takes to run its DAX query and render. You start recording and refresh the visuals to get these numbers for Report1.
  2. Sort the Duration (ms) column in descending order. With the recording done, sorting by duration shows the slowest operation first, so you identify the slowest DAX query. (The other sort option, "by DAX query time", is a distractor that is not part of the five correct actions.)
  3. Copy the first query to DAX Studio. Performance analyzer lets you copy the DAX query of a visual, which you then paste into DAX Studio to analyze it outside the report.
  4. Enable Query Timings and Server Timings, then run the query. DAX Studio only collects the timing traces if these two options are on before executing the query.
  5. View the Server Timings tab. This tab splits the total duration into formula engine (FE) time and storage engine (SE) time, which is the comparison the scenario asks for. "View the Query Timings tab" is not used because the FE/SE breakdown is shown in Server Timings.
  • Official documentation: Use Performance analyzer to examine report element performance and Troubleshoot DAX performance by using DAX Studio

q089.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model contains 15 tables.

You need to programmatically change each column that ends in the word Key to meet the following requirements:

  • Hide the column.
  • Set Nullable to False
  • Set Summarize By to None.
  • Set Available in MDX to False.
  • Mark the column as a key column.

What should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Tabular Editor

Why it is correct: The requirement is to change the same set of properties (Hidden, Nullable, Summarize By, Available in MDX, Is Key) on every column whose name ends in "Key" across 15 tables, programmatically. Tabular Editor supports C# scripts (Advanced Scripting) and the Best Practice Analyzer, with which you can loop through all the columns, filter by name and set all the properties in one run. It connects to a semantic model, including one in a Fabric workspace through the XMLA endpoint, and saves the changes back.

  • Official documentation: External tools in Power BI Desktop and Power BI usage scenarios: Advanced data model management
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Power BI Desktop lets you edit column properties in the UI, but only manually (although you can multi-select columns, you still have to find them across 15 tables) and it offers no scripting to apply changes by name pattern. Several of the listed properties are not even exposed there.

  • Official documentation: Work with Modeling view in Power BI Desktop

B. ALM Toolkit

Why it is incorrect: ALM Toolkit is used to compare two semantic model schemas and deploy the differences between them (a diff/merge tool). It is not meant to bulk-edit properties of columns.

  • Official documentation: External tools in Power BI Desktop

D. DAX Studio

Why it is incorrect: DAX Studio is for writing and running DAX queries and analyzing their performance. It is not a model authoring tool and cannot modify column metadata.

q090.stem:
-

You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model.

You plan to implement calculation groups.

You need to create a calculation item that will change the context from the selected date to month-to-date (MTD).

How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First drop-down: CALCULATE
  • Second drop-down: SELECTEDMEASURE

The complete expression is CALCULATE ( SELECTEDMEASURE (), DATESMTD ( 'Date'[Date] ) ).

First selection: CALCULATE. A calculation item must change the filter context in which the measure that is being used is evaluated. CALCULATE evaluates an expression in a modified filter context, and here the modification is the DATESMTD filter that moves the context from the selected date to the month-to-date period. GENERATE is a table function that returns a cross join of tables, so it cannot return the scalar value a calculation item must return. MEASURE is not a DAX function for use in an expression (it is the keyword used in a query-scoped DEFINE MEASURE statement).

  • Official documentation: Create calculation groups in Power BI

Second selection: SELECTEDMEASURE. Inside a calculation item, SELECTEDMEASURE() is a placeholder that refers to whichever measure is currently being evaluated in the visual. That makes the same MTD logic reusable for every measure in the model. SELECTEDVALUE returns the value of a column when only one value is in the filter context, so it is for column values and not for measures. COMBINEVALUES concatenates values into a string for multi-column relationships and is unrelated.

  • Official documentation: SELECTEDMEASURE function (DAX) and Calculation groups - Analysis Services

q091.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI report named Report1 that uses a Fabric semantic model.

Users discover that Report1 renders slowly.

You open Performance analyzer and identify that a visual named Orders By Date is the slowest to render. The duration breakdown for Orders By Date is shown in the following table.

What will provide the greatest reduction in the rendering duration of Report1?
options: Optimize the DAX query of Orders By Date by using DAX Studio.
Change the visual type of Orders By Date.
Reduce the number of visuals in Report1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Reduce the number of visuals in Report1.

Why it is correct: The Performance analyzer table splits the time of the slowest visual into three parts: DAX query = 27 ms, Visual display = 39 ms and Other = 1047 ms. Almost the entire duration (about 94%) is in "Other". Microsoft defines "Other" as the time the visual spends preparing queries, waiting for other visuals to finish, and performing other background processing. In other words, Orders By Date is not slow because of its own query or its own drawing; it is slow because it is queued behind the other visuals on the page, which are rendered and queried competitively. The thing that reduces that waiting time the most is to have fewer visuals competing on the page (for example by splitting content into several pages or removing redundant visuals), which lowers the number of concurrent queries and the rendering work for the whole report.

  • Official documentation: Use Performance Analyzer to examine report element performance - Power BI
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Enable automatic page refresh.

Why it is incorrect: Automatic page refresh makes a report re-query its data source at a fixed interval so that the visuals show fresh data. It does not speed anything up; on the contrary, each refresh triggers new queries and more rendering work. It addresses data freshness, not render duration.

  • Official documentation: Use Performance Analyzer to examine report element performance - Power BI

B. Optimize the DAX query of Orders By Date by using DAX Studio.

Why it is incorrect: DAX Studio is a good tool to tune slow queries, but the exhibit shows the DAX query takes only 27 ms. Even if you made it instantaneous you would save at most 27 ms out of roughly 1,113 ms in total. The bottleneck is the "Other" category (1047 ms), which a DAX optimization does not address.

  • Official documentation: Use Performance Analyzer to examine report element performance - Power BI

C. Change the visual type of Orders By Date.

Why it is incorrect: Changing the visual type could only influence the "Visual display" component, which is just 39 ms. It would not reduce the 1047 ms that the visual waits for other visuals and background processing, so the gain would be marginal.

  • Official documentation: Use Performance Analyzer to examine report element performance - Power BI

q092.stem:
You have a custom Direct Lake semantic model named Model1 that has one billion rows of data.

You use Tabular Editor to connect to Model1 by using the XMLA endpoint.

You need to ensure that when users interact with reports based on Model1, their queries always use Direct Lake mode.

What should you do?
options: From Model, configure the Default Mode option.
From Partitions, configure the Mode option.
From Model, configure the Storage Location option.
From Model, configure the Direct Lake Behavior option.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: From Model, configure the Direct Lake Behavior option.

Why it is correct: In a Direct Lake semantic model, queries can fall back to DirectQuery mode when Direct Lake cannot be used efficiently (for example when the table is very large, as with the one billion rows here, or when guardrails of the capacity are exceeded). This behavior is controlled by the model-level DirectLakeBehavior property, which has three values: Automatic (default, fallback allowed), DirectLakeOnly (all queries use Direct Lake mode only; fallback is disabled and an error is returned if the data cannot be loaded into memory) and DirectQueryOnly. Because you are connected to Model1 through the XMLA endpoint with Tabular Editor, you select the Model object and set Direct Lake Behavior to DirectLakeOnly, which guarantees that report queries always use Direct Lake mode.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - Fallback behavior and Direct Lake: how it works
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. From Model, configure the Default Mode option.

Why it is incorrect: Default Mode is a model property that sets the default storage mode (Import, DirectQuery, Dual) for new tables. It does not control whether a Direct Lake model may fall back to DirectQuery at query time, so it cannot force queries to stay in Direct Lake mode.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - Fallback behavior

B. From Partitions, configure the Mode option.

Why it is incorrect: A Direct Lake table partition already has its mode set to Direct Lake; changing the partition mode is how you would convert a table to another storage mode, not how you prevent fallback. The fallback is governed by the model-level DirectLakeBehavior property, not by the partition Mode.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - Fallback behavior

C. From Model, configure the Storage Location option.

Why it is incorrect: Storage Location refers to where the model data is stored (for example large semantic model storage format). It has nothing to do with the query mode or the DirectQuery fallback of a Direct Lake model.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake: how it works

You create a semantic model by using Microsoft Power BI Desktop. The model contains one security role named SalesRegionManager and the following tables:

  • Sales
  • SalesRegion
  • SalesAddress

You need to modify the model to ensure that users assigned the

SalesRegionManager role cannot see a column named Address in SalesAddress.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Open the model in Tabular Editor.
  • Step 2: Select the Address column in SalesAddress.
  • Step 3: Set Object Level Security to None for SalesRegionManager.

Analysis:

Step 1 - Open the model in Tabular Editor. Object-level security (OLS) cannot be configured in the Power BI Desktop interface; the Power BI documentation explicitly says that you must use an external tool such as Tabular Editor to define OLS on tables and columns. That is why "Open the model in Power BI Desktop" is not part of the sequence: the Desktop designer lets you create the roles (the model already has SalesRegionManager) but not set table/column permissions.

Step 2 - Select the Address column in SalesAddress. OLS is applied per object, so you must first pick the exact object to protect, here the single column Address (not the whole SalesAddress table). In Tabular Editor you expand the table, select the column and then the Object Level Security property shows each role.

Step 3 - Set Object Level Security to None for SalesRegionManager. The OLS permission values are Default (inherit, which is the permission level for the role), Read and None. Setting None for the role hides the column: for members of SalesRegionManager the column behaves as if it did not exist, and visuals that use it show an error or are not available. Default would leave the permission unchanged, so it would not hide anything.

Why the other actions are wrong: "Set the Hidden property to True" only hides the column from the report view/field list; it is not a security feature, since a user with Build permission can still show hidden fields and query them with DAX or in Analyze in Excel. "Set Object Level Security to Default" restores the standard behavior (no restriction) for the role.

  • Official documentation: Object-level security (OLS) - Microsoft Fabric

q094.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model that contains measures. The measures use multiple CALCULATE functions and a FILTER function.

You are evaluating the performance of the measures.

In which use case will replacing the FILTER function with the KEEPFILTERS function reduce execution time?
options: when the FILTER function uses a nested calculate function
when the FILTER function references a measure
when the FILTER function references columns from multiple tables
when the FILTER function references a column from a single table that uses Import mode

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: when the FILTER function uses a nested calculate function

Why it is correct: KEEPFILTERS changes how a filter argument is combined with the existing filter context of CALCULATE: instead of replacing the filters already applied to a column, it intersects with them. When the table expression passed to CALCULATE is built with FILTER over an iterator that contains a nested CALCULATE, a context transition occurs for every row, which is expensive. Using KEEPFILTERS keeps the existing filters in place and avoids the extra work of overriding and re-evaluating the filter context, which is the use case in which replacing FILTER with KEEPFILTERS can reduce execution time. In the other options (a measure, columns from multiple tables, a single Import table) FILTER is behaving as a plain row filter, and replacing it with KEEPFILTERS does not give a performance advantage.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but Microsoft's performance guidance is to replace FILTER over a column with a Boolean filter expression, and KEEPFILTERS is mainly a semantic tool (it intersects with the existing filter context instead of overwriting it) that the documentation does not tie to nested CALCULATE. Options A, C and D can each be argued depending on the case meant, and none is explicitly backed by the documentation. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: KEEPFILTERS function (DAX) and Avoid using FILTER as a filter argument
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. when the FILTER function references a measure

Why it is incorrect: If the FILTER condition references a measure, the measure must be evaluated for each row of the table being iterated (with context transition). The measure reference is evaluated per row regardless of KEEPFILTERS, and a Boolean filter expression cannot reference a measure directly either, so KEEPFILTERS does not remove that cost.

  • Official documentation: Avoid using FILTER as a filter argument

C. when the FILTER function references columns from multiple tables

Why it is incorrect: FILTER is the appropriate way to apply a condition that involves columns of several tables, since Boolean filter expressions can only reference columns of a single table. KEEPFILTERS controls how the resulting filter is merged with the existing context, but it does not make a multi-table filter cheaper to compute.

  • Official documentation: Avoid using FILTER as a filter argument

D. when the FILTER function references a column from a single table that uses Import mode

Why it is incorrect: This is the case where the best optimization is to replace FILTER with a simple Boolean filter expression (for example Sales[Color] = "Red"), which the engine optimizes natively, not with KEEPFILTERS. The storage mode (Import) does not make KEEPFILTERS a performance feature.

  • Official documentation: Avoid using FILTER as a filter argument

q095.stem:
You have a semantic model named Model1. Model1 contains five tables that all use Import mode. Model1 contains a dynamic row-level security (RLS) role named HR. The HR role filters employee data so that HR managers only see the data of the department to which they are assigned.

You publish Model1 to a Fabric tenant and configure RLS role membership. You share the model and related reports to users.

An HR manager reports that the data they see in a report is incomplete.

What should you do to validate the data seen by the HR Manager?
options: Select Test as role to view the data as the HR role.
Filter the data in the report to match the intended logic of the filter for the HR department.
Select Test as role to view the report as the HR manager.
Ask the HR manager to open the report in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Select Test as role to view the data as the HR role.

Why it is correct: When a user reports that the data in a report is incomplete and the semantic model uses RLS, the standard way to validate what that user sees is to use Test as role in Power BI (Desktop with View > View as, or in the service from the semantic model's Security page). You choose the HR role, and the report is rendered with the role's filter applied, so you can compare the result with the intended logic (the department assigned to the HR manager) and spot errors in the filter expression or in the underlying mapping table. Because the role is dynamic, testing also lets you check the DAX filter (for example one that uses USERPRINCIPALNAME()) and the department-to-user mapping.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but in the Power BI service Test as role also lets you add a specific user ("Now viewing as"), so option C (viewing the report as the HR manager) is nearly equivalent and arguably reproduces the manager's exact view when the problem lies in that user's mapping or membership. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Validate roles
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Filter the data in the report to match the intended logic of the filter for the HR department.

Why it is incorrect: Applying a report filter only changes what the report displays for you; it does not reproduce how the RLS role filters the data for the HR manager. You would not be validating the role itself, and a report-level filter cannot reveal whether the RLS expression or the membership is wrong.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI

C. Select Test as role to view the report as the HR manager.

Why it is incorrect: This is not the expected answer for this question: the role is the unit to test, and Test as role lets you select the HR role (roles, not people, are what you define in the model). With dynamic RLS you can additionally impersonate a specific user in the service, which makes this a very close alternative in practice, but the expected answer is to test as the HR role (A).

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI

D. Ask the HR manager to open the report in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.

Why it is incorrect: RLS defined in the model is not enforced for the author in Power BI Desktop in the same way; the Desktop experience opens the file/model with its own data, and the manager would not necessarily have access to the model. It also pushes the troubleshooting onto the end user instead of validating the role as the model owner.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Sales.Products.

Sales.Products contains the following columns.

You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the following columns.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • HighestSellingPrice: GREATEST
  • TradePrice: COALESCE

Analysis:

HighestSellingPrice = GREATEST(ListPrice, WholesalePrice, AgentPrice). The requirement is the highest value across three columns of the same row. GREATEST is the T-SQL scalar function that returns the maximum value from a list of expressions, and it ignores NULL arguments as long as at least one value is not NULL (WholesalePrice and AgentPrice are nullable, ListPrice is not, so there is always a value). MAX is wrong because it is an aggregate function that works over the rows of one column (it takes a single expression, not a list of columns). COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value, not the largest, so with ListPrice first it would always return ListPrice. IIF takes a boolean condition and two results, so it cannot take three columns like this.

TradePrice = COALESCE(...). The requirement is "AgentPrice if present, otherwise WholesalePrice if present, otherwise ListPrice", which is the definition of COALESCE: it evaluates its arguments in order and returns the first one that is not NULL. CHOOSE selects an item by index position, not by NULL checks. IIF handles only a single condition. MAX would return the highest price rather than the first available one. (Note: for the exact logic described, the arguments would need to be in the order AgentPrice, WholesalePrice, ListPrice; the exhibit keeps the order ListPrice, WholesalePrice, AgentPrice.)

  • Official documentation: GREATEST (Transact-SQL), COALESCE (Transact-SQL), IIF (Transact-SQL), CHOOSE (Transact-SQL) and MAX (Transact-SQL)

You have a Fabric notebook that has the Python code and output shown in the following exhibit.

Which type of analytics are you performing?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: descriptive

Why it is correct: The notebook code plots a histogram of the tip amounts of a sampled taxi dataset with Matplotlib and shows the distribution of the values (how many trips fall in each tip range). That answers the question "what happened / what is the data like?", which is exactly descriptive analytics: summarizing historical data through statistics and visualizations (counts, distributions, averages). There is no attempt to explain the cause (diagnostic), to forecast future values with a model (predictive) or to recommend an action (prescriptive).

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. diagnostic

Why it is incorrect: Diagnostic analytics answers "why did it happen?" by drilling down, correlating variables or looking for root causes. A single histogram of one column does not compare factors or look for causes.

  • Official documentation: Understand data analytics types

C. prescriptive

Why it is incorrect: Prescriptive analytics recommends actions ("what should we do?"), usually using optimization or simulation on top of predictions. The notebook only shows a distribution and recommends nothing.

  • Official documentation: Understand data analytics types

D. predictive

Why it is incorrect: Predictive analytics builds models (for example regression or machine learning) to forecast "what will happen". The code only plots existing sampled data and does not train or apply any model.

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Sales.Orders.

Sales.Orders contains the following columns.

You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the following columns.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • PeriodDate: DATETRUNC
  • DayName: weekday

Analysis:

PeriodDate = DATETRUNC(month, OrderDate). The requirement is a date representing the first day of the month of OrderDate. DATETRUNC(datepart, date) truncates the input date to the specified part, so with month it returns the first day of that month as a date (for example 2025-03-17 becomes 2025-03-01). DATEPART returns an integer with just that part (the month number, 3), not a date. DATEFROMPARTS needs year, month and day arguments, not (month, OrderDate). DATE_BUCKET takes a bucket width and an origin (DATE_BUCKET(month, 1, OrderDate)), so the shown signature (month, OrderDate) does not fit it.

DayName = DATENAME(weekday, OrderDate). DATENAME returns the character string name of the specified datepart. With weekday it returns the name of the day of the week (for example "Wednesday"). day would return the day of the month as a string ("17"), and dayofyear would return the number of the day in the year ("76"), neither of which is a name.

  • Official documentation: DATETRUNC (Transact-SQL), DATENAME (Transact-SQL), DATEPART (Transact-SQL), DATEFROMPARTS (Transact-SQL) and DATE_BUCKET (Transact-SQL)

q100.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains JSON files in OneLake. The files have one billion items.

You plan to perform time series analysis of the items.

You need to transform the data, visualize the data to find insights, perform anomaly detection, and share the insights with other business users. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • Use parallel processing.
  • Minimize the duplication of data.
  • Minimize how long it takes to load the data.

What should you use to transform and visualize the data?
options: the PySpark library in a Fabric notebook
the pandas library in a Fabric notebook
a Microsoft Power BI report that uses core visuals

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: the PySpark library in a Fabric notebook

Why it is correct: The scenario has one billion items stored as JSON files in OneLake and three constraints: use parallel processing, minimize duplicating data and minimize load time. A Fabric notebook running PySpark reads the files in place from OneLake (no copy needed) and distributes the transformation across the executors of the Spark cluster, so it meets the parallel processing requirement and scales to this volume. The notebook also lets you visualize the result with built-in charts or libraries and run anomaly detection on the time series, and the results can be shared with business users from the Fabric workspace.

  • Official documentation: What is Apache Spark compute in Microsoft Fabric? and Notebook visualization in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. the pandas library in a Fabric notebook

Why it is incorrect: pandas runs on a single node and loads the whole dataset in the memory of the driver, so it does not provide distributed (parallel) processing and cannot reasonably handle one billion items. Loading the data would also take much longer.

  • Official documentation: What is Apache Spark compute in Microsoft Fabric?

C. a Microsoft Power BI report that uses core visuals

Why it is incorrect: A Power BI report with core visuals is a visualization layer; it does not by itself transform the JSON files nor perform the anomaly detection on one billion items, and importing that volume would duplicate the data and lengthen the load. It would require a transformation engine such as Spark first.

  • Official documentation: Notebook visualization in Microsoft Fabric

q101.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains customer churn data stored as Parquet files in OneLake. The data contains details about customer demographics and product usage.

You create a Fabric notebook to read the data into a Spark DataFrame. You then create column charts in the notebook that show the distribution of retained customers as compared to lost customers based on geography, the number of products purchased, age, and customer tenure.

Which type of analytics are you performing?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: descriptive

Why it is correct: Descriptive analytics answers the question "what happened?". It summarizes historical data with counts, distributions and aggregations, typically shown as tables and charts. In the scenario you read the churn Parquet files into a Spark DataFrame and build column charts that show how retained customers compare to lost customers by geography, number of products, age and tenure. You are only describing the existing distribution of the data. You are not investigating the root cause of the churn, you are not training a model to forecast who will leave, and you are not recommending any action. That is exactly the definition of descriptive analytics, and exploratory charting in a Fabric notebook is the typical way to do it.

  • Official documentation: Understand data analytics types - Microsoft Learn and Explore data analytics - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. diagnostic

Why it is incorrect: Diagnostic analytics answers "why did it happen?". It drills down, correlates variables and looks for root causes (for example, testing which factor actually drives customers to leave). Plotting the distribution of retained versus lost customers by several attributes only shows what the data looks like; it does not establish causes. The scenario never asks for an explanation of the churn.

  • Official documentation: Understand data analytics types - Microsoft Learn

C. prescriptive

Why it is incorrect: Prescriptive analytics answers "what should we do?". It recommends actions or decisions, usually on top of predictions and optimization. The notebook produces only charts and recommends nothing, so it is not prescriptive.

  • Official documentation: Overview of data analysis - Microsoft Learn

D. predictive

Why it is incorrect: Predictive analytics answers "what is likely to happen?". It uses statistical or machine learning models trained on historical data to forecast future outcomes, such as the probability that a given customer will churn. The scenario reads data and draws column charts but trains no model and produces no forecast, so it is not predictive.

  • Official documentation: Explore data analytics - Microsoft Learn

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model contains data about retail stores.

You need to write a DAX query that will be executed by using the XMLA endpoint. The query must return the total amount of sales from the same period last year.

How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (function used in VAR _LYSales =): SUMMARIZE
  • Second box (after RETURN): _LYSales

Detailed analysis:

First box. The variable _LYSales must hold the total sales for the same period of the previous year, and the expression passes [Total Sales] and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Orders'[Order Date]) as arguments. The expected selection for this box is SUMMARIZE, which is the function used to build the prior-year result in the query. The other alternatives are: CALCULATETABLE returns a table (not a scalar total), FILTER needs a table and a Boolean condition, and SUMMARIZECOLUMNS builds a grouped table from column references and also does not take a measure plus a filter table in this form.

  • Official documentation: SUMMARIZE function (DAX), CALCULATE function (DAX), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR function (DAX)

Second box. In a DAX query that is run through the XMLA endpoint, the query must end with EVALUATE followed by a table expression. After RETURN you reference the variable you just defined, _LYSales, so the query returns the value you computed. [Total Sales] would return the current-period measure and ignore the prior-year calculation. { _LYSales } would wrap the value in a table constructor, which is a valid way to return a scalar from EVALUATE, but it is not the expected selection here. VAR is a keyword, not a value to return.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the arguments shown (a measure followed by a time-intelligence table function used as a filter) match the signature of CALCULATE, which evaluates an expression in a modified filter context, whereas SUMMARIZE expects a table as its first argument. For the first box, CALCULATE could therefore also be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: DAX queries, SUMMARIZECOLUMNS function (DAX)

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a Microsoft Power BI report.

You are exploring a new semantic model.

You need to display the following column statistics:

  • Count
  • Average
  • Null count
  • Distinct count
  • Standard deviation

Which Power Query function should you run?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Table.Profile

Why it is correct: Table.Profile(table) returns a table with one row per column of the input table and a set of statistics for it: minimum, maximum, average, standard deviation, count, null count and distinct count (where applicable). That is exactly the list of column statistics required (count, average, null count, distinct count and standard deviation). It is the M function behind the column profiling that Power Query shows when you explore a new dataset.

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Table.schema

Why it is incorrect: Table.Schema returns metadata about the structure of the table (column names, positions, type names, nullability and so on), not statistics computed over the data values such as average or standard deviation.

  • Official documentation: Table.Profile - Power Query M

B. Table.view

Why it is incorrect: Table.View creates a table whose behavior is defined by custom handlers (for query folding and similar scenarios in connector development). It computes no column statistics.

C. Table.FuzzyGroup

Why it is incorrect: Table.FuzzyGroup groups rows whose key values are similar (fuzzy matching) and aggregates them. It is a grouping function, not a profiling function, and it does not return count, null count, distinct count or standard deviation per column.

Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals. Some question sets might have more than one correct solution, while others might not have a correct solution.

After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return to it. As a result, these questions will not appear in the review screen.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains a Delta table named Customer.

When you query Customer, you discover that the query is slow to execute. You suspect that maintenance was NOT performed on the table.

You need to identify whether maintenance tasks were performed on Customer.

Solution: You run the following Spark SQL statement:

DESCRIBE DETAIL customer -

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: The goal is to find out whether maintenance tasks (OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and so on) have been run on the Customer table. You have a Fabric workspace that uses the default Spark starter pool and runtime version 1.2.

You plan to read a CSV file named Sales_raw.csv in a lakehouse, select columns, and save the data as a Delta table to the managed area of the lakehouse.

Sales_raw.csv contains 12 columns.

You have the following code.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Statement 1 (The Spark engine will read only the SalesOrderNumber, OrderDate, CustomerName and UnitPrice columns from Sales_raw.csv): Yes
  • Statement 2 (The Year column replaces the OrderDate column in the table): No
  • Statement 3 (Adding inferSchema='true' to the options will increase the execution time of the query): Yes

Statement 1 - Yes. Spark evaluates DataFrames lazily: .load() and .select() only build a logical plan, and nothing is read until the .saveAsTable() action runs. The Catalyst optimizer then pushes the projection down to the CSV data source, which applies column pruning, so only the four selected columns are parsed and materialized from the 12-column file.

Statement 2 - No. withColumn("Year", year("OrderDate")) adds a new column called Year derived from OrderDate; it does not drop or replace OrderDate, because the column name used in withColumn is different from the existing one. The resulting table therefore has five columns: SalesOrderNumber, OrderDate, CustomerName, UnitPrice and Year. Only a call with the same name (withColumn("OrderDate", ...)) would replace the original column. The Year column is then used by partitionBy('Year') to partition the Delta table.

Statement 3 - Yes. By default, the CSV reader treats every column as a string (and, here, the header option only names the columns). With inferSchema='true' Spark must make an additional pass over the data to sample/scan the values and infer the data types, so the execution time increases. For large files it is faster and more predictable to provide the schema explicitly.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks statement 1 as Yes, but a CSV file is a row-oriented text format, so every line is still physically scanned from storage even though only the selected columns are parsed; read that way, the statement could be argued as "No". Check it against the linked documentation.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named model1. The two largest columns in model1 are shown in the following table.

You need to optimize model1. The solution must meet the following

requirements:

  • Reduce the model size.
  • Increase refresh performance when using Import mode.
  • Ensure that the datetime value for each sales transaction is available in the model.

What should you do on each column? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • TransactionKey: Remove the column.
  • SaleDateTime: Split the column.

TransactionKey - Remove the column. This column holds an incrementing surrogate key with 2,500,350,000 distinct values and a compressed size of 160 GB. The Vertipaq engine of Import mode stores data in a columnar way and compresses it based on repeated values, so a column in which every row is different (cardinality equal to the number of rows) cannot be compressed and is the biggest contributor to model size and to refresh time. The requirement is to reduce the model size and speed up refresh, and the only datetime information that must remain is the sale datetime; a surrogate key of a fact table is not needed for analysis, aggregation or relationships (nothing references it), so the best action is to remove it from the model. Microsoft guidance states that unnecessary high-cardinality columns, such as fact table surrogate keys, should be removed. Alternatives: "Change the data type" would not make the unique values compressible; "Split the column" does not make sense for a key; "Truncate the data" would delete rows or values and is not a modeling optimization for the column.

SaleDateTime - Split the column. This column has 6,850,273 distinct values because it stores the date and the time to the second. The requirement says that the datetime of each sale must still be available in the model, so the column cannot be removed or truncated. Splitting it into two columns, a Date column and a Time column, drops the cardinality dramatically: there are only a few thousand distinct dates and at most 86,400 distinct times of the day, so both columns compress very well and the combined size is much smaller than that of the original column. The full datetime can still be reconstructed from the date and time columns when needed (for example with a measure), and the Date column can be related to a date dimension. Alternatives: "Remove the column" would lose the datetime information; "Truncate the data" (for example to the date or the hour) loses the time precision, so the requirement would not be met; "Change the data type" (for example datetime to date) also loses the time part, and changing it to text would increase the size.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a data warehouse named DW1. DW1 contains a table named DimCustomer. DimCustomer contains the fields shown in the following table.

You need to identify duplicate email addresses in DimCustomer. The solution must return a maximum of 1,000 records.

Which four T-SQL statements should you run in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate statements from the list of statements to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  1. SELECT TOP(1000) CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*)
  2. FROM DimCustomer
  3. GROUP BY CustomerAltKey
  4. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

Analysis. The goal is to find email addresses (stored in CustomerAltKey) that appear more than once in DimCustomer and to return at most 1,000 rows. A T-SQL query is written with the clauses in this logical order: SELECT, FROM, GROUP BY and HAVING.

  • Statement 1 - SELECT TOP(1000) CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*): it selects the email and the number of times it appears and, thanks to TOP(1000), limits the number of rows returned to 1,000, which meets the "maximum of 1,000 records" requirement. The other SELECT, without TOP, would not limit the result.
  • Statement 2 - FROM DimCustomer: it specifies the source table and must come right after the SELECT list.
  • Statement 3 - GROUP BY CustomerAltKey: it groups the rows by email, so COUNT(*) returns the number of rows for each distinct address.
  • Statement 4 - HAVING COUNT(*) > 1: it keeps only the groups that contain more than one row, which are the duplicates. HAVING is the clause used to filter on the result of aggregates after the grouping.

Why the other statements are wrong: LIMIT 1000 is not supported by T-SQL (it is the syntax of MySQL, PostgreSQL and similar engines; T-SQL uses TOP or OFFSET ... FETCH), so it would produce a syntax error in a Fabric warehouse. WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 is invalid because the WHERE clause is evaluated before grouping and cannot contain aggregate functions; aggregates are filtered with HAVING. The plain SELECT CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*) would work for finding duplicates but would not enforce the 1,000-record maximum unless combined with LIMIT, which does not exist in T-SQL.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - HAVING (Transact-SQL), TOP (Transact-SQL) and T-SQL surface area in Microsoft Fabric

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named WH1.

You run the following T-SQL query against WH1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Statement 1 (Dimension.GetDirectReports is a scalar T-SQL function): Yes
  • Statement 2 (The Dimension.GetDirectReports function will run only once when the query runs): No
  • Statement 3 (The output rows will include at least one row for each row in the Dimension.Employee table): Yes

Statement 1 - Yes. Dimension.GetDirectReports is accepted as a T-SQL user-defined function that is invoked once per employee row and whose returned columns are projected as gdr.[WWI Employee ID] and gdr.Employee.

Statement 2 - No. The APPLY operator invokes the right-side expression once for each row of the left-side table (here Dimension.Employee), passing the employee key as a parameter. It therefore executes many times, once per employee, and not once for the whole query.

Statement 3 - Yes. OUTER APPLY works like a left outer join: when the function returns no rows for an employee (an employee without direct reports), the left row is still returned with NULL values in the function columns. Therefore the result contains at least one row for every row of Dimension.Employee. In contrast, CROSS APPLY would discard the employees for which the function returns an empty result.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks statement 1 as Yes, but the function is used on the right side of OUTER APPLY, which requires a table-valued function (or a derived table), so it more likely behaves as a table-valued function than as a scalar one, which would make statement 1 "No". The proposed replacement, NOT(CALCULATE(COUNTROWS('Order Item')) < 0), does not improve the execution and also changes the result:

  1. COUNTROWS never returns a negative number: it returns a positive count or blank. The condition < 0 is therefore always false and NOT(...) is always true, so the filter no longer removes any customer. The query returns all the customers, including those without order items, instead of only those with orders. A tuning change must keep the same results.
  2. The expression still contains a CALCULATE with a context transition evaluated for every customer (row context to filter context), which is the costly part of the original query, so the number of storage engine and formula engine operations is not reduced in any meaningful way.

The solution therefore does not meet the goal of reducing the execution time while keeping the query meaningful.

A. Yes

Why it is incorrect: The replacement NOT(CALCULATE(COUNTROWS('Order Item')) < 0) is always true, because a row count can never be negative, so the filter stops filtering and the result of the query changes (all customers are returned). It also keeps the per-customer CALCULATE evaluation, so it is not a real optimization. Therefore, the solution does not meet the goal.

q120.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI Premium Per User (PPU) workspace that contains a semantic model.

You have an Azure App Service app named App1 that modifies row-level security (RLS) for the model by using the XMLA endpoint.

App1 requires users to sign in by using their Microsoft Entra credentials to access the XMLA endpoint.

You need to configure App1 to use a service account to access the model.

What should you do first?
options: Add a managed identity to the workspace.
Upgrade the workspace to Premium capacity.
Add a managed identity to App1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Add a managed identity to App1.

Why it is correct: App1 is an Azure App Service app that currently authenticates to the XMLA endpoint with interactive user sign-in (Microsoft Entra credentials). To make it use a service account instead, the app needs a non-human identity in Microsoft Entra ID that it can use to obtain tokens without storing credentials. For an App Service app this is done by enabling a managed identity on the app itself (the identity is created as a service principal in Microsoft Entra ID and is managed by Azure). This is the first step: once App1 has an identity, you can allow service principals to use the Fabric/Power BI APIs in the tenant settings, add that identity to the workspace with a suitable role (for example Member or Contributor/Admin), and then use it with the XMLA endpoint to change the RLS. Premium Per User workspaces already support XMLA read/write, so no capacity change is needed.

  • Official documentation: How to use managed identities for App Service and Azure Functions and Automate Premium workspace and semantic model tasks with service principals
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Add a managed identity to the workspace.

Why it is incorrect: The identity that must authenticate belongs to the application that calls the XMLA endpoint (App1), not to the workspace. A workspace identity is used for outbound authentication of Fabric items to data sources, not for letting an external app sign in as a service account. Moreover, App1 has no identity yet that could be granted access to the workspace, so creating the identity for App1 comes first.

  • Official documentation: Automate Premium workspace and semantic model tasks with service principals

B. Modify the XMLA Endpoint setting.

Why it is incorrect: The XMLA endpoint is already usable by the app (it currently connects to it with user credentials), and Premium Per User workspaces support read/write operations through the endpoint. Changing the endpoint mode (Read Only / Read Write) does not give the app a service account identity, so it does not solve the requirement.

  • Official documentation: Connect to a semantic model with client applications and tools by using the XMLA endpoint

C. Upgrade the workspace to Premium capacity.

Why it is incorrect: A Premium Per User workspace already provides the XMLA endpoint, and service principals can be used with it, so upgrading to a Premium capacity is not required. It would also add cost without addressing the missing app identity.

  • Official documentation: Manage Premium Per User

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named WH1.

You have source data in a CSV file that has the following fields:

  • SalesTransactionID
  • SaleDate
  • CustomerCode
  • CustomerName
  • CustomerAddress
  • ProductCode
  • ProductName
  • Quantity
  • UnitPrice

You plan to implement a star schema for the tables in WH1. The dimension tables in WH1 will implement Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD) logic.

You need to design the tables that will be used for sales transaction analysis and load the source data.

Which type of target table should you specify for the CustomerName,

CustomerCode, and SaleDate fields? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • CustomerCode: Dimension
  • CustomerName: Dimension
  • SaleDate: Dimension

Analysis: The source CSV mixes transaction-level facts (SalesTransactionID, Quantity, UnitPrice) with descriptive attributes of customers, products and dates. In a star schema the descriptive attributes go into dimension tables and the measurable events go into a fact table. The question asks only about the three fields that describe who and when, and all three belong to dimension tables.

CustomerCode = Dimension. CustomerCode is the business key of the customer. In a dimension table that implements Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD) logic, the business key is kept next to a surrogate key and the validity columns (start date, end date, current flag), so that several versions of the same customer can coexist. The fact table would only hold the surrogate key of the customer as a foreign key, never the descriptive attributes. A fact table is wrong because the code is not a numeric measure. A factless fact table records events or coverage with only foreign keys and is not where a business key is stored. A junk dimension groups unrelated low-cardinality flags and indicators, which does not describe a customer.

  • Official documentation: Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse: Dimension tables

CustomerName = Dimension. CustomerName (together with CustomerAddress) is a descriptive attribute that can change over time. Type 2 SCD is precisely the technique for preserving the history of such attributes by inserting a new row in the dimension when a tracked attribute changes. That requirement only makes sense in a dimension table. Storing the name in the fact table would duplicate it on every sale and break history tracking. It is not a junk dimension (that is for miscellaneous flags such as payment type or order status) and not a factless fact.

  • Official documentation: Implement slowly changing dimensions - Design dimensional models in Microsoft Fabric and Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric

SaleDate = Dimension. A date is the classic role-playing dimension in a star schema. Rather than keeping the raw date in the fact table, you load a date dimension (year, quarter, month, day of week, fiscal period...) and the fact table keeps a key that references it. This makes time-based analysis possible (by month, by quarter, year-over-year) without computing those attributes in every query. A date is not a measure, so Fact is wrong, and it is a standard dimension rather than a junk dimension. Note that the date dimension is normally not an SCD, because dates do not change.

  • Official documentation: Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse: Dimension tables and Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse: Fact tables
