q122.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You are creating a Fabric Data Factory pipeline.

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Lookup

Why it is correct: The Lookup activity in a Fabric Data Factory pipeline can run a stored procedure against a data source such as a warehouse and return the result set to the pipeline. The output (for example @activity('Lookup1').output.firstRow.ActiveCustomers) can then be referenced by any downstream activity, such as a Set variable, an If Condition or a Copy data activity. Since the stored procedure returns the number of active customers and the average sales and these values must be consumed later in the pipeline, Lookup is the activity designed for that purpose.

  • Official documentation: Use the Lookup activity to look up data from a data source - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Get metadata

Why it is incorrect: Get Metadata retrieves metadata about data (for example the structure, size, last modified date or existence of a file, folder or table). It does not execute a stored procedure or return the rows that a procedure produces.

  • Official documentation: Use the Get Metadata activity to look up data from a data source - Microsoft Fabric

B. Copy data

Why it is incorrect: Copy data moves data from a source to a destination. It can use a stored procedure as a source, but its output only exposes run statistics (rows read, rows written, throughput), not the values returned by the procedure, so the downstream activities cannot consume the customer count or the average sales.

  • Official documentation: How to copy data using copy activity - Microsoft Fabric

D. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: Append variable only adds a value to an existing array variable of the pipeline. It does not connect to a warehouse and cannot execute a stored procedure. At most it could store a value that was previously retrieved by another activity.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains a fact table named FactSales that has one billion rows.

You run the following T-SQL statement.

CREATE TABLE test.FactSales AS CLONE OF dbo.FactSales;

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • A replica of dbo.FactSales is created in the test schema by copying the metadata only: Yes
  • Additional schema changes to dbo.FactSales will also apply to test.FactSales: No
  • Additional data changes to dbo.FactSales will also apply to test.FactSales: No

Analysis: CREATE TABLE test.FactSales AS CLONE OF dbo.FactSales; creates a zero-copy clone of the table in the Fabric warehouse. The statement is fast even for a table with one billion rows because it does not copy data files.

Statement 1, Yes. A table clone is created by copying only the metadata of the source table. The clone points to the same underlying Parquet files in OneLake, so no data is physically duplicated and no extra storage is consumed at creation time. The clone can be placed in a different schema of the same warehouse, which is what happens here (test schema).

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse

Statement 2, No. After the clone is created, it is an independent table. DDL changes applied later to dbo.FactSales (adding a column, for instance) are not propagated to test.FactSales, and the same is true in the other direction.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse

Statement 3, No. Data changes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) made to the source after the clone is created are not reflected in the clone, and changes to the clone do not affect the source. Existing data files are shared until one of the tables is modified; new or rewritten files then belong only to the table that was changed. This is why a clone is useful for testing, backups and point-in-time analysis, and it is not a replication or synchronization mechanism.

  • Official documentation: Tutorial: Clone a table using T-SQL in Microsoft Fabric

You have an Amazon Web Services (AWS) subscription that contains an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket named bucket1.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named LH1.

In LH1, you plan to create a OneLake shortcut to bucket1.

You need to configure authentication for the connection.

Which two values should you provide? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: the secret access key
  • Option D: the access key ID

Why it is correct: An Amazon S3 shortcut in OneLake authenticates with the credentials of an AWS IAM user. When you create the connection in the lakehouse you provide the bucket URL (in the format https://BucketName.s3.RegionCode.amazonaws.com) and the IAM user's access key ID and secret access key. These two values together act as the user name and password for AWS programmatic access. The IAM user needs at least read and list permissions on the bucket (for example s3:GetObject, s3:GetBucketLocation and s3:ListBucket).

  • Official documentation: Create an Amazon S3 shortcut - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. the shared access signature (SAS) token

Why it is incorrect: SAS tokens are an Azure Storage concept (for Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 or Blob Storage). AWS S3 does not use them.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts - Microsoft Fabric

C. the access ID

Why it is incorrect: "Access ID" is not the name of an AWS credential. The identifier of an IAM user's key pair is the access key ID, which is option D. The S3 connection dialog asks for the access key ID and the secret access key.

  • Official documentation: Create an Amazon S3 shortcut - Microsoft Fabric

E. the certificate thumbprint

Why it is incorrect: A certificate thumbprint belongs to certificate-based authentication of service principals in Microsoft Entra ID. The S3 shortcut does not support it.

  • Official documentation: Create an Amazon S3 shortcut - Microsoft Fabric

q125.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a data warehouse.

You need to load rows into a large Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD). The solution must minimize resource usage.

Which T-SQL statement should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: UPDATE AND INSERT

Why it is correct: A Type 2 slowly changing dimension keeps history: when a tracked attribute changes you close the current row (set the end date and the current flag to false) with an UPDATE and add a new version of the row with an INSERT. Applying only the changed or new rows with these two statements touches the minimum amount of data in a large dimension, which minimizes resource usage and preserves history. In the Fabric warehouse the MERGE statement is listed among the T-SQL limitations of the surface area (it was not available), so the supported pattern is the combination of UPDATE and INSERT statements.

  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area - Microsoft Fabric and Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse: Load tables
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. MERGE

Why it is incorrect: MERGE is the statement many people would use for SCD loads in SQL Server, but the T-SQL surface area of Fabric Data Warehouse lists it as a limitation (not supported), so it is not an available choice for this scenario.

  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area - Microsoft Fabric

C. TRUNCATE TABLE and INSERT

Why it is incorrect: Truncating the dimension and reloading it removes all the historical versions, which defeats the purpose of Type 2 SCD. It also reprocesses the whole large table on each load, which maximizes resource usage rather than minimizing it.

  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric

D. CREATE TABLE AS SELECT

Why it is incorrect: CTAS creates a new table from a query result. Rebuilding the entire dimension this way rewrites all the data on every load and loses the history that cannot be recomputed from the current source. It is a bulk transformation tool, not an incremental load technique.

  • Official documentation: Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse: Load tables

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: spark.read.format("delta").load("Tables/ResearchProduct")

Why it is correct: The case study says that Lakehouse1 (in Productline1ws) contains a shortcut named ResearchProduct pointing to the Delta data in storage1, and that all Research data in the lakehouses must be presented as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer. A shortcut that points to a Delta table is created directly under the Tables folder of the lakehouse, so it is shown as a table named ResearchProduct. Its relative path in the lakehouse is therefore Tables/ResearchProduct, and in a Fabric notebook you read it with spark.read.format("delta").load("Tables/ResearchProduct").

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. spark.sql("SELECT * FROM Lakehouse1.Tables.ResearchProduct")

Why it is incorrect: In Spark SQL a lakehouse table is referenced as Lakehouse1.ResearchProduct (or as schema.table). The Tables folder is part of the file path, not of the table name, so Lakehouse1.Tables.ResearchProduct is not a valid identifier.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse and Delta tables - Microsoft Fabric

B. spark.read.format("delta").load("Tables/productline1/ResearchProduct")

Why it is incorrect: The case does not define a productline1 subfolder or schema. The shortcut is called ResearchProduct and it is located directly in Tables. Loading from Tables/productline1/ResearchProduct would fail because that path does not exist.

C. external_table(ResearchProduct)

Why it is incorrect: external_table() is a KQL function used in Kusto queries to read an external table defined in an eventhouse (KQL database). It is not a Spark syntax and cannot be used in a notebook to read a lakehouse shortcut, and the requirement is explicitly to use Fabric notebooks.

You create new tables in LH1.

options: Disable Query Caching for the default semantic model.
From the settings pane of LH1, enable Sync the default Power BI semantic model.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: From the settings pane of LH1, enable Sync the default Power BI semantic model.

Why it is correct: Each lakehouse has a default semantic model. In the lakehouse settings there is a Default Power BI semantic model section with the option Sync the default Power BI semantic model. When it is enabled, tables that you create in the lakehouse (and the changes to them) are automatically added to the default semantic model, so you do not have to add them manually from the SQL analytics endpoint or the semantic model.

answer.incorrect:

A. Disable Query Caching for the default semantic model.

C. Enable Refresh for the default semantic model.

Why it is incorrect: Refresh reloads or reframes data of the tables that are already part of the model. It does not add new tables to the model. The metadata sync of new lakehouse tables is controlled by the sync setting.

D. From the Endorsement and discovery settings of LH1, select Make discoverable.

Why it is incorrect: Make discoverable lets users find the item in the OneLake catalog/data hub even if they have no access yet. It is a governance feature unrelated to the contents of the default semantic model.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: Adding user objects to the list of synced objects in Microsoft Entra Connect does not change what the USERNAME() function returns, so the solution does not meet the goal. USERNAME() is a DAX information function that reports the identity of the user who is running the query in the current context; it does not look anything up in a directory and it has no dependency on which AD DS object types are in the Entra Connect sync scope. The scenario already says that contoso.com syncs with the Microsoft Entra tenant, so the people who sign in to the Fabric service already have identities in the tenant. A blank result is therefore not fixed by widening the sync scope. If the requirement is explicitly to return the user principal name (UPN), DAX provides a dedicated function, USERPRINCIPALNAME(), whose purpose is exactly that, and the dynamic RLS pattern in Power BI is normally built on the UPN of the signed-in user matched against a column or mapping table in the model.

Changing the sync configuration is an identity-infrastructure change in the on-premises/Entra layer; it is not a change to the semantic model measure, which is where the behavior the question complains about lives.

It does not: the value produced by USERNAME() depends on how the function is evaluated for the querying principal, not on the list of objects that Entra Connect synchronizes, and in this scenario the AD DS domain already syncs with the tenant. To obtain the UPN deterministically you use USERPRINCIPALNAME() in the model's DAX, which is the function designed to return the UPN.

You define sas_token as a variable in the first cell of Notebook1 and store a shared access signature (SAS) token in the variable.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • customers is a pandas DataFrame: No
  • If a delta table named Customers does NOT exist, an error will be generated: No
  • The source data is located in the customers folder in a container named contacts: Yes

Statement 1: "customers is a pandas DataFrame" is No. spark.read.parquet(...) is a method of the SparkSession reader and it returns a Spark DataFrame (pyspark.sql.DataFrame), which is distributed and lazily evaluated. It is not a pandas DataFrame. A pandas DataFrame would only appear if the code used pandas.read_parquet or called .toPandas() on the Spark DataFrame. The follow-on code, customers.write.format("delta")..., is the Spark DataFrameWriter API, which a pandas DataFrame does not have. The Fabric documentation distinguishes the Spark API (used to write Delta tables) from the Pandas API (which works through the default lakehouse mount point).

  • Official documentation: Use a notebook to load data into your lakehouse

Statement 2: "If a delta table named Customers does NOT exist, an error will be generated" is No. saveAsTable("Customers") with .format("delta") and .mode("overwrite") creates the table when it does not exist and replaces its contents when it does. The write mode overwrite does not require a pre-existing target (an error on a missing target would be the behavior of an UPDATE/MERGE or of insertInto, not of saveAsTable). In a Fabric lakehouse Delta is also the default table format, so the table is created in the Tables section of the default lakehouse. The "error" alternative would only be true for the errorifexists mode when the table does exist, which is the opposite case.

  • Official documentation: Use a notebook to load data into your lakehouse and Lakehouse and Delta Lake tables

Statement 3: "The source data is located in the customers folder in a container named contacts" is Yes. The path wasbs://contacts@contoso.blob.core.windows.net/customers?{sas_token} follows the pattern wasbs://<container>@<storage account>.blob.core.windows.net/<path>. The part before the @ is the container (contacts), the host is the storage account contoso, and /customers is the folder (path) inside the container. The ?{sas_token} suffix is the shared access signature appended as the query string to authorize access; it is not part of the folder name. The f-string substitutes the token stored in the sas_token variable defined in the first cell. So the data is read from the customers folder of the contacts container.

  • Official documentation: Use a notebook to load data into your lakehouse (Spark read/write of Parquet and Delta in a notebook).

q133.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named DW1 and a

lakehouse named LH1. DW1 contains a table named Sales.Product. LH1 contains a table named Sales.Orders.

You plan to schedule an automated process that will create a new point-in-time (PIT) table named Sales.ProductOrder in DW1. Sales.ProductOrder will be built by using the results of a query that will join Sales.Product and Sales.Orders. You need to ensure that the types of columns in Sales.ProductOrder match the column types in the source tables. The solution must minimize the number of operations required to create the new table.

Which operation should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS)

Why it is correct: The requirements are: create a new table Sales.ProductOrder in the warehouse DW1, populate it with the result of a query that joins a warehouse table (Sales.Product) with a lakehouse table (Sales.Orders), have the column types match the source types, and use as few operations as possible. CTAS does everything in a single statement: it creates the destination table and loads it with the query result, and the column names and data types of the new table are derived from the SELECT result, so they match the source columns (you only cast when you need a different type). From a warehouse you can reference a lakehouse in the same workspace with a three-part name (LH1.Sales.Orders), so the join between DW1.Sales.Product and LH1.Sales.Orders is possible within the CTAS query. Because it is a plain T-SQL statement it can also be scheduled (for example in a data pipeline) to rebuild the point-in-time table.

  • Official documentation: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (Transact-SQL) and Ingest data into your Warehouse using Transact-SQL
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. INSERT INTO

Why it is incorrect: INSERT INTO ... SELECT only appends rows to a table that already exists. You would first have to run a CREATE TABLE statement defining every column and data type manually (an extra operation, and a chance of mismatching the source types) and then the INSERT. That is two operations instead of one, and the requirement is to minimize them. INSERT is the right tool for incremental loads into a table whose schema you control, not for creating the table.

  • Official documentation: Ingest data into your Warehouse using Transact-SQL / Create tables in Fabric Data Warehouse

C. CREATE TABLE AS CLONE OF

Why it is incorrect: A table clone creates a zero-copy copy of one existing table as of a point in time. It cannot take the result of a query, so it cannot join Sales.Product and Sales.Orders, and it cannot clone a lakehouse table into the warehouse in that way. The requirement is a new table built from a join, which a clone cannot express. (The "point-in-time" wording in the question is about the content being a snapshot of the query result, not about the clone feature.)

  • Official documentation: Tables in data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric (table-creation options available in the warehouse).

D. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW AS SELECT

Why it is incorrect: The question asks for a table (a point-in-time table) whose data is physically created by an automated process. A materialized view is a view object, not a table, and the supported way to create a table from a query result in a Fabric warehouse is CTAS. A view would also not produce a static point-in-time snapshot the way a scheduled CTAS does.

  • Official documentation: Tables in data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric / CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (Transact-SQL)

You have a Fabric tenant that contains the semantic model shown in the following exhibit.

Use the drop-down menus to select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented in the graphic.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Querying SQL views from the warehouse of the model will cause a fallback to [answer choice] mode: DirectQuery
  • Row and column security is [answer choice]: undefined

Box 1: DirectQuery. In a Direct Lake semantic model on SQL analytics endpoints, queries stay in Direct Lake mode only if the model does not reference tables that are based on unmaterialized SQL views. Direct Lake reads Delta/Parquet files from OneLake, and a view has no files of its own; when a query touches one, the engine falls back to DirectQuery, sending the query to the SQL analytics endpoint of the warehouse. That is what "fallback" means in Direct Lake: the only mode it falls back to is DirectQuery. Automatic is not a storage mode but one of the values of the Direct Lake behavior property that decides whether fallback is allowed, and Direct Lake is the mode being left, not the destination. The remedy documented by Microsoft is to materialize the view as a Delta table.

Note about the exhibit: the model's Direct Lake behavior is set to Direct Lake Only, which disables fallback, so in practice such a query would fail with an error instead of silently switching. The question nevertheless asks which mode a fallback goes to, and the answer is DirectQuery.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the exhibit shows Direct Lake behavior set to "Direct Lake Only", which disables fallback, so a query hitting an unmaterialized SQL view would fail with an error instead of falling back (see the linked Direct Lake documentation). It could therefore be argued that box 1 should read "Direct Lake". DirectQuery is the expected answer because it is the only mode a fallback can go to, and the question is worded imprecisely. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview / how Direct Lake works (fallback and views) and Analyze query processing for Direct Lake

Box 2: undefined. In the Model pane of the exhibit, Roles (0) shows that no role exists in the semantic model, so no row-level security (RLS) filters and no column/object-level security (OLS) permissions are defined at the model level. Nothing in the graphic shows RLS or OLS configuration, so the only supportable choice is "undefined". "configured to use OLS" and "configured to use RLS" would require at least one role carrying table/column permissions or row filters. (Security enforced in the warehouse SQL analytics endpoint would be a separate, SQL-level configuration that the exhibit does not show.)

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI and Direct Lake overview

q135.stem:
Note: This section contains one or more sets of questions with the same scenario and problem. Each question presents a unique solution to the problem. You must determine whether the solution meets the stated goals.

More than one solution in the set might solve the problem. It is also possible that none of the solutions in the set solve the problem.

After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return. As a result, these questions do not appear on the Review Screen.

Your network contains an on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) domain named contoso.com that syncs with a Microsoft Entra tenant by using Microsoft Entra Connect.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model.

You enable dynamic row-level security (RLS) for the model and deploy the model to the Fabric service.

You query a measure that includes the USERNAME() function, and the query returns a blank result.

You need to ensure that the measure returns the user principal name (UPN) of a user.

Solution: You create a role in the model.

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: Creating a role in the model does not change what a USERNAME() measure returns. A role in a semantic model is a container for RLS filter expressions and for table/column permissions, and it is evaluated only to restrict which rows or objects the members of that role can see. A measure that calls USERNAME() simply returns the identity of the user running the query; the existence of a role does not alter how that identity is presented, so the blank result is not resolved, and the measure still does not become a function that returns the UPN. The dedicated DAX function for the UPN is USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Roles are the second half of dynamic RLS (the role filter uses USERPRINCIPALNAME() or USERNAME() to compare to a column), not a way to change the function's result.

  • Official documentation: USERNAME function (DAX) and Configure row-level security with the dynamic method
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Yes

Why it is incorrect: Defining a role only adds filter expressions and permissions for the members of the role. It does not change the value returned by USERNAME() in a measure, and it does not convert that value to the UPN. The scenario already enabled dynamic RLS, and the measure still returns blank, so adding a role does not meet the goal; you would replace or complement the expression with USERPRINCIPALNAME().

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI / USERPRINCIPALNAME function (DAX)

q136.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains two workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2 and a user named User1.

You need to ensure that User1 can perform the following tasks:

  • Create a new domain.
  • Create two subdomains named subdomain1 and subdomain2.
  • Assign Workspace1 to subdomain1.
  • Assign Workspace2 to subdomain2.

The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.

Which role should you assign to User1?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Fabric admin

Why it is correct: The first task is to create a new domain, and in Microsoft Fabric only a Fabric admin (tenant-level admin role) can create domains. The documentation states this explicitly: "To create domain, you must be a Fabric admin." The other tasks are also covered by this role: creating subdomains is allowed to Fabric admins (and to the domain admins of the parent domain) and assigning workspaces to a domain or subdomain is available in the admin portal to Fabric admins and domain admins. Since the single role that satisfies all four tasks, including the creation of the domain itself, is Fabric admin, it is also the least-privileged choice that works. A domain admin could manage subdomains and workspace assignments of a domain, but only after a Fabric admin had created that domain, so it cannot cover the first requirement.

  • Official documentation: Fabric domains and Administration overview
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. domain admin

Why it is incorrect: Domain admins can create subdomains, associate workspaces with the domain and define domain contributors, but only for domains they administer, and a domain admin cannot create the domain itself (the role is assigned to a domain that a Fabric admin has created). Because the user must be able to create a new domain, this role is insufficient. This is a tempting choice, but it fails on the first requirement.

  • Official documentation: Fabric domains (roles and permissions)

B. domain contributor

Why it is incorrect: A domain contributor is a workspace admin who has been authorized to assign their own workspaces to a domain (or change an existing assignment) from the workspace settings. Contributors cannot create domains or subdomains and do not have access to the Domains tab in the admin portal.

  • Official documentation: Fabric domains (domain contributors) / Domains best practices

D. workspace Admin

Why it is incorrect: Workspace Admin is a role inside a single workspace. It controls the items and membership of that workspace, but it has no authority over the tenant-level domain structure: it cannot create domains or subdomains, and it can only assign the workspace to a domain if it is also authorized as a domain contributor.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric

You have a Fabric tenant that contains three users named User1, User2, and User3. The tenant contains a security group named Group1. User1 and User3 are members of Group1.

The tenant contains the workspaces shown in the following table.

The tenant contains the domains shown in the following table.

User1 creates a new workspace named Workspace3.

You assign Domain1 as the default domain of Group1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • User2 is assigned the Contributor role for Workspace3: No
  • User3 is assigned the Viewer role for Workspace3: No
  • User3 is assigned the Contributor role for Workspace1: No

Statement 1: No. User1 creates Workspace3, so User1 is the workspace Admin of Workspace3 (the creator becomes Admin). Nothing in the scenario grants User2 any role in Workspace3. User2 is Admin of Workspace2 and of Domain2, but a role in another workspace, or a domain role, does not carry over to a different workspace. Workspace roles are assigned per workspace.

Statement 2: No. User3 is a member of Group1, and Domain1 is made the default domain of Group1. The default domain only controls the domain assignment of workspaces created by members of the group (a new workspace created by User1, a member of Group1, is assigned to Domain1 automatically) and makes those users domain contributors for those workspaces. It does not add User3 to the access list of Workspace3. Domain assignment and workspace access are independent: workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) must be granted explicitly in the workspace.

Statement 3: No. User1 is the Admin of Workspace1 and no role is given to User3 on that workspace. Being a member of Group1 or having Domain1 as default domain does not grant a workspace role. "Domain contributor" is a domain-level capability to assign workspaces to a domain, not the workspace Contributor role.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric and Fabric domains (default domain and domain contributors)

q138.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse named Warehouse1 that contains a table named Table1. Table1 contains customer data.

You need to implement row-level security (RLS) for Table1. The solution must ensure that users can see only their respective data.

Which two objects should you create? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: FUNCTION
  • Option E: SECURITY POLICY

Why it is correct: Row-level security in a Fabric warehouse is implemented with two T-SQL objects. First, a predicate function, an inline table-valued function (CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS TABLE) that contains the filtering logic, for example comparing a column of the row with USER_NAME() so that each user only qualifies for their own rows. Second, a security policy (CREATE SECURITY POLICY ... ADD FILTER PREDICATE ... ON <table>) that binds the function to Table1 and turns enforcement on. Together they make each user see only their respective customer rows. The function defines which rows are allowed and the security policy defines where and when the predicate is applied.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security in Fabric data warehousing and CREATE SECURITY POLICY (Transact-SQL)
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. DATABASE ROLE

Why it is incorrect: A database role groups principals so that permissions can be granted to them together. It is not part of the RLS mechanism: the Fabric documentation example needs only a predicate function and a security policy, and "users see only their own data" is achieved by the predicate comparing the row to the querying user. Roles can complement RLS (for example to grant SELECT) but are not one of the two required objects.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security in Fabric data warehousing

B. STORED PROCEDURE

Why it is incorrect: A stored procedure is a callable routine, and a user could simply bypass it by querying the table directly. RLS filter predicates must be inline table-valued functions bound through a security policy, so a stored procedure cannot act as the predicate.

  • Official documentation: CREATE SECURITY POLICY (Transact-SQL)

C. CONSTRAINT

Why it is incorrect: Constraints (CHECK, PRIMARY KEY, and so on) enforce data integrity on data that is written; they do not filter the rows that a user reads. A constraint therefore cannot limit each user to their own rows. Row-level access is enforced by a security policy.

  • Official documentation: Implement row-level security (Secure a Microsoft Fabric data warehouse)

q139.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Lakehouse1 contains a table named Table1. Table1 contains the following data.

You need to perform the following actions:

  • Load the data from Table1 into a star schema.
  • Create a product dimension table named DimProduct and a fact table named FactSales.

Which three columns should you include in DimProduct?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: ProductColor, ProductID, and ProductName.

Why it is correct: In a star schema, a dimension table describes a business entity (here, the product) and holds a unique key plus descriptive attributes used to filter and group, while a fact table stores the events or observations (the transactions) with the foreign keys to the dimensions and the numeric measures. In Table1, the product entity is described by ProductID (the unique key), ProductName and ProductColor (descriptive attributes). Those three columns therefore belong in DimProduct. TransactionID, Date (which would normally link to a date dimension) and SalesAmount (the measure) belong in FactSales, together with ProductID as the foreign key to DimProduct.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. ProductName, SalesAmount, and TransactionID.

Why it is incorrect: SalesAmount is a numeric measure and TransactionID identifies each transaction, so both are fact-level columns that describe events. Putting them in the product dimension would mix grain and would leave DimProduct without its unique key ProductID.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

C. Date, ProductID, and TransactionID.

Why it is incorrect: Date and TransactionID are attributes of the transaction (the fact grain), not of the product. This set would describe a fact table, and it contains no descriptive product attributes.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

D. ProductID, ProductName, and SalesAmount

Why it is incorrect: It correctly includes the key and the name, but SalesAmount is a measure that varies for each transaction. In a dimension it would not be unique per product and it would not be summarized from the fact table. The product color, a real descriptive attribute, is the column that should be there instead.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

q140.stem:
-

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a Dataflow Gen2 query. The query returns the following data.

You need to filter the results to ensure that only the latest version of each customer’s record is retained. The solution must ensure that no new columns are loaded to the semantic model.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence in Power Query Editor? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Group by CustomerID and calculate the max version date per customer ID.
  • Step 2: Filter the query where the version date value equals the max version date value.
  • Step 3: Remove duplicates based on CustomerID.
  • Step 4: Remove the max version date column.

Why this order: The goal is to keep only the latest version of each customer's record, and the result must not load any new column to the semantic model.

  1. Group by CustomerID and calculate the max version date per customer ID. This is the first step because the latest version has to be known per customer. The grouping computes the maximum VersionDate for each CustomerID, which provides the reference value (the "max version date") against which every record can be compared.
  2. Filter the query where the version date value equals the max version date value. After the max is available next to each record, a filter that compares VersionDate with the max keeps only the newest row of each customer and discards the older versions. Filtering must come after the aggregate exists, which is why it cannot be first.
  3. Remove duplicates based on CustomerID. If two rows of a customer share the same latest timestamp, the filter keeps both; removing duplicates on CustomerID guarantees a single row per customer.
  4. Remove the max version date column. The helper column created in step 1 is only needed to filter. The requirement says that no new columns may be loaded to the semantic model, so it has to be removed at the end, after it has been used.

Why the other actions are not in the answer: the All Rows variant of the grouping and Expand the All Rows detail column are an alternative route (group by with All Rows, then expand) that adds extra steps and nested tables; the selected path uses the simple max aggregation instead. Also, "Remove the max version date column" must come last: if it were removed before the filter, the filter would have nothing to compare with.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this sequence, but a plain Group by in Power Query returns only CustomerID and the max column, so the filter step would not work exactly as described. A technically sound pattern is Group by with All Rows plus the max, filter, expand the All Rows column, and remove the max column (or sort and remove duplicates). Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: For the modelling context (keeping one current row per entity in a dimension) see Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

links.t: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

q141.stem:
-

You have a Microsoft Power Bl project that contains a file named definition.pbir. definition.pbir contains the following JSON.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • definition.pbir is in the PBIR-Legacy format: No
  • The semantic model referenced by definition.pbir is located in the Power BI service: No
  • When the related report is opened, Power BI Desktop will open the semantic model in full edit mode: Yes

Statement 1 - "definition.pbir is in the PBIR-Legacy format": No. The definition.pbir file is the entry-point file of a Power BI Desktop project report: it holds the overall report settings and the pointer to the semantic model. The file itself is part of the current PBIR project structure and is not a "legacy" artifact; the format (PBIR-Legacy or PBIR) is determined by how the report definition is stored next to it, in a report.json file or in the definition folder. The version property controls which report definition formats are allowed: with "version": "1.0" (as in the exhibit) the report definition must be stored as PBIR-Legacy in a report.json file, whereas version 4.0 or higher allows either PBIR-Legacy (report.json) or PBIR (the definition folder).

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop project report folder - definition.pbir

Statement 2 - "The semantic model referenced is located in the Power BI service": No. The datasetReference contains "byPath": { "path": "../Sales.Dataset" } and "byConnection": null. A byPath reference is a relative path to a semantic model folder that lives next to the report folder in the same project (here, the Sales.Dataset folder). A model located in the Power BI service / a Fabric workspace would be referenced with byConnection and a connection string (for example semanticmodelid=...). Because byConnection is null, the model is local, not in the service.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop project report folder - datasetReference (byPath / byConnection)

Statement 3 - "Power BI Desktop will open the semantic model in full edit mode": Yes. The documentation states that when a byPath reference is used, opening the .pbir file in Power BI Desktop also opens the semantic model alongside the report, in full edit mode, so you can edit report and model together. In contrast, with a byConnection reference Power BI Desktop opens the report as a live connection and does not open the model in edit mode.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the documentation says that "version": "1.0" in definition.pbir requires the report definition to be stored as PBIR-Legacy (report.json), so "Yes" for statement 1 could also be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop project report folder - byPath behavior
  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects overview

q142.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

You plan to deploy a semantic model named Model1 by using the XMLA

endpoint.

You need to optimize the deployment of Model1. The solution must minimize how long it takes to deploy Model1.

What should you do in Workspace1?
options: Select Small semantic model storage format.
Select Users can edit data models in the Power BI service.
Set Enable Cache for Shortcuts to On.
Select Large semantic model storage format.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Select Large semantic model storage format.

Why it is correct: The Large semantic model storage format uses a different, more efficient storage and write path (segment-based, on-demand loading) designed for big models. Microsoft documents that when it is enabled, XMLA write operations (such as deploying or refreshing through tools that use the XMLA endpoint) are faster, and it recommends enabling it whenever you plan to use XMLA-based tools for write operations, even if the model is not strictly "large". Since the requirement is to minimize deployment time through the XMLA endpoint, enabling the Large format in the workspace/model settings is the right action.

  • Official documentation: Large semantic models in Power BI Premium
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Select Small semantic model storage format.

Why it is incorrect: The small storage format is the default and it does not give the XMLA write-performance benefit of the large format. It also caps models at a limited size. Choosing it would not minimize deployment time.

  • Official documentation: Large semantic models in Power BI Premium

B. Select Users can edit data models in the Power BI service.

Why it is incorrect: This workspace setting enables web-based data modeling for users (editing the model in the browser). It is a permission/authoring feature and has no effect on how fast a deployment through the XMLA endpoint runs.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model modes in the Power BI service

C. Set Enable Cache for Shortcuts to On.

Why it is incorrect: Caching for OneLake shortcuts reduces egress cost and latency when reading external shortcut data (for example, S3 or GCS). It does not influence the deployment of a semantic model metadata/definition through XMLA.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts

q143.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI project that contains a semantic model.

You plan to use Azure DevOps for version control.

You need to modify the .gitignore file to prevent the data values from the data sources from being pushed to the repository.

Which file should you reference?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: cache.abf

Why it is correct: In a Power BI Desktop project (PBIP), the semantic model folder contains a cache.abf file: an Analysis Services backup (ABF) file with a local cached copy of the model and its data as of the last edit. It is the only file in the list that stores the actual data values loaded from the data sources, and the documentation says it should be included in .gitignore (or other source-control exclusions); Git ignores it by default in the generated .gitignore. Excluding it keeps data out of the Azure DevOps repository and avoids large binary files. The localSettings.json file only holds user/computer-specific settings, not data.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but localSettings.json is also excluded from source control by default and could be argued; only cache.abf, however, holds data values, while localSettings.json holds just user/computer-specific settings. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop project semantic model folder - cache.abf
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. unappliedChanges.json

Why it is incorrect: It stores Power Query changes that you saved with "Apply later" (unfinished query work). It is part of the model definition and is saved in Git by default; excluding it is optional and only done to avoid affecting other developers. It contains no data values.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop project semantic model folder - unappliedChanges.json

C. localSettings.json

Why it is incorrect: It contains semantic model settings that apply only to the current user and computer. It should indeed be excluded from source control (and is ignored by default), but its reason is that the settings are personal, not that it holds data values. The file that holds the data is cache.abf.

D. model.bim

Why it is incorrect: model.bim is the TMSL definition of the model (metadata: tables, columns, measures, relationships), available when the project is saved in TMSL format. It is the artifact you want to version in Git and it does not contain the data values.

To make Model1 accessible through XMLA you must change the workspace License mode (called workspace type in newer UI) to Premium per-user, Premium capacity or a Fabric capacity (also making sure the capacity's XMLA Endpoint setting is Read Write if you need write operations). You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named LH1.

You need to deploy a new semantic model. The solution must meet the

following requirements:

  • Support complex calculated columns that include aggregate functions, calculated tables, and Multidimensional Expressions (MDX) user hierarchies.
  • Minimize page rendering times.

How should you configure the model? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Mode: Import
  • Query Caching: On

Mode - Import. The requirements are calculated columns that use aggregate functions, calculated tables and MDX user hierarchies. Import mode keeps the data in the in-memory VertiPaq engine and supports the full set of DAX modeling features, including calculated columns, calculated tables and user hierarchies. Direct Lake is the wrong choice here: a Direct Lake table cannot have calculated columns/tables that reference Direct Lake columns, and Direct Lake table user-defined hierarchies are not supported (the documented limitations). DirectQuery also restricts calculated columns and tables (and sends queries to the source, making rendering slower), so it fails the performance requirement as well.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - considerations and limitations
  • Official documentation: Semantic model modes in the Power BI service

Query Caching - On. Query caching lets the capacity keep query results locally, so the initial page of a report opens faster and the data source does less work. It is available for Import semantic models on Premium/Fabric capacities. Setting it to On explicitly turns the feature on for this model, which supports the goal of minimizing page rendering times. Off disables it, and Capacity default is "Off" unless the capacity admin changed it, so neither guarantees the benefit.

  • Official documentation: Query caching in Power BI Premium

q147.stem:
-

You have the following KQL query.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • The query excludes sales that have a Status of Cancelled: Yes
  • The query calculates the total sales of each product category for the last 30 days: Yes
  • The query includes product categories that have had zero sales during the last 30 days: No

Statement 1 - Yes. | where Status != "Cancelled" is a filter predicate: only rows whose Status is different from "Cancelled" continue down the pipeline, so cancelled sales are excluded before aggregation.

Statement 2 - Yes. where OrderDate >= ago(30d) keeps only orders from the last 30 days, and summarize TotalSales = sum(SalesAmount) by ProductCategory groups the remaining rows by category and sums SalesAmount. The result is therefore the total sales per product category for the last 30 days (excluding cancelled ones).

Statement 3 - No. summarize ... by only produces groups that exist in the input rows. A category with no sales in the last 30 days has no rows after the where filters, so it never appears in the output. Furthermore, the final | where TotalSales > 0 removes any group whose total is zero or negative, which would also remove categories whose sales net to zero. Both effects mean zero-sales categories are not included.

  • Official documentation: KQL quick reference (where, summarize, ago)

q148.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named SalesOrderDetail, SalesOrderDetail contains three columns named OrderQty, ProductID and SalesOrderlD. SalesOrderDetail contains one row per combination of

SalesOrderlD and ProductID.

You need to calculate the proportion of the total quantity of each sales order represented by each product within the sales order.

Which T-SQL statement should you run?
options:
SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(PARTITION BY ProductID) * 100
  AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(ORDER BY SalesOrderID) * 100
  AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(ORDER BY ProductID) * 100
  AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(PARTITION BY SalesOrderID) * 100
  AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: the statement that computes SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY SalesOrderID)
SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY SalesOrderID) * 100
   AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProduct
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

Why it is correct: The goal is the share of each product's quantity within its own sales order. The window function SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY SalesOrderID) returns, on every row, the total quantity of that order (rows are not collapsed, as they would be with GROUP BY). Dividing the row's OrderQty by that total (multiplying by 1. forces decimal division instead of integer division) and by 100 gives the percentage each product represents within the order. Partitioning by SalesOrderID restarts the total for every order.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - OVER clause (Transact-SQL)
  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductID)

Why it is incorrect: It partitions by product, so the denominator is the total quantity of that product across all orders. The result is each order line's share of the product's total, not the product's share of its order.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - OVER clause (Transact-SQL)

B. SUM(OrderQty) OVER (ORDER BY SalesOrderID)

Why it is incorrect: With no PARTITION BY, the whole result set is a single partition, and with an ORDER BY the aggregate becomes a running (cumulative) total ordered by SalesOrderID. The denominator would be a growing cumulative quantity across orders, not the order's total.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - OVER clause (Transact-SQL)

C. SUM(OrderQty) OVER (ORDER BY ProductID)

Why it is incorrect: Same problem as B, ordered by ProductID: a running total over the whole table rather than the total per sales order.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - OVER clause (Transact-SQL)

q149.stem: Which syntax should you use in a notebook to access the Research division data for Productline1?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

Why it is correct: The case says that in Productline1ws a lakehouse named Lakehouse1 is created with a shortcut to storage1 named ResearchProduct, that the data is in delta format, that all Research data in the lakehouses must appear as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer, and that notebooks must be used. A shortcut that points to Delta data is created at the top level of the Tables section, so it is recognized as a table. From a notebook with Lakehouse1 as default lakehouse, the relative path Tables/ResearchProduct plus the delta format reads it. Shortcuts under Tables can only be created at the top level, so there is no sub-folder.

B. spark.read.format("delta").load("Files/ResearchProduct")

C. spark.sql("SELECT * FROM Lakehouse1.productline1.ResearchProduct")

Why it is incorrect: It addresses a schema named productline1, but the case describes no schema in Lakehouse1 (productline1 is only the product line name; the shortcut is ResearchProduct). Without a schema-enabled lakehouse containing that schema, the name does not resolve (tables would live in the default dbo schema).

Why it is incorrect: It adds a productline1 sub-folder that does not exist. The shortcut was created directly as ResearchProduct, and OneLake does not support shortcuts in subdirectories of Tables.

You have a Fabric lakehouse named Lakehouse1 that contains the following data.

You need build a T-SQL statement that will return the total sales amount by OrderDate only for the days that are holidays in Australia. The total sales amount must sum the quantity multiplied by the price on each row in the dbo.sales table.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Aggregate expression: Sum(s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice)
  • Join type: Inner

Aggregate expression - Sum(s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice). The total sales amount must be the sum of quantity multiplied by price per row, grouped by OrderDate. Therefore the multiplication happens inside the aggregate. s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice without SUM would be a non-aggregated expression and fail with GROUP BY s.OrderDate. Sum(s.Quantity) * s.UnitPrice multiplies a total by a single, non-grouped price column (invalid under GROUP BY and not the sum of row amounts), and Sum(s.Quantity) * Sum(s.UnitPrice) multiplies two totals, which gives a different (wrong) number.

  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse

Join type - Inner. The result must only include days that are holidays in Australia. An INNER JOIN returns only the matching pairs of rows (sales whose OrderDate equals a holiday date) and discards unmatched rows; the WHERE on countryOrRegion = 'Australia' then filters the holidays. A Cross join would produce a Cartesian product, and Full outer/Right outer keep unmatched rows (for example holidays without sales, or sales on non-holidays), which does not meet "only the days that are holidays" (and a WHERE on the nullable side would effectively behave like an inner join anyway, but the intent is the inner join).

  • Official documentation: FROM clause plus JOIN (Transact-SQL)

q151.stem:
-

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a warehouse named DW1. DW1 contains two tables named Employees and Sales. All users have read access to Dw1.

You need to implement access controls to meet the following requirements:

  • For the Sales table, ensure that the users can see only the sales data from their respective region.
  • For the Employees table, restrict access to all Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
  • Maintain access to unrestricted data for all the users.

What should you use for each table? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Employees: Column-level security
  • Sales: Row-level security (RLS)

Employees: Column-level security. The requirement is to hide the Personally Identifiable Information (PII) columns (for example name, national ID, phone, salary) while every user keeps access to the non-sensitive columns of the same table. That is exactly what column-level security (CLS) does in a Fabric warehouse: you use T-SQL GRANT SELECT ON Employees(<allowed columns>) TO <user or role> so that the PII columns are simply not included. A query that touches a restricted column fails with a "SELECT permission was denied on the column" error, while queries over the permitted columns work. Because all users already have read access to DW1, CLS lets you narrow it at column granularity without creating extra views or duplicating the table.

  • Official documentation: Column-level security in Fabric data warehousing

Sales: Row-level security (RLS). Here the restriction is not about which columns are visible but about which rows: each user must see only the sales of their own region. RLS is implemented with an inline table-valued function that acts as a filter predicate (for example comparing the Region column with the user's identity or a mapping table) and a CREATE SECURITY POLICY that binds the predicate to the Sales table. The filtering is enforced in the database tier and is silent, so users still query the Sales table normally but get only the rows of their region, including from Power BI reports built on top of the warehouse.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security in Fabric data warehousing

Why the other options are wrong for both boxes:

  • Column-level security for Sales: CLS hides entire columns for a user; it cannot make a user see only the rows that belong to their region. Hiding the Region column would not filter any data.

  • Row-level security for Employees: RLS removes rows, so applying it would hide whole employees (including their non-PII data) instead of just the PII columns, which breaks the requirement to "maintain access to unrestricted data for all the users".

  • Item permissions: Item permissions (sharing the warehouse and the associated SQL permissions such as ReadData) work at the level of the whole item. They cannot restrict individual rows or columns inside a table, and all users already have read access to DW1.

  • Workspace permissions: Workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) apply to every item in the workspace and are even coarser than item permissions. They cannot separate PII columns or regional rows.

  • Official documentation: Security for data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric and Permission model - Microsoft Fabric

q152.stem:
You need to create a Microsoft Power BI file that will be used to create multiple reports. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • The file must include predefined data source connections.
  • The file must include the report structure and formatting.
  • The file must NOT contain any data.

Which file format should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: PBIT

Why it is correct: A Power BI template file (.pbit) is designed precisely for this scenario. It stores the report definition (pages, visuals, formatting, theme), the data model (tables, relationships, measures) and the queries, including the data source connections, but it does not contain any data. When someone opens the template, Power BI Desktop prompts for the required parameters or credentials and loads the data from the sources, creating a new .pbix report. That satisfies the three requirements: predefined data source connections, report structure and formatting, and no data in the file. It can be reused to create as many reports as needed.

  • Official documentation: Create and use report templates in Power BI Desktop
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. PBIDS

Why it is incorrect: A Power BI data source file (.pbids) is a small JSON file that only holds the connection information for a single data source (server, database, connection type). When opened, Power BI Desktop starts the Get Data experience against that source. It contains no report pages, visuals or formatting, so it fails the requirement to include the report structure and formatting.

  • Official documentation: Data sources in Power BI Desktop

C. PBIX

Why it is incorrect: A .pbix file is the regular Power BI Desktop file. It includes the report, the model and the connections, but it also stores the imported data (the compressed model cache). This violates the requirement that the file must not contain any data. Exporting the report as a template (.pbit) is what removes the data.

  • Official documentation: Create and use report templates in Power BI Desktop

D. PBIP

Why it is incorrect: A Power BI Project (.pbip) saves a report and a semantic model as a folder of plain-text definition files, mainly for source control, CI/CD and programmatic edits. It is a development format, not a distributable template: it is not opened by a user to spawn new reports with prompted parameters, and the project can include a local data cache that is only excluded through .gitignore. It is not the file format intended for creating multiple reports from a predefined structure.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects overview

q153.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a single semantic model that has two Microsoft Power BI reports.

You have a Microsoft 365 subscription that contains a data loss prevention (DLP) policy named DLP1.

You need to apply DLP1 to the items in Workspace1.

What should you do?
options: Apply a certified endorsement to the semantic model.
Apply sensitivity labels to the semantic model and reports.
Apply a master data endorsement to the semantic model.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Apply sensitivity labels to the semantic model and reports.

Why it is correct: Data loss prevention (DLP) policies for Fabric and Power BI are defined in the Microsoft Purview portal and evaluate items based on conditions such as sensitivity labels and sensitive information types. A policy such as DLP1 therefore takes effect on the items in Workspace1 when those items carry the label (or contain the sensitive content) that the policy's conditions target. Applying the appropriate sensitivity labels to the semantic model and to the two reports is the way to make DLP1 apply to them, and the semantic model is one of the item types that DLP policies evaluate (on publish, refresh, and so on).

  • Official documentation: Get started with data loss prevention policies for Fabric and Power BI and Information protection in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Create a workspace identity.

Why it is incorrect: A workspace identity is an automatically managed service principal that the workspace uses to authenticate to resources protected by Microsoft Entra ID, such as firewall-enabled storage accounts through trusted workspace access. It has nothing to do with Microsoft Purview DLP policies.

  • Official documentation: Workspace identity in Microsoft Fabric

B. Apply a certified endorsement to the semantic model.

Why it is incorrect: Certification is a governance badge that tells users the item is reliable and meets the organization's quality standards. It affects discoverability and trust, not security: DLP policy conditions do not use endorsement, and it only covers the semantic model, not the reports.

  • Official documentation: Endorsement overview - Microsoft Fabric

D. Apply a master data endorsement to the semantic model.

Why it is incorrect: Master data is another endorsement badge that marks an item as a core, single source of truth. Like certification, it is only a label for discovery and trust; it does not trigger or scope DLP policies.

  • Official documentation: Endorsement overview - Microsoft Fabric

q154.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1 and a user named User1. User1 is assigned the Contributor role for Workspace1.

You plan to configure Workspace1 to use an Azure DevOps repository for version control.

You need to ensure that User1 can commit items to the repository.

Which two settings should you enable for User1? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options: Users can sync workspace items with GitHub repositories
Users can create and use Data workflows
Users can synchronize workspace items with their Git repositories

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option C: Users can create Fabric items
  • Option D: Users can synchronize workspace items with their Git repositories

Why it is correct: Git integration is controlled by tenant settings, and the ones needed here are listed in the Git prerequisites. "Users can synchronize workspace items with their Git repositories" is the core switch that allows users to sync a workspace with an Azure DevOps repository (it is enabled by default and can be limited to specific security groups). "Users can create Fabric items" is also required so that users can work with Fabric items (lakehouses, warehouses, notebooks, and so on) that are saved to and committed from the repository. User1 already has the Contributor role, so the role is not the missing piece; the tenant switches must apply to User1 (for example by being a member of the security group they are scoped to).

  • Official documentation: Get started with Git integration - Microsoft Fabric and Git integration tenant settings
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Users can sync workspace items with GitHub repositories

Why it is incorrect: This switch is only needed when the workspace is connected to a GitHub repository. The scenario uses an Azure DevOps repository, so this setting is not required.

  • Official documentation: Git integration tenant settings

B. Users can create and use Data workflows

Why it is incorrect: This tenant setting relates to Data workflows (Apache Airflow-based orchestration in Data Factory). It is not part of the Git integration prerequisites, and committing items to a repository does not depend on it.

q155.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a data pipeline named Pipeline1 and a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You perform the following actions:

  • Create a workspace named Workspace2.
  • Create a deployment pipeline named DeployPipeline1 that will deploy items from Workspace1 to Workspace2.
  • Add a folder named Folder1 to Workspace1.
  • Move Lakehouse1 to Folder1.
  • Run DeployPipeline1.

Which structure will Workspace2 have when DeployPipeline1 is complete?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: \Pipeline1 \Folder1\Lakehouse1

Why it is correct: When you deploy to a stage whose workspace is empty (Workspace2 is new), deployment pipelines copy all the supported items from the source and create them in the target. Pipeline1 is in the root of Workspace1, so it is created in the root of Workspace2. Lakehouse1 was moved to Folder1 before the deployment; deployment pipelines apply the folder hierarchy of the deployed items, and if the folder does not exist in the target it is created first. Therefore Workspace2 ends up with \Pipeline1 and \Folder1\Lakehouse1. Folder structure is only deployed because an item inside the folder is deployed, and the data pipeline in the root is not placed inside Folder1.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process - Microsoft Fabric and Introduction to deployment pipelines
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. \Folder1\Pipeline1 \Folder1\Lakehouse1

Why it is incorrect: Only Lakehouse1 was moved to Folder1. Pipeline1 stays in the root of Workspace1, and the deployment preserves each item's own path, so Pipeline1 is not placed in Folder1.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process - Microsoft Fabric

B. \Pipeline1 \Lakehouse1

Why it is incorrect: This ignores the folder. Deployment pipelines apply the folder hierarchy of the deployed items, creating the folder in the target workspace if it does not exist, so Lakehouse1 does not land in the root.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines

D. \Folder1\Lakehouse1

Why it is incorrect: It omits Pipeline1. A data pipeline is a supported item type for deployment pipelines, and the run deploys all the supported items from Workspace1 (not only those in the folder), so Pipeline1 must also appear in Workspace2.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines

q156.stem:
Your company has a finance department.

You have a Fabric tenant, an Azure Storage account named storage1, and a Microsoft Entra group named Group1. Group1 contains the users in the finance department.

You need to create a new workspace named Workspace1 in the tenant. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • Ensure that the finance department users can create and edit items in Workspace1.
  • Ensure that Workspace1 can securely access storage1 to read and write data.
  • Ensure that you are the only admin of Workspace1.
  • Minimize administrative effort.

You create Workspace1.

Which two actions should you perform next? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
options: Assign the Contributor role to Group1.
Assign the Admin role to yourself.
Assign the Contributor role to each finance department user.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: Assign the Contributor role to Group1.
  • Option B: Create a workspace identity.

Why it is correct: Two things are needed after creating the workspace.

  1. Finance users can create and edit items, with minimal effort: The Contributor role allows creating and modifying content. Assigning it to the Microsoft Entra group Group1 (instead of to each user) minimizes administrative effort, because membership changes are handled in Entra and not in the workspace.
  2. Secure access to storage1 for reading and writing: A workspace identity is a managed service principal tied to the workspace. Once created, you grant that identity an Azure RBAC role on the storage account (for example Storage Blob Data Contributor) and use trusted workspace access, so items in the workspace can securely read and write the firewall-protected storage without managing keys or secrets.

The Admin requirement needs no action: the person who creates a workspace is automatically its Admin, and nobody else receives that role.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric, Workspace identity in Microsoft Fabric and Trusted workspace access
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

C. Assign the Admin role to yourself.

Why it is incorrect: It is redundant. The user who creates a workspace already holds the Admin role in it, so there is nothing to assign, and this action does not address either the finance access or the storage requirement.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric

D. Assign the Contributor role to each finance department user.

Why it is incorrect: It gives the right permission level, but it is not the most efficient way: each user would have to be added and maintained individually. The requirement to minimize administrative effort is met by assigning the role once to Group1.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric

q157.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains the workspaces shown in the following table.

You have a deployment pipeline named Pipeline1 that deploys items from Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST. In Pipeline1, all items that have matching names are paired.

You deploy the contents of Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST by using

Pipeline1.

What will the contents of Workspace_TEST be once the deployment is complete?
options: Lakehouse1 - Lakehouse2 - Notebook1 - Notebook2 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Lakehouse1 - Lakehouse2 - Notebook1 - Notebook2 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

Why it is correct: Deployment pipelines work with paired items. Workspace_TEST was populated independently, so Lakehouse2 and Notebook2 have no counterpart in Workspace_DEV and are not paired with anything. During deployment:

  • Lakehouse1, Notebook1 and Pipeline1 exist only in Workspace_DEV, so they are new items and are copied to Workspace_TEST.
  • SemanticModel1 exists in both workspaces with the same name and, as the question states, the items with matching names are paired, so the DEV version overwrites the TEST one (a single SemanticModel1 remains).
  • Lakehouse2 and Notebook2 exist only in the target. Items that do not exist in the source stage remain as they are; deployment never deletes them.

The result is the union of both sets: Lakehouse1, Lakehouse2, Notebook1, Notebook2, Pipeline1 and SemanticModel1.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines and Understand the deployment process
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Lakehouse1 - Notebook1 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: It assumes that the target is replaced by the source (a mirror). Deployment pipelines do not delete target items that are missing from the source, so Lakehouse2 and Notebook2 stay in Workspace_TEST.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines

C. Lakehouse2 - Notebook2 - SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: It assumes nothing new is copied. Unpaired items from the source (Lakehouse1, Notebook1, Pipeline1) are created in the target during a deployment; only items that are paired are overwritten.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process

D. Lakehouse2 - Notebook2 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: It copies Pipeline1 but forgets Lakehouse1 and Notebook1. All supported items in the source stage are deployed, so they must also appear in Workspace_TEST.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace_DEV.

Workspace_DEV contains the semantic models shown in the following table.

Workspace_DEV contains the dataflows shown in the following table.

You create a new workspace named Workspace_TEST.

You create a deployment pipeline named Pipeline1 to move items from

Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST.

You run Pipeline1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • DF1 will be deployed to Workspace_TEST: No
  • Data from Model1 will be deployed to Workspace_TEST: Yes
  • The scheduled refresh policy for Model1 will be deployed to Workspace_TEST: Yes

DF1 will be deployed to Workspace_TEST: No. DF1 is a Dataflow Gen1. In this scenario it is not carried to the test stage by the deployment pipeline. Marking "Yes" would assume every dataflow type is deployed as is, which is not the expected answer here.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines

Data from Model1 will be deployed to Workspace_TEST: Yes. Model1 has a scheduled refresh policy configured, and the semantic model is treated as deployed together with its content. "No" is not the expected answer for this question.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process

The scheduled refresh policy for Model1 will be deployed to Workspace_TEST: Yes. The refresh policy configured on Model1 travels with the semantic model, whereas Model2, which has no policy configured, would simply have nothing to carry.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the official documentation says that deployment pipelines copy metadata, not data, and lists the refresh schedule among the semantic model properties that are not copied, so "No" could be argued for the last two statements (unless "refresh policy" means an incremental refresh policy, which is metadata and is copied). Dataflows are also listed among the supported items, so "Yes" could be argued for DF1. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process
