q159.stem:
-

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains two tables named DimDate and Trips.

DimDate contains the following fields.

Trips contains the following fields.

You need to compare the average miles per trip for statutory holidays versus non-statutory holidays.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (the MilesPerTrip expression): (sum(t.tripDistance)/count(t.tripID))
  • Second box (the clause before d.IsHoliday): group by

First box: (sum(t.tripDistance)/count(t.tripID)). Average miles per trip is the total miles travelled divided by the number of trips. sum(t.tripDistance) is the numerator (tripDistance holds miles per trip) and count(t.tripID) is the denominator, evaluated for each group. The result is one MilesPerTrip value per value of IsHoliday. (Both operands are integers, so T-SQL performs integer division; in a real solution you would cast one operand to decimal or use avg(t.tripDistance), but among the options this is the correct formula.)

  • (count(t.tripID) / sum(t.tripDistance)) is inverted: it returns trips per mile.

  • Sum(t.tripDistance)/t.tripID mixes an aggregate with a non-aggregated column, which is invalid without grouping by tripID and would give the distance per individual trip, not the average.

  • Official documentation: GROUP BY (Transact-SQL)

Second box: group by. To compare statutory holidays (IsHoliday = 1) against non-holidays (0) you need one aggregated row per IsHoliday value, which is what GROUP BY d.IsHoliday produces. It is also required by the rule that every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list (here d.IsHoliday) must appear in the GROUP BY clause.

  • order by only sorts the output; with aggregates in the SELECT list and no GROUP BY, the statement would fail and it would not compute per-group averages.

  • where d.IsHoliday would filter the rows (keeping only one kind of day, and it needs a comparison for a bit column) instead of producing the two groups side by side, so it cannot compare holidays against non-holidays in a single result.

  • Official documentation: GROUP BY (Transact-SQL) and SELECT - ORDER BY clause (Transact-SQL)

GROUP BY (Transact-SQL)
SELECT - ORDER BY clause (Transact-SQL)

q160.stem:
-

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named LH1 and a warehouse named DW1. LH1 contains a table named signindata that is in the dbo schema.

You need to create a stored procedure in DW1 that deduplicates the data in the signindata table.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (after AS): BEGIN
  • Second box (after SELECT): DISTINCT

First box: BEGIN. The procedure body is delimited by BEGIN ... END, and the statement ends with the END that closes it. BEGIN opens that statement block, which is the syntax that pairs with the final END.

  • BEGIN DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION starts a distributed transaction (a transaction spanning remote servers through MSDTC) and does not open a block that the final END can close. It is also unnecessary here because the procedure only reads from a lakehouse in the same workspace, using the three-part name LH1.dbo.signindata.

  • SET is a statement for assigning options or variable values; it is not a block opener and cannot pair with END.

  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse

Second box: DISTINCT. The goal is to deduplicate the signindata rows. SELECT DISTINCT PersonID, FirstName, LastName returns each unique combination of those columns once, removing duplicate rows (NULLs are treated as equal). Because the procedure queries the lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint (read-only) and cannot modify the source table, returning the distinct rows is the way to deliver the deduplicated data.

  • GROUP BY is a separate clause that goes after FROM; it cannot be placed right after SELECT in the select list, and it would only make sense with aggregates.

  • TOP (100) PERCENT WITH TIES does not remove duplicates: it returns the top 100 percent of rows, which is all of them, and WITH TIES requires an ORDER BY clause.

  • Official documentation: SELECT clause (Transact-SQL) and GROUP BY (Transact-SQL)

links.t: T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse

GROUP BY (Transact-SQL)

q161.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You are creating a Fabric Data Factory pipeline.

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Lookup

Why it is correct: The pipeline has to run a stored procedure in a warehouse and hand the values it returns (number of active customers and average sales) to the downstream activities. The Lookup activity can retrieve a dataset from any supported data source, including a Fabric warehouse, and it can run a stored procedure as its query. Its output (the first row, or the whole result set if "First row only" is cleared) is exposed as activity output, so later activities reference it with expressions such as @activity('Lookup1').output.firstRow.ActiveCustomers. That is exactly the "returned values must be available downstream" requirement. Note that the plain Stored procedure activity runs the procedure but does not return a result set to the pipeline, which is why Lookup is the right choice here.

  • Official documentation: Use the Lookup activity to look up data from a data source and How to use Stored procedure activity
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Get metadata

Why it is incorrect: Get metadata returns metadata about data (for example file or folder names, sizes, last-modified dates, structure, column count, existence). It does not execute a stored procedure and cannot return the business values (active customers, average sales) that the procedure computes.

  • Official documentation: Use the Get Metadata activity to look up data from a data source

B. Switch

Why it is incorrect: Switch is a control-flow activity that evaluates an expression and runs one of several branches of activities depending on the value. It does not connect to a warehouse and does not execute stored procedures or return data.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

D. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: Append variable adds a value to an existing array-type pipeline variable. It is a way of storing something that already exists in the pipeline; it cannot run a stored procedure in a warehouse or produce its result.

  • Official documentation: Use the Append Variable activity in Fabric

How to use Stored procedure activity

q162.stem:
-

You have the following T-SQL statement.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Statement 1 (returns Region values when a Sales item has a RefundStatus of Refunded): Yes
  • Statement 2 (only returns TransactionDate values that occurred during the current year): Yes
  • Statement 3 (TotalRevenue aggregates SalesAmount values that have a RefundStatus of Refunded): No

Statement 1 - Yes. The CASE expression lives inside the SUM, in the SELECT list. It is not a filter: the WHERE clause only restricts by year. Rows with RefundStatus = 'Refunded' are therefore not removed from the result set; they still belong to their ProductCategory/Region group, so that Region appears in the output (their contribution to TotalRevenue is simply 0). Had the refund condition been in the WHERE clause, the region could disappear if all its rows were refunded.

  • Official documentation: FROM clause plus JOIN, APPLY, PIVOT (Transact-SQL) (query reference for how rows are filtered and grouped)

Statement 2 - Yes. The predicate YEAR(TransactionDate) = YEAR(GETDATE()) in the WHERE clause keeps only the rows whose transaction date falls in the current calendar year; every other year is discarded before grouping. This is the sense in which the statement is true (the query operates only on current-year transactions), even though the column itself is not projected in the SELECT list.

  • Official documentation: YEAR (Transact-SQL)

Statement 3 - No. The CASE WHEN RefundStatus <> 'Refunded' THEN SalesAmount ELSE 0 END adds SalesAmount only when the status is not Refunded; refunded rows contribute 0. So TotalRevenue excludes refunded amounts, the opposite of what the statement claims. The operator <> means "not equal to".

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but Statement 2 is debatable: the WHERE clause limits the rows to the current year, yet TransactionDate is not in the SELECT list, so read literally the query does not return TransactionDate values and the statement could be argued as No. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: FROM clause plus JOIN, APPLY, PIVOT (Transact-SQL)

q163.stem:
-

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains the following data.

The data has the following characteristics:

  • Each customer is assigned a unique CustomerID value.
  • Each customer is associated to a single SalesRegion value.
  • Each customer is associated to a single CustomerAddress value.
  • The Customer table contains 5 million rows.
  • All foreign key values are non-null.

You need to create a view to denormalize the data into a customer dimension that contains one row per distinct CustomerID value. The solution must minimize query processing time and resources.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First drop-down (join to SalesLT.SalesRegion): left outer join
  • Second drop-down (join to SalesLT.Address): A.AddressID = CA.AddressID

First drop-down - left outer join. The view must contain one row per distinct CustomerID. Customer is the driving table (5 million rows) and each customer has a single SalesRegion, so the join to SalesRegion cannot multiply rows. A left outer join keeps every customer even if a matching SalesRegion row were missing (Fabric warehouse foreign keys are declared but not enforced, so referential integrity is not guaranteed by the engine), which protects the requirement of one row per customer. This is the accepted choice for the first drop-down. A full outer join is wrong because it would also bring in SalesRegion rows that have no customer (regions with no customers), producing rows with a NULL CustomerID and breaking the one-row-per-customer rule, and it is the most expensive join. An inner join would silently drop customers without a matching region, so it is not the expected answer for this question.

  • Official documentation: Understand joins concepts and syntax and FROM clause plus JOIN, APPLY, PIVOT (Transact-SQL)

Second drop-down - A.AddressID = CA.AddressID. CustomerAddress is the bridge table (PK CustomerID + AddressID, FKs to Customer and Address), so Address must be joined through the AddressID that CustomerAddress carries. C.AddressID = CA.AddressID is wrong because Customer has no AddressID column according to the table description (its only foreign key is SalesRegionID). C.CustomerID = A.CustomerID is wrong because Address has only AddressID as primary key and no CustomerID. Together with CA.AddressType = 'Main Office', the join to CustomerAddress is restricted to one address per customer, which keeps the result at one row per CustomerID.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but for the first drop-down an inner join could also be argued: all foreign keys are non-null and each customer has exactly one region, so an inner join would return the same rows and is usually cheaper, which fits "minimize query processing time and resources". A left outer join is only safer if orphaned keys are possible, which Fabric warehouse does not prevent. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Use inner joins

links.t: Understand joins concepts and syntax
FROM clause plus JOIN, APPLY, PIVOT (Transact-SQL)
Use inner joins

q164.stem:
You have a query in Microsoft Power BI Desktop that contains two columns named Order_Date and Shipping_Date.

You need to create a column that will calculate the number of days between Order_Date and Shipping_Date for each row.

Which Power Query function should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Duration.Days

Why it is correct: In Power Query, subtracting two date values ([Shipping_Date] - [Order_Date]) returns a duration value. Duration.Days extracts the days component of a duration as a number, so a custom column such as = Duration.Days([Shipping_Date] - [Order_Date]) yields the number of days between the two dates for every row.

  • Official documentation: Duration.Days - Power Query M and Duration functions
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. DateTime.LocalNow

Why it is incorrect: It returns the current local date and time as a datetime value; it takes no column inputs and does not compute a difference between two columns.

  • Official documentation: Today's date in Power Query custom columns

C. Duration.From

Why it is incorrect: Duration.From converts a value (for example a number or text) into a duration. It does not calculate the difference between two dates, and it would not return the day count as a number by itself.

  • Official documentation: Duration functions

D. Date.AddDays

Why it is incorrect: Date.AddDays adds a number of days to a date and returns another date. The requirement is the opposite: obtain the number of days between two dates.

  • Official documentation: Date.AddDays - Power Query M

q165.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model.

You need to modify object-level security (OLS) for the model.

What should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Tabular Editor

Why it is correct: Object-level security (OLS) restricts access to tables and columns of a semantic model through table/column permissions on roles. The Power BI Desktop and Fabric service interfaces let you create roles and define row-level security, but they do not expose the table and column permission settings needed for OLS. Microsoft's documentation states that OLS is configured by using external tools such as Tabular Editor (which modifies the model metadata, for example the MetadataPermission of a table or column per role) and then published to the service.

  • Official documentation: Object-level security (OLS) and Object-level security in Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. the Fabric service

Why it is incorrect: In the Fabric service you can manage role membership (assign users and groups to roles) and test roles, but you cannot define OLS permissions on tables and columns there.

  • Official documentation: Object-level security (OLS)

B. Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Desktop's Manage roles dialog configures RLS filters. It has no option to restrict tables or columns for a role (OLS); that requires a tool that edits the model's tabular metadata directly.

  • Official documentation: Restrict access to Power BI model objects

C. ALM Toolkit

Why it is incorrect: ALM Toolkit is a schema comparison and deployment tool for semantic models (it compares and merges metadata between models). It is not an authoring tool for defining role permissions such as OLS.

  • Official documentation: Object-level security (tabular models)

q166.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model that contains a measure named TotalSalesAmount. TotalSalesAmount returns a sales revenue amount that is translated into a selected currency.

You need to ensure that the value returned by TotalSalesAmount is formatted to use the correct currency symbol.

What should you include in the solution?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: a dynamic format string

Why it is correct: A dynamic format string lets a measure carry a DAX expression that decides its format string depending on context. For a revenue measure converted to the currency the user selects, the format string expression can return the proper symbol and pattern (for example "€#,0.00" or "$#,0.00") based on the selected currency, so the value is shown with the correct symbol without changing the value itself or creating text measures.

  • Official documentation: Create dynamic format strings for measures
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. a field parameter

Why it is incorrect: Field parameters let report users switch which fields or measures appear in a visual (for example swapping the axis or the measure). They change what is shown, not how a measure's value is formatted.

  • Official documentation: Use field parameters in Power BI

B. a linguistic schema

Why it is incorrect: A linguistic schema defines synonyms and phrasing for Q&A natural-language queries over the model. It has no effect on number or currency formatting.

  • Official documentation: Create dynamic format strings for measures (formatting is controlled by format strings, not by the linguistic schema)

D. the WINDOW DAX function

Why it is incorrect: WINDOW returns a range of rows within a partition and is used for window calculations (running totals, moving averages). It does not control how a result is formatted.

  • Official documentation: WINDOW function (DAX)

q167.stem:
You plan to use Fabric to store data.

You need to create a data store that supports the following:

  • Writing data by using T-SQL
  • Multi-table transactions
  • Dynamic data masking

Which type of data store should you create?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: warehouse

Why it is correct: The three requirements point to a Fabric warehouse: it is the store that supports writing data with T-SQL (full DML and DDL), multi-table transactions (ACID transactions that span several tables, with snapshot isolation) and dynamic data masking to obfuscate sensitive column values for non-privileged users.

  • Official documentation: Transactions in Warehouse tables and Dynamic data masking in Fabric data warehousing
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. KQL database

Why it is incorrect: A KQL database is queried with Kusto Query Language and ingests streaming/time-series data. Data is not written by T-SQL DML, and it does not offer multi-table T-SQL transactions.

  • Official documentation: Kusto query set - Microsoft Fabric

B. lakehouse

Why it is incorrect: A lakehouse is written with Spark. Its SQL analytics endpoint is read-only for the Delta tables (you can create views and security, but cannot INSERT/UPDATE data in tables through T-SQL), and multi-table transactions are a warehouse capability. Dynamic data masking is configurable on the endpoint, but the write-with-T-SQL and transaction requirements rule the lakehouse out.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric decision guide: Choose between Warehouse and Lakehouse and SQL analytics endpoint of the lakehouse

D. semantic model

Why it is incorrect: A semantic model is an analytical layer for reports and measures (DAX); it is not a data store you write to with T-SQL and it has no T-SQL transaction support.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric decision guide: Choose between Warehouse and Lakehouse

q168.stem:

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 uses the Pro license mode and contains a semantic model named Model1.

You have an Azure DevOps organization.

You need to enable version control for Workspace1. The solution must ensure that Model1 is added to the repository.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  1. Assign Workspace1 to a Fabric capacity.
  2. Connect Workspace1 to a Git provider.
  3. Sync Workspace1 with the repository.

1. Assign Workspace1 to a Fabric capacity. Workspace1 uses the Pro license mode, and Git integration is only available for workspaces on a Fabric (or Premium) capacity. Therefore the first step is to change the license/capacity of the workspace; without it the Git connection cannot be created.

  • Official documentation: Get started with Git integration

2. Connect Workspace1 to a Git provider. Once on a capacity, you open Workspace settings > Git integration, choose Azure DevOps, and select the organization, project, repository and branch. This is what actually enables version control for the workspace.

  • Official documentation: Get started with Git integration

3. Sync Workspace1 with the repository. After connecting, the workspace and the repository must be synchronized; when the Git branch is empty, the initial sync commits the workspace items (including Model1) to the repository. This is what guarantees Model1 ends up in the repo.

  • Official documentation: Basic concepts in Git integration

Why the other actions are wrong: Create a deployment pipeline is part of a release process between stages, not of enabling version control. Configure branch policies in Azure DevOps is optional governance on the repository branch and does not add Model1 to the repo.

  • Official documentation: Manage branches in Fabric workspaces

q169.stem:
-

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Enterprise.

Enterprise contains a semantic model named Model1. Model1 contains a date parameter named Date1 that was created in Power Query.

You build a deployment pipeline named Enterprise Data that includes two stages named Development and Test. You assign the Enterprise workspace to the Development stage.

You need to perform the following actions:

  • Create a workspace named Enterprise [Test] and assign the workspace to the Test stage.
  • Configure a rule that will modify the value of Date1 when changes are deployed to the Test stage.

Which two settings should you use? To answer, select the appropriate settings in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Create the workspace Enterprise [Test] and assign it to the Test stage: the green workspace icon (Deploy to this stage or Assign a workspace) in the Test stage.
  • Configure a rule that changes Date1 on deployment to Test: the Deployment rules icon at the top right of the Test stage card.

Assign a workspace / create the Test workspace. In an empty stage of a deployment pipeline, the "Deploy to this stage or Assign a workspace" area lets you assign an existing workspace or deploy from the previous stage, which creates a new workspace (named, by default, after the source with the stage name in brackets, e.g. Enterprise [Test]) and assigns it to the stage. This is the setting for the first requirement.

  • Official documentation: Get started with deployment pipelines and The deployment pipelines process

Deployment rules. Rules are configured per target stage (here Test) and are applied when content is deployed into it. A parameter rule can replace the value of a Power Query parameter such as Date1 in a semantic model. The Deployment rules button is in the target stage, not in Development, and not in pipeline Settings. The pencil icon only edits the stage name/description and Manage access/Settings concern pipeline permissions and general settings.

  • Official documentation: Create deployment rules

q170.stem:
-

You have two Microsoft Power BI queries named Employee and Retired Roles.

You need to merge the Employee query with the Retired Roles query. The solution must ensure that duplicate rows in each query are removed.

Which column and Join Kind should you use in Power Query Editor? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Column: Division (the matching column between Employee and Retired Roles; in the Merge dialog it is the column highlighted in the Employee table)
  • Join Kind: Inner (only matching rows)

Column - Division. A merge requires one or more columns with the same meaning in both queries. Retired Roles exposes Division (and Role) while Employee contains Division, Role, etc.; Division is the matching column for this merge.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview

Join Kind - Inner. An inner join keeps only the rows that match in both tables, so the result consists solely of employees whose division (and role) exists in Retired Roles, with no unmatched rows from either side; this is the accepted option for the "duplicate rows removed" requirement. The alternatives do not fit: Left Outer keeps every row from Employee, Right Outer every row from Retired Roles, and Full Outer all rows from both, so none of them eliminates non-matching/duplicate rows; Left Anti and Right Anti return only the rows with no match, which is the opposite of keeping the intersection.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but an inner join does not by itself remove duplicates, and the dialog also shows Role as a second matching column (Retired Roles shows Division = 2, Role = 1). Inner is the closest option offered; removing duplicates properly would need a Remove Duplicates step before merging. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Inner join, Left outer join, Left anti join, Right anti join

q171.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1 and a user named User1. Workspace1 contains a warehouse named DW1.

You share DW1 with User1 and assign User1 the default permissions for DW1.

What can User1 do?
options: Build reports by using the default dataset.
Read data from the tables in DW1.
Connect to DW1 via the Azure SQL Analytics endpoint.
Read the underlying Parquet files from OneLake.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Connect to DW1 via the Azure SQL Analytics endpoint.

Why it is correct: When you share a warehouse and leave all the optional check boxes cleared, the recipient only gets the default Read permission on the item. In a Fabric warehouse this permission is the equivalent of the SQL CONNECT permission: it lets the user connect to the warehouse through its SQL (TDS) connection string, which is the SQL analytics endpoint (the option text says "Azure SQL Analytics endpoint", which is a loose reference to it), and nothing more. The user does not get SELECT on the tables, does not get access to the files in OneLake and does not get the right to build on the semantic model. Those capabilities require additional permissions chosen at sharing time (for example Read all data using SQL / ReadData, Read all OneLake data / ReadAll, or Build reports on the default semantic model / Build), or a SQL GRANT executed afterwards.

  • Official documentation: Share your warehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric and Connectivity to data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Build reports by using the default dataset.

Why it is incorrect: Building reports on the default semantic model is controlled by the separate Build permission, which is an optional check box in the sharing dialog ("Build reports on the default semantic model"). It is not part of the default Read permission, so User1 cannot build reports on the default dataset until that option is granted.

  • Official documentation: Share your warehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric

B. Read data from the tables in DW1.

Why it is incorrect: This is the tempting answer chosen by some commenters, but the default Read permission only allows connecting to the endpoint (like CONNECT in SQL Server). Reading table data requires the additional Read all data using SQL (ReadData) permission selected during sharing, or granular SELECT permissions granted with T-SQL. Without them, User1 can connect but queries against the tables are denied.

  • Official documentation: Share your warehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric

D. Read the underlying Parquet files from OneLake.

Why it is incorrect: Access to the underlying Delta/Parquet files in OneLake is granted by the Read all Apache Spark / Read all OneLake data (ReadAll) permission, which is also optional and not part of the default permission. Without it, the user cannot access the files directly through the OneLake endpoint.

  • Official documentation: Share your warehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric / OneLake overview

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1 and a user named DBUser. Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

DBUser does NOT have access to the tenant.

You grant DBUser access to Lakehouse1 as shown in the following exhibit.

Use the drop-down menus to select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented in the graphic.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • DBUser can read the data in Lakehouse1 by using the: OneLake endpoint
  • DBUser can query the data in Lakehouse1 by using: OneLake file explorer

Analysis of the exhibit: DBUser was granted access to the lakehouse with only one additional permission, Read all Apache Spark. Read all SQL endpoint data and Build reports on the default semantic model are not selected. Also, DBUser has no access to the tenant (no workspace role), so everything depends on the item-level share.

First box: OneLake endpoint. The "Read all Apache Spark" permission (ReadAll) gives read access to the data files of the lakehouse in OneLake. That access is exercised through the OneLake endpoint (the ADLS Gen2-compatible API at onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com) and through Spark. The other choices are wrong: the default semantic model can only be used with the item share, but the share dialog itself warns that reading directly in the lakehouse needs additional permissions, and a default semantic model being merely readable is not "reading the data in the lakehouse"; the Tabular Data Stream (TDS) endpoint is the SQL analytics endpoint connection, and reading tables through it would require the Read all SQL endpoint data permission, which was not granted.

Second box: OneLake file explorer. OneLake file explorer is the Windows client that surfaces OneLake items and their files in File Explorer; it works against the OneLake endpoint, so it is consistent with the ReadAll permission and lets the user browse and work with the lakehouse files and tables. A KQL queryset queries KQL databases (eventhouses), not lakehouses. SSMS connects through the TDS (SQL analytics) endpoint, which would require the SQL endpoint data permission that DBUser does not have.

  • Official documentation: How lakehouse sharing works - Microsoft Fabric

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.

You have three groups named Group1, Group2, and Group3.

You need to assign a workspace role to each group. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege and meet the following requirements:

  • Group1 must be able to write data to Workspace1, but be unable to add members to Workspace1.
  • Group2 must be able to configure and maintain the settings of Workspace1.
  • Group3 must be able to write data and add members to Workspace1, but be unable to delete Workspace1.

Which workspace role should you assign to each group? To answer, drag the appropriate roles to the correct groups. Each role may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Group1: Contributor
  • Group2: Admin
  • Group3: Member

Group1 - Contributor. Group1 must write data to the workspace but must not add members. The Contributor role can create, edit and delete content and write data in the workspace, but it cannot manage membership. The Viewer role is read-only, so it is not enough, and Member or Admin would grant more privilege than needed (they can add people), which violates least privilege.

Group2 - Admin. Configuring and maintaining the settings of the workspace (workspace settings, permissions, deleting or renaming the workspace) is exclusive to the Admin role. Member and Contributor cannot do it.

Group3 - Member. Group3 needs to write data and add members, but must not be able to delete the workspace. Member can write content and add members or other users with lower roles (Member, Contributor, Viewer), but cannot delete the workspace or change workspace-level settings; deleting is reserved for Admin. Admin would be excessive because it can delete the workspace.

q174.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant named Tenant1 that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You need to add data to Lakehouse1 from a CSV file in an Azure Storage account outside of Fabric. The solution must minimize development effort.

What should you use to add the data?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: shortcut

Why it is correct: The requirement is to make a CSV file stored in an Azure Storage account outside of Fabric available in Lakehouse1 while minimizing development effort. A OneLake shortcut to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (or Blob-compatible storage) creates a pointer in the lakehouse Files section to the external location. No pipeline, code or transformation needs to be built, no data is copied or duplicated, and the file is immediately visible to Fabric engines. It is just configuration with a connection, so it is the lowest effort option.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts - Microsoft Fabric and Create an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 shortcut
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. copy job

Why it is incorrect: A copy job does move the file into the lakehouse, and it is simple, but it still requires creating and configuring a job (source, destination, mapping, schedule) and it duplicates the data. A shortcut needs less effort because there is nothing to copy or run.

  • Official documentation: What is the Copy job in Data Factory for Microsoft Fabric

C. pipeline

Why it is incorrect: A data pipeline with a Copy activity can load the CSV into the lakehouse, but it is orchestration tooling that requires more design and maintenance (activities, connections, parameters, triggers). It is more development effort than a shortcut for a simple file.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric decision guide: choose a data integration strategy

D. Dataflow Gen2

Why it is incorrect: Dataflow Gen2 uses Power Query to extract, transform and load data. It is meant for transformations and is the heaviest option for just exposing a CSV file; no transformation is required in this scenario.

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Table1. Table1 contains the following data.

You need to create a T-SQL statement that meets the following requirements:

  • Outputs the item name of each item and returns a null value if the item name is longer than 20 characters
  • Outputs the PurchaseDate value in the format of МММ dd, yy

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • ItemName: ,try_cast(item_name as varchar(20))
  • PurchaseDate: ,convert(varchar, purchase_date, 7)

ItemName. The requirement is to output the item name and return NULL when it is longer than 20 characters. TRY_CAST is the "safe" conversion: instead of raising an error when the conversion cannot be performed, it returns NULL, and among the offered options it is the best fit for the requirement. convert(varchar(max), item_name) simply returns the full value with no length restriction, so it does not satisfy the requirement. convert(varchar(20), item_name) truncates or fails rather than returning NULL by design.

PurchaseDate. The target format is MMM dd, yy (for example Apr 20, 22). In the T-SQL CONVERT function, style 7 produces exactly Mon dd, yy. Style 109 produces Mon dd yyyy hh:mi:ss:mmmAM (four-digit year with time) and style 112 produces yyyymmdd (ISO basic, no separators), so neither matches.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but strictly speaking TRY_CAST(x AS varchar(20)) does not return NULL for strings longer than 20 characters: explicit conversions between character types silently truncate, and TRY_CAST only returns NULL when the conversion fails (for example, an invalid format). A true NULL-if-too-long result would need CASE WHEN LEN(item_name) > 20 THEN NULL ELSE item_name END, which none of the options offers, so try_cast is the best available choice. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: TRY_CAST (Transact-SQL)
  • Official documentation: CAST and CONVERT (Transact-SQL), date and time styles

You have a Fabric warehouse named Warehouse1 that contains a table named dbo.Product.

dbo.Product contains the following columns.

You need to use a T-SQL query to add a column named PriceRange to

dbo.Product. The column must categorize each product based on UnitPrice. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • If UnitPrice is 0, PriceRange is "Not for resale".
  • If UnitPrice is less than 50, PriceRange is "Under $50".
  • If UnitPrice is between 50 and 250, PriceRange is "Under $250“.
  • In all other instances, PriceRange is "$250+".

How should you complete the query? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • PriceRange = CASE
  • Before '$250+': ELSE
  • Last target (after '$250+'): END

Analysis. To categorize each row by ranges of UnitPrice in a query, you use a searched CASE expression. It starts with CASE, evaluates each WHEN ... THEN ... branch in order, falls back to ELSE for "all other instances" (UnitPrice of 250 or more, giving '$250+') and must be closed with END.

  • BEGIN and END as a pair delimit statement blocks in T-SQL, and BEGIN is not valid at the start of a column expression; only END closes CASE, and the same END keyword is used.

  • IF and WHILE are control-of-flow statements that cannot be used inside a SELECT column expression to return a value. For inline conditional logic you need CASE (or IIF).

  • Official documentation: CASE (Transact-SQL)

q177.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You are creating a Fabric Data Factory pipeline.

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Script

Why it is correct: The Script activity in a Fabric Data Factory pipeline runs SQL (including EXEC of a stored procedure) against a warehouse and, when the script returns a result set, exposes that result in the activity output (result sets and rows affected). Downstream activities can then reference it through dynamic content expressions such as the output of the activity, so the active customer count and average sales can be used later in the pipeline.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: Append variable only adds a value to an existing array variable of the pipeline. It does not connect to a warehouse nor execute a stored procedure.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric

C. Stored procedure

Why it is incorrect: The Stored procedure activity does execute a stored procedure in a warehouse, but it is designed to run the procedure (for example to perform data modifications) and does not surface the values returned by the procedure as an output usable by downstream activities. Since the requirement is that the returned values must be available downstream, the Script activity is the one to use.

  • Official documentation: How to use the Stored procedure activity

D. Get metadata

Why it is incorrect: Get metadata retrieves metadata of data (files, folders, tables, structure) from a data store. It does not execute stored procedures.

q178.stem:

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains the following data.

You need to create a T-SQL statement that will denormalize the tables and include the ContractType and StartDate attributes in the results. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • Include attributes from matching rows in the Contract table.
  • Ensure that all the rows from the Employee table are preserved.
  • Return the total number of employees per contract type for all the contract types that have more than two employees.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Join type: LEFT OUTER JOIN
  • Filter on the aggregated count: HAVING

Join type - LEFT OUTER JOIN. The query starts from Employee AS e. The requirements are to include attributes from matching rows of Contract and to ensure all rows of Employee are preserved. That is the definition of a left outer join with Employee on the left: every employee is returned, with ContractType set to NULL where there is no matching contract. INNER JOIN would drop employees without a contract, RIGHT OUTER JOIN would preserve Contract rows instead of Employee rows, and CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product with no join condition, which makes no sense here.

Second box - HAVING. The final query groups by ContractType and must only return contract types having more than two employees, a condition on an aggregate (COUNT(DISTINCT EmployeeID) > 2). Aggregate functions cannot be used in WHERE, because WHERE filters rows before grouping; the filter on aggregated values belongs in HAVING. LIMIT is not T-SQL syntax (T-SQL uses TOP), and CONTAINS is a full-text predicate, not a clause.

  • Official documentation: FROM clause plus JOIN, APPLY, PIVOT (Transact-SQL)
  • Official documentation: HAVING (Transact-SQL)

You have a KQL database that contains a table named Readings.

You need to query Readings and return the results shown in the following table.

How should you complete the query? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (computing the previous values): | extend
  • Second box (final column list): | project

First box - extend. prev() is a window function that returns the value of a column in a previous row of a serialized row set; sort by Datetime produces a serialized set, so prev(MeterReading) and prev(Datetime) can be used. Adding new calculated columns (PrevMeterReading, PrevTimestamp) to every row while keeping the existing ones is exactly what extend does. summarize would aggregate rows, evaluate invokes plugins, and lookup enriches a table with another table, so none of them fit.

Second box - project. The expected output contains only the columns City, Area, MeterReading, Datetime, PrevMeterReading, PrevDatetime, listed in that order. project selects and orders the columns to be returned. extend would add rather than select columns and summarize would require aggregation. (The exhibit names the extended column PrevTimestamp but the projected one PrevDatetime; this appears to be a typo in the question, the intended logic is extend followed by project.)

q180.stem:

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named DW1. DW1 contains the following tables and columns.

You need to summarize order quantities by year and product. The solution must include the yearly sum of order quantities for all the products in each row.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • SELECT ... (SO.ModifiedDate) AS OrderDate: YEAR
  • GROUP BY: ROLLUP(YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate), P.Name)

First box - YEAR. The requirement is to summarize by year, so the date has to be reduced to its year component: YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate) AS OrderDate. CAST and CONVERT need a target data type argument, so they do not match the shape X (SO.ModifiedDate) and do not extract the year.

Second box - ROLLUP. The query must give order quantities by year and product, and also include the yearly total for all products on its own row. ROLLUP(year, product) produces the detail rows (year, product), a subtotal row for each year (product NULL) and a grand total. A plain GROUP BY YEAR(...), P.Name gives only the detail rows, with no subtotal. CUBE creates subtotals for every combination, including per-product totals across all years, which are not requested. GROUPING SETS with the sets shown would need to be written explicitly and omits the grand total; ROLLUP is the concise hierarchical aggregate designed for this.

  • Official documentation: YEAR (Transact-SQL)

q181.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains multiple semantic models, including a model named Model1. Model1 is updated by using an XMLA endpoint.

You need to increase the speed of the write operations of the XMLA endpoint.

What should you do?
options: Delete any unused semantic models from Workspace1.
Select Large semantic model storage format for Workspace1.
Configure Model 1 to use the Direct Lake storage format.
Delete any unused columns from Model1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Select Large semantic model storage format for Workspace1.

Why it is correct: Model1 is written to through the XMLA endpoint (for example by Tabular Editor, SSMS, ALM Toolkit or a deployment pipeline). The way to make those write operations faster is to enable the Large semantic model storage format. With this format, the service uses a different, optimized storage layout for the model, which is what improves the performance of XMLA write operations (processing and metadata changes) on big models, and it also removes the 10 GB model size limit. The setting is applied per semantic model (in the model settings) or as the default for the workspace, so selecting it for Workspace1 covers Model1. Nothing in the other options changes how data is written through the endpoint.

  • Official documentation: Large semantic models in Power BI Premium and Fabric and Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Delete any unused semantic models from Workspace1.

Why it is incorrect: Semantic models in a workspace are independent items. Removing models that nobody uses frees capacity memory and tidies the workspace, but it does not change the storage format or the way XMLA writes to Model1 are executed, so the write speed of the endpoint is not improved in a meaningful way.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint

C. Configure Model 1 to use the Direct Lake storage format.

Why it is incorrect: Direct Lake is a storage mode that reads Delta tables from OneLake directly into memory. It is a different way of loading data into the model, not a way to speed up XMLA write operations, and it would force a redesign of Model1 (data must live in Delta tables in a lakehouse or warehouse). Large semantic model storage format is the setting the documentation ties to faster XMLA writes.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview

D. Delete any unused columns from Model1.

Why it is incorrect: Removing unused columns reduces model size and can speed up refresh and queries, but it is a modeling optimization, not a configuration of the XMLA write path. It also means changing the model design, whereas the requirement is simply to speed up the endpoint writes, which the large model storage format addresses directly.

  • Official documentation: Large semantic models in Power BI Premium and Fabric

q182.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.

You need to create a semantic model named Model1 and publish Model1 to Workspace1. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • Can revert to previous versions of Model1 as required.
  • Identifies differences between saved versions of Model1.
  • Uses Microsoft Power Bl=I Desktop to publish to Workspace1.
  • Can edit item definition files by using Microsoft Visual Studio Code.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
options: Save Model1 in Power BI Desktop as a PBIT file.
Enable users to edit data models in the Power BI service.
Save Model1 in Power BI Desktop as a PBIP file.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Enable Git integration for Workspace1.
  • Option D: Save Model1 in Power BI Desktop as a PBIP file.

Why it is correct: The four requirements split into two needs.

  • Version history, revert and compare versions are source control features. Enabling Git integration on Workspace1 connects the workspace to a Git repository (Azure DevOps or GitHub), so every change to Model1 is committed, you can compare versions through diffs and you can revert to a previous commit.
  • Publishing from Power BI Desktop and editing item definition files in Visual Studio Code require the model to be saved as a Power BI Project (PBIP). A PBIP stores the semantic model and report as a folder of text-based definition files (TMDL/TMSL for the model, PBIR/JSON for the report), which are readable by humans, diff-friendly and editable in VS Code. Desktop can still publish the project to the workspace, and the same folder structure is what Git integration in Fabric understands.

Together, PBIP gives the editable text-based files and Git integration gives history, diff and revert.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects (PBIP) overview, Power BI Desktop projects and Git integration and Manage Power BI content in version control
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Save Model1 in Power BI Desktop as a PBIT file.

Why it is incorrect: A PBIT is a Power BI template: a single packaged file that contains the model and report definition but no data. It is a binary-style container, not a folder of editable item definition files, so it cannot be edited properly in VS Code, and it provides no version history or diff of saved versions. It is meant for sharing reusable starting points, not for source control.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects (PBIP) overview

C. Enable users to edit data models in the Power BI service.

Why it is incorrect: This tenant/workspace setting lets people edit a model in the browser (web modeling). It has nothing to do with saving versions, comparing them, publishing from Desktop or working with definition files in VS Code, so it covers none of the requirements.

  • Official documentation: Manage Power BI content in version control

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that is assigned to a newly created Fabric capacity named Capacity1.

You create a semantic model named Model1 and deploy Model1 to Workspace1.

You need to publish changes to Model1 directly from Tabular Editor.

What should you do?
options: For Workspace1, create a managed private endpoint.
For Capacity1, set XMLA Endpoint to Read Write.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: For Capacity1, set XMLA Endpoint to Read Write.

Why it is correct: Tabular Editor connects to a semantic model through the XMLA endpoint of the workspace. By default the endpoint of a capacity is Read Only, which lets client tools query but not change the model. To deploy or save changes made in Tabular Editor to Model1 you need read-write XMLA, and that is configured in the capacity settings (the XMLA Endpoint option, set to Read Write) in the Fabric admin portal or the capacity settings. Because Workspace1 is assigned to the newly created Capacity1, this is the setting you have to change.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint and Manage semantic models with the XMLA endpoint
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. For Workspace1, enable Git integration.

Why it is incorrect: Git integration synchronizes workspace items with a repository for version control. It does not open a write channel for third-party tools such as Tabular Editor; those still need the XMLA endpoint to be read-write.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects and Git integration

B. For Model1, enable external sharing.

Why it is incorrect: External sharing controls whether guest users from other organizations can consume content. It is unrelated to how Tabular Editor connects to and writes to the model.

C. For Workspace1, create a managed private endpoint.

Why it is incorrect: Managed private endpoints are used for outbound secure connections from Fabric workloads (for example Spark) to data sources. They do not configure the inbound XMLA endpoint that client tools use, and they do not enable write operations.

q184.stem:

You are creating a report and a semantic model in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.

The Value measure has the expression shown in the following exhibit.

Use the drop-down menus to select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented in the graphic.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • A [answer choice] was added to the Value measure: dynamic format string
  • The Value measure can return values formatted as: percentages or whole numbers

Analysis of each selection:

  1. Dynamic format string. The Format drop-down in the exhibit shows Dynamic, and the formula bar shows a SWITCH(SELECTEDVALUE(Metric[Metric]), ...) expression that returns a format string ("#", "0.00%", "#,###") instead of a value. That expression is the format string expression of the measure, which is exactly what a dynamic format string is: the measure keeps returning its numeric value, while the format applied to it changes according to the user's selection in the Metric slicer. A calculation group would be a separate table with calculation items (although a calculation item can also carry a format string expression), a data category only classifies a field (for example as a URL or city), and a synonym is an alternative name for Q&A/Copilot.

  2. Percentages or whole numbers. The three branches of the SWITCH are: "# of Customers" gets "#" (a whole number), "Gross Margin %" gets "0.00%" (a percentage with two decimals), and every other metric (Gross Margin, Total COGS, Total Revenue) falls to the default "#,###" (a whole number with thousands separator). So the measure shows whole numbers or percentages, never plain decimals, which rules out "percentages only" (the other metrics are whole numbers), "whole numbers only" (Gross Margin % is a percentage) and "percentages or decimals" (no format shows decimal digits except as part of the percentage).

  • Official documentation: Create dynamic format strings for measures and Use custom format strings in Power BI Desktop

Use custom format strings in Power BI Desktop

q185.stem:
-

You have a Fabric lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You have the data sources shown in the following table.

You need to ingest data from both data sources into Lakehouse1. The solution must minimize maintenance and development time.

What should you use to ingest the data into each data source? To answer, drag the appropriate options to the correct data sources. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Datasource1: A Dataflow Gen2
  • Datasource2: An eventstream

Analysis of each selection:

  1. Datasource1 (Azure SQL managed instance, CDC enabled, 500,000+ rows and 20 GB daily): A Dataflow Gen2 is the selected tool. Dataflow Gen2 is the low-code Power Query experience of Fabric, it has a native connector for Azure SQL managed instance and it can write straight to a lakehouse destination, so it minimizes development and maintenance effort, and it scales to this data volume. A Dataflow Gen1 cannot write to a lakehouse (it only stores in Power BI managed storage), and a notebook would need custom Spark code and maintenance, which contradicts the requirement. A pipeline with a Copy activity is the main alternative: it is the high-throughput tool for large batch copies and can also copy from a SQL managed instance.

  2. Datasource2 (machine data streamed to an Azure event hub): An eventstream is the Fabric Real-Time Intelligence item built to capture streaming data. It has an Azure Event Hubs source and a lakehouse destination, so streaming data from the event hub lands in Lakehouse1 with no code. Dataflows and Copy activities are batch tools that are not designed to continuously consume an event hub, and a notebook would require writing and running a Spark Structured Streaming job.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks Dataflow Gen2 for Datasource1, but a pipeline with a Copy activity (high-volume batch copy that supports incremental and CDC-based patterns) or mirroring could also be argued for a 500,000+ row, 20 GB daily load from Azure SQL managed instance; Dataflow Gen2 fits best on the low-code "minimize development time" argument. Check it against the linked documentation.

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that uses the Premium Per User (PPU) license mode and contains a semantic model named Model1.

Large semantic model storage format is selected for Model1.

You need to ensure that tables imported into Model1 are written automatically to Delta tables in OneLake.

What should you do for Model1 and Workspace1? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Model1: Enable OneLake integration.
  • Workspace1: Change the license mode to Fabric capacity.

Analysis of each selection:

  1. Model1: Enable OneLake integration. The OneLake integration for semantic models feature automatically writes the data of import-mode tables to Delta tables in OneLake, in addition to keeping them in the model. It is switched on per model (once the model uses the large semantic model storage format, which is already the case here), so this is the setting that meets the requirement. Query caching only stores query results to speed up report loads, and query scale-out distributes query load across read-only replicas; neither writes anything to OneLake.

  2. Workspace1: Change the license mode to Fabric capacity. OneLake integration needs the workspace to be on a Fabric (F) or Premium (P) capacity. A workspace in Premium Per User license mode is not supported, so the workspace has to be moved to a Fabric capacity. A workspace identity is used for trusted access/authentication to external data sources and OneLake user-delegated SAS tokens are a way to give temporary access to OneLake data; neither activates the Delta export of the model.

  • Official documentation: OneLake integration for semantic models, Large semantic models in Power BI Premium and Fabric and Power BI semantic model scale-out

You have a Fabric eventhouse named Eventhouse1 that contains a table named Weatherdata. A sample of the data in Weatherdata is shown in the following table.

You plan to use a KQL queryset to manipulate the data in Eventhouse1. The result set must have the following columns.

You need to build the query.

Which four KQL statements should you use in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate statements from the list of statements to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers (in order):

  1. Weatherdata
  2. | extend Delta_temperature = Temperature - prev(Temperature)
  3. | summarize Delta_temperature = sum(Temperature) -sum(prev(Temperature)) by Datetime
  4. | sort by Datetime asc

Analysis of each selection:

  1. Weatherdata starts every KQL query: a query must begin with the table that is the source of the tabular data flowing through the pipe operators.
  2. extend Delta_temperature = Temperature - prev(Temperature) is how you compute the difference between the current row and the preceding one. prev() returns the value of the previous row of a serialized row set, so subtracting it from the current Temperature gives the delta. The alternatives are wrong: next(Temperature,1) looks at the following row (and the subtraction would be inverted in meaning), and prev(Temperature,2) looks two rows back instead of the immediately preceding row.
  3. summarize ... by Datetime is the third statement in the sequence. Grouping by Datetime leaves one row per timestamp and produces the Delta_temperature column in the result set.
  4. sort by Datetime asc orders the output chronologically so the deltas read in time order.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this sequence, but prev() needs a serialized (for example sorted) row set, so in practice the sort would come before the extend, and prev() is not valid inside summarize, which would also drop the Lat/Long columns. A more conventional query is Weatherdata | sort by Datetime asc | extend Delta_temperature = Temperature - prev(Temperature). Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: prev() function, next() function, serialize operator and Window functions overview

q188.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains an eventstream named Eventstream1.

Eventstream1 reads data from an Azure event hub named Eventhub1.

Eventhub1 contains the following columns.

You need to add a continuous percentile calculation to the Payload column. The solution must minimize development effort.

What should you do?
options: Add a KQL queryset to Workspace1.
Add a Group by transformation to Eventstream1.
Add a Manage fields transformation to Eventstream1.
Add an Aggregate transformation to Eventstream1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Add an Aggregate transformation to Eventstream1.

Why it is correct: The calculation must be applied to the incoming events themselves while they are inside the eventstream, with the least possible development work. The eventstream event processor editor is a no-code canvas, and its Aggregate transformation is the operator for computing an aggregation over the stream; you pick the column (Payload), choose the function and let the eventstream emit the calculated value continuously as new events arrive. No query language, extra item or code is needed, which satisfies "minimize development effort".

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks Aggregate, but the Fabric eventstream documentation lists only sum, minimum, maximum and average for the Aggregate transformation, while Group by offers more aggregation options (including continuous percentile functions), so Group by (option B) could also be argued for a continuous percentile. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric event streams overview and Process data streams in Fabric event streams
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Add a KQL queryset to Workspace1.

Why it is incorrect: A KQL queryset lets you write and run KQL queries against data that is already stored in an eventhouse/KQL database. You would first have to ingest the stream into an eventhouse and then write the percentile query yourself (for example with percentile()), which is more development effort and does not change the data while it flows through Eventstream1.

  • Official documentation: percentiles() aggregation function

B. Add a Group by transformation to Eventstream1.

Why it is incorrect: Group by calculates aggregations across all events in a time window (tumbling, hopping, sliding, session or snapshot) and groups by one or more fields. The scenario asks for a continuous calculation on the Payload column, not a windowed aggregate per group, so the Aggregate transformation is the expected answer for this question, although Group by does offer more aggregation options in practice.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric event streams overview

C. Add a Manage fields transformation to Eventstream1.

Why it is incorrect: Manage fields only adds, removes, renames or changes the data type of columns (and can add built-in date/time functions). It is for shaping the schema and does not compute percentile aggregations.

  • Official documentation: Process data streams in Fabric event streams

q189.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Table1. Table1 contains three columns named SalesAmount, ProductCategory, and

TransactionDate.

You need to create a Microsoft Power BI query that will calculate the total sales amount of each product category for transactions that occurred during the last quarter.

Which two actions should you perform in the visual query editor? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
options: For the TransactionDate column, select Remove duplicates.
For the TransactionDate column, select Keep top rows and set Number of rows to 90.
For the TransactionDate column, select Filter rows and set the value to last quarter.
For the ProductCategory column, select Group by and sum the SalesAmount column.
For the SalesAmount column, select Transformation number column - Standard, select Add, and then set the value to 90.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option B: For the TransactionDate column, select Keep top rows and set Number of rows to 90.
  • Option D: For the ProductCategory column, select Group by and sum the SalesAmount column.

Why they are correct: The result must be the total sales amount per product category restricted to a recent period. The solution combines two steps of the visual query editor (Power Query-style operations over the warehouse table):

  • Group by on ProductCategory, summing SalesAmount produces exactly the aggregate requested: one row per category with the total sales amount. This step is essential in any solution.
  • Keep top rows with 90 rows on TransactionDate is the restricting step: it keeps a limited slice of the table (the most recent rows by date) before the aggregation, so only the recent window feeds the sum.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks Keep top rows (90), but keeping 90 rows does not really implement "last quarter" (it keeps a number of rows, not a date range), whereas Filter rows with a date condition for the last quarter (option C) is the logical way to express it, so C + D could also be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Choose a data transformation strategy and Microsoft Fabric decision guide: copy activity, dataflow, or Spark
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. For the TransactionDate column, select Remove duplicates.

Why it is incorrect: Remove duplicates deletes repeated values and would throw away legitimate transactions that share a date, which corrupts the total instead of limiting it to a period.

  • Official documentation: Choose a data transformation strategy

C. For the TransactionDate column, select Filter rows and set the value to last quarter.

Why it is incorrect: This is not the expected answer for this question. The Filter rows dialog works with comparison conditions on explicit values rather than a relative "last quarter" preset, so the expected solution uses a top-rows step instead. In practice, though, a date filter is the more natural way to express "last quarter".

  • Official documentation: Choose a data transformation strategy

E. For the SalesAmount column, select Transformation number column - Standard, select Add, and then set the value to 90.

Why it is incorrect: This would add 90 to every sales amount, altering the measure itself. The number 90 is meant for a count of rows or days, never for adding to the amounts.

  • Official documentation: Choose a data transformation strategy

You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model.

You need to identify any surrogate key columns in the model that have the Summarize By property set to a value other than to None. The solution must minimize effort.

What should you use?
options: Performance Analyzer in Power BI Desktop
Model explorer in Microsoft Power BI Desktop
Model view in Microsoft Power BI Desktop

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Model view in Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is correct: In Model view, you can select several columns, or all columns of several tables, and the Properties pane applies the changes to every selected field, so you can see and fix the Summarize by property (and others such as Hidden) in bulk. This lets you scan the surrogate key columns, spot the ones whose Summarize by is not None, and set them to None in a few clicks, which is the lowest-effort approach compared with opening each column in Data view.

A. Performance Analyzer in Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Performance Analyzer records how long each report visual takes to load and which DAX queries it runs. It does not show or edit column properties such as Summarize by.

B. Model explorer in Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Model explorer is a tree view of the model objects (tables, columns, measures, relationships) with the number of items in each node. It helps you navigate the model but is not where you review and bulk-edit the Summarize by value across columns, which is done in the Properties pane of Model view.

D. DAX Formatter in DAX Studio

Why it is incorrect: DAX Formatter only reformats DAX expressions for readability. It has no view of column properties like Summarize by.

q191.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.

You use a dataflow to load a new dataset from OneLake to the warehouse.

You need to add a Power Query step to identify the maximum values for the numeric columns.

Which function should you include in the step?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Table.Profile

Why it is correct: The requirement is to add a Power Query step in the dataflow that identifies the maximum values for the numeric columns of the new dataset. Table.Profile is the Power Query M function designed for exactly this: it returns a table with one row per column of the input table, and for each column it calculates profile statistics where they apply, namely minimum, maximum, average, standard deviation, count, null count and distinct count. A single step therefore gives you the maximum of every numeric column at once, which is what the "column profiling" feature of the Power Query editor is built on. The result can then be inspected or filtered before the data is loaded into the warehouse.

  • Official documentation: Table.Profile - Power Query M
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Table.Range

Why it is incorrect: Table.Range returns a subset of rows of a table, starting at a given offset and for a given number of rows. It is a row-slicing function by position; it does not calculate any statistics and does not look at the values of the numeric columns, so it cannot identify their maximum values.

  • Official documentation: Table.Range - Power Query M

B. Table.MaxN

Why it is incorrect: Table.MaxN returns the N rows of a table that have the largest values for one column (or comparison criteria) that you specify. It returns rows, not a per-column maximum, and it works on a single criterion at a time. To get the maximum of every numeric column you would need to repeat it for each column and still extract the value; the profile function gives all of them in a single step.

  • Official documentation: Table.MaxN - Power Query M

q192.stem:
-

You have a Fabric warehouse named Warehouse1 that contains a table named TaxiTrips.

TaxiTrips contains the following columns.

You need to create a query that shows the top three taxi companies based on the total miles traveled.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • SELECT ...: Top (3)
  • Second box (after FROM): GROUP BY company
  • Third box (before DESC): ORDER BY sum(tripDistance)

The completed statement is SELECT TOP (3) company AS TaxiCompany, sum(passengerCount) AS TotalPassengers, sum(tripDistance) TotalDistance FROM [Warehouse1].[dbo].[TaxiTrips] GROUP BY company ORDER BY sum(tripDistance) DESC;

Analysis of each selection:

  1. Top (3). The requirement is the top three companies, and the Fabric warehouse uses the T-SQL dialect. In T-SQL the number of rows returned is limited with TOP (n) placed right after SELECT; combined with ORDER BY ... DESC, it returns the three companies with the highest total miles. Limit (3) is not valid T-SQL (it belongs to MySQL, PostgreSQL and Spark SQL). FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY is valid T-SQL, but it is part of the ORDER BY clause (ORDER BY ... OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY) and cannot be placed right after SELECT.

    • Official documentation: TOP (Transact-SQL) and SELECT - ORDER BY clause (Transact-SQL)

  2. GROUP BY company. The query uses the aggregate sum() together with the non-aggregated column company, so every non-aggregated column in the select list must appear in GROUP BY. You must group by the real column name company. GROUP BY TaxiCompany is wrong because TaxiCompany is a column alias defined in the SELECT list, and T-SQL evaluates GROUP BY before SELECT, so the alias is not visible there. ORDER BY tripDistance is not a grouping clause at all and would leave company ungrouped, causing an error.

    • Official documentation: SELECT (Transact-SQL)

  3. ORDER BY sum(tripDistance) (followed by DESC). The ranking must be based on the total miles per company, so the sort expression must be the aggregate. ORDER BY tripDistance would sort by a non-aggregated, non-grouped column and is invalid in a grouped query (and it would not represent the total anyway). GROUP BY company was already used and cannot be repeated before DESC. Sorting descending by the aggregate and then applying TOP (3) returns the three companies with the greatest total distance.

    • Official documentation: SELECT - ORDER BY clause (Transact-SQL)

q193.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains the workspaces shown in the following table.

You have a deployment pipeline named Pipeline1 that deploys items from Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST. In Pipeline1, all items that have matching names are paired.

You deploy the contents of Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST by using

Pipeline1.

What will the contents of Workspace_TEST be once the deployment is complete?
options: Lakehouse1 - Lakehouse2 - Notebook1 - Notebook2 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1 -

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Lakehouse1, Lakehouse2, Notebook1, Notebook2, Pipeline1, SemanticModel1

Why it is correct: A deployment pipeline only overwrites an item in the target stage when that item is paired with the source item. Items that exist in the source but are not paired in the target are copied as new items, and items that exist only in the target are left untouched. Applying this to the scenario:

  • Lakehouse1, Notebook1 and Pipeline1 exist in Workspace_DEV but have no paired counterpart in Workspace_TEST, so they are created as new items in Workspace_TEST.
  • SemanticModel1 has the same name in both workspaces and, according to the question, items with matching names are paired, so the one in Workspace_TEST is overwritten with the DEV version (it remains a single item).
  • Lakehouse2 and Notebook2 exist only in Workspace_TEST. They have no source counterpart, so the deployment does not delete or change them.

The final content of Workspace_TEST is therefore the union of both: Lakehouse1, Lakehouse2, Notebook1, Notebook2, Pipeline1 and SemanticModel1.

  • Official documentation: Get started with deployment pipelines - Microsoft Fabric and Assign a workspace to a deployment pipeline (item pairing)
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Lakehouse2, Notebook2, SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: This would mean that the new items from DEV (Lakehouse1, Notebook1, Pipeline1) were not deployed. A deployment copies every supported item that does not yet exist in the target stage; only items that are already paired are overwritten rather than duplicated.

  • Official documentation: Get started with deployment pipelines - Microsoft Fabric

B. Lakehouse1, Notebook1, Pipeline1, SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: This answer assumes that the deployment replaces the whole content of the target workspace so that it becomes a mirror of DEV, removing Lakehouse2 and Notebook2. Deployment pipelines do not delete items from the target stage that have no counterpart in the source stage; those items "remain as is".

  • Official documentation: Get started with deployment pipelines - Microsoft Fabric

D. Lakehouse2, Notebook2, Pipeline1, SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: It includes Pipeline1 and SemanticModel1 but omits Lakehouse1 and Notebook1, which exist in DEV, are not paired in TEST and are therefore deployed as new items. Nothing in the scenario excludes lakehouses or notebooks from the deployment.

  • Official documentation: Assign a workspace to a deployment pipeline (item pairing)
